knowledge_statements.title: Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard algebraic definition of a convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space. A subset \(C\subseteq V\) is convex if
\[
(\forall x,y\in C)(\forall \lambda\in[0,1])\qquad \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, for every integer \(m\geq 1\), all points \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\), and all coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq 0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1\), one has \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i\in C\). Under this universal-quantifier convention, the empty set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is convex when it contains every line segment joining two of its points, equivalently every finite convex combination of its points.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is convex}\iff (\forall x,y\in C)(\forall \lambda\in[0,1])\;\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in C.\)

notation.meaning: Subset whose convexity is being defined.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine, convex, and conic generation hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space \(E\). All combinations below have finite support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional algebraic hulls are considered; no topological closure is implicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine combination of \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in S\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). It is convex when also \(\lambda_i\geq0\), and conic when the normalization is omitted while \(\lambda_i\geq0\). The corresponding generated sets are \[\operatorname{aff}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\},\] \[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\},\] and \[\operatorname{cone}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.\] They are respectively the smallest affine set, convex set, and convex cone containing \(S\). In particular, \(S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\operatorname{aff}S\), while \(\operatorname{cone}S\) belongs to the homogeneous rather than normalized branch of the hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set S, affine generation permits finite coefficients summing to one, convex generation additionally requires nonnegative coefficients, and conic generation requires nonnegative coefficients without normalization. The sets of all such combinations are the affine hull, convex hull, and conic hull, respectively, and each is the smallest set of its structural class containing S. Thus S is contained in its convex hull, which is contained in its affine hull; the conic hull is the corresponding homogeneous construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}S\), \(\operatorname{conv}S\), and \(\operatorname{cone}S\) are the affine-, convex-, and conic-generation closures of \(S\) under the displayed finite combinations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}S=\bigcap\{A:S\subseteq A,\ A\text{ affine}\}\) and \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcap\{C:S\subseteq C,\ C\text{ convex}\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), every generated point uses only these listed generators.
If \(0\in S\), then \(\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\operatorname{cone}S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex set is closed under finite convex combinations, and every affine set is closed under finite affine combinations.
\(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{conv}S\) and \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{aff}S)=\operatorname{aff}S\).
boundary_notes: The algebraic convex hull need not be closed; its closure is a separate construction.
Infinite sums, integrals, and probability barycenters are not part of these finite-support definitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine sets and affine combinations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) with its usual real vector-space structure, and let \(A\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real affine geometry; the empty set may be treated separately by convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(A\) is affine if \[x,y\in A,\ \theta\in\mathbb{R}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta x+(1-\theta)y\in A.\] Equivalently, \(A\) contains every finite affine combination \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\) of its points, where \(m\geq1\), \(x_i\in A\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), with no sign restriction on the coefficients. If \(A\neq\varnothing\) and \(a\in A\), then its direction set is \(L=A-a=\{x-a:x\in A\}\); affineness is equivalent to \(L\) being a linear subspace, in which case \(A=a+L\). Thus an affine set is precisely a translate of a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset A of real n-space is affine when it contains the full line through any two of its points. Equivalently, it contains every finite combination of its points whose real coefficients sum to one. For a nonempty affine set and any base point a in it, A minus a is a linear subspace L, independent of the chosen base point, and A equals the translate a plus L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is affine}\iff(\forall a\in A)(A-a\text{ is a linear subspace})\), and then \(A=a+(A-a)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(A\) is affine if and only if it is closed under all finite affine combinations of its elements.
For nonempty \(A\), affineness is equivalent to the existence of \(a\in E\) and a linear subspace \(L\subseteq E\) such that \(A=a+L\).
special_cases_latex: A singleton \(\{a\}\) is the affine set \(a+\{0\}\).
A solution set \(\{x:Mx=b\}\), when nonempty, is affine with direction \(\ker M\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every affine set is convex because \([0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}\).
Translations and affine images of affine sets are affine.
boundary_notes: Closure under convex combinations alone defines convexity, not affineness.
The representation \(A=a+L\) requires \(A\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: direction subspace parallel to the affine set A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine equivalence of equal-dimensional affine sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of affine subsets of a fixed Euclidean space under ambient affine automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M_1,M_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be affine sets with \dim M_1=\dim M_2. Then there exists a bijective affine transformation T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n such that T(M_1)=M_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two affine subsets of the same Euclidean space having the same dimension are carried to one another by an affine automorphism of the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Foundational Affine-Geometry Definitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine subspaces, linear functionals, affine hyperplanes, affine combinations, affine independence, and affine hulls over the real scalar field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space. An affine subspace is a translate \(A=L+u\) of a linear subspace \(L\leq V\), and \(\dim A=\dim L\). If \(\dim A=1\), then \(A=\{u+\tau v:\tau\in\mathbb R\}\) for some \(v\neq0\). A linear functional is a map \(f:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(f(\alpha u+\beta v)=\alpha f(u)+\beta f(v)\). If \(f\not\equiv0\), then \(\{x\in V:f(x)=\gamma\}\) is an affine hyperplane. A sum \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i v_i\) is an affine combination when \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\). Points \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) are affinely independent if \(\sum_i\alpha_i v_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\alpha_i=0\) imply \(\alpha_i=0\) for every \(i\). For \(X\subseteq V\), \(\operatorname{aff}(X)\) is the set of all finite affine combinations of points of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine subspace is a translate of a linear subspace and has the same dimension. Nonzero linear functionals define affine hyperplanes through their level sets. Affine combinations have coefficients summing to one, affine independence excludes nontrivial affine dependence, and the affine hull consists of all finite affine combinations.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a real vector space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A=L+u,\quad \dim A=\dim L,\quad f\not\equiv0\Rightarrow\{x:f(x)=\gamma\}\text{ is an affine hyperplane},\quad \operatorname{aff}(X)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i:x_i\in X,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\right\}.

children.top_down_role: Translated linear structure and its associated directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direction space of a nonempty affine set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty affine set and choose any \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The correspondence is for nonempty affine sets in finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The direction space parallel to \(A\) is \[\operatorname{dir}(A):=A-a=\{x-a:x\in A\}.\] This set is a linear subspace and is independent of the selected base point: for all \(a,b\in A\), \(A-a=A-b\). Consequently, \[A=a+\operatorname{dir}(A)=\{a+v:v\in\operatorname{dir}(A)\}.\] Conversely, for every linear subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the translate \(a+L\) is affine and has \(\operatorname{dir}(a+L)=L\). Hence nonempty affine sets correspond to pairs consisting of a direction subspace and one coset of that subspace; changing the base point within the same coset does not change the affine set or its directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty affine set A, subtracting any point a of A produces its direction subspace. This subspace does not depend on which point of A is chosen, and A is recovered as a plus that subspace. Conversely, translating any linear subspace by any point produces an affine set whose direction space is the original subspace. Base points differing by a direction vector determine the same translate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dir}(A)=A-a\) is well defined independently of \(a\in A\), and \(A=a+\operatorname{dir}(A)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a fixed subspace \(L\), \(a+L=b+L\iff a-b\in L\).
\(x-y\in\operatorname{dir}(A)\) for every \(x,y\in A\), and every direction is such a difference.
special_cases_latex: \(\operatorname{dir}(\{a\})=\{0\}\).
If \(A=\{x:Mx=b\}\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{dir}(A)=\ker M\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Two nonempty affine sets with a common point and the same direction space are equal.
Translation of \(A\) changes its base-point coset but not its direction space.
boundary_notes: An empty affine set has no base point, so this definition does not assign it a direction space.
The origin belongs to \(A\) exactly when \(A\) itself is a linear subspace.

notation.meaning: linear direction subspace parallel to A
the translate or coset of L through a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection Closure of Affine Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: When affine sets are required to be nonempty, the intersection must be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((A_j)_{j\in J}\) is a family of affine subsets of a real vector space and \(\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j\neq\varnothing\), then \(\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j\) is affine. Under a convention admitting the empty affine set, the qualification is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty intersection of affine sets is affine.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is affine if and only if \((1-t)x+ty\in A\) for every \(x,y\in A\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a nonempty affine subset of a real vector space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention that affine sets are nonempty; under conventions allowing the empty affine set, add it separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(A\subseteq V\) be nonempty. The set \(A\) is affine precisely when, for every \(x,y\in A\) and every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), one has \((1-t)x+ty\in A\). Equivalently, for every integer \(m\geq 1\), every \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in A\), and all \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), one has \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty subset of a real vector space is affine exactly when it contains every affine combination of its points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parallel Affine Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-based parallelism for affine sets and its restriction to translates of the same shape and dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For affine sets \(M,L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(M\) to be parallel to \(L\) if and only if there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(M=L+a\). This is an equivalence relation on the affine subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Under this definition, affine sets of different dimensions, such as a line and a plane, are not parallel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two affine sets are parallel when one is a translate of the other. This is an equivalence relation and, unlike broader informal usage, does not call affine sets of different dimensions parallel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\parallel L\iff \exists a\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ such that }M=L+a;\qquad \parallel\text{ is an equivalence relation on the affine subsets of }\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine sets as translated linear subspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translated-subspace representation of a nonempty affine set, independence of its direction subspace from the chosen base point, and the induced dimension definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is affine and $x_0\in C$, then $V:=C-x_0$ is a linear subspace and $C=x_0+V$. Moreover, $C-x_1=V$ for every $x_1\in C$, so the direction subspace is independent of the chosen base point, and $\dim C$ is defined as $\dim V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating a nonempty affine set by any of its points produces a linear subspace. Thus the affine set is that subspace plus an offset. The resulting direction subspace is independent of the chosen point, and its dimension defines the dimension of the affine set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V:=C-x_0\text{ is a linear subspace},\qquad C=x_0+V,\qquad (\forall x_1\in C)\;C-x_1=V,\qquad \dim C:=\dim V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tucker representation of a nontrivial affine set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-graph representation of a proper positive-dimensional affine set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^N\) be an affine set of dimension \(n\), where \(0<n<N\), and let \(m=N-n\). There exist a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and coefficients \(\alpha_{ij},\alpha_i\) such that, for every \(x=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)\),
\[
x\in M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \xi_{\pi(n+i)}=\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_{ij}\xi_{\pi(j)}+\alpha_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Such a system is a Tucker representation of \(M\) and realizes \(M\) as the graph of an affine map \(\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\). There are only finitely many coordinate-ordered Tucker representations of \(M\), and their number is at most \(N!\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every n-dimensional affine set in R^N with 0 < n < N can, after a permutation of coordinates, be represented exactly as the graph of an affine map from R^n to R^(N−n). This necessary-and-sufficient coordinate system is called a Tucker representation. There are finitely many coordinate-ordered Tucker representations, at most N!.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\pi\in S_N\;\exists(\alpha_{ij},\alpha_i)\;\forall x=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N):\;x\in M\iff \bigl[\xi_{\pi(n+i)}=\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_{ij}\xi_{\pi(j)}+\alpha_i\ \forall i=1,\ldots,m\bigr],\qquad \#\{\text{coordinate-ordered Tucker representations of }M\}\le N!.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lines and Affine Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of a line and an affine subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct points \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the line through \(x\) and \(y\) is \(\{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}\). A set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is affine if and only if \((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y\in M\) for every \(x,y\in M\) and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence Criteria for Affine Translates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The criteria compare affine translates through their direction spaces and one base-point displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=a+L\) and \(B=b+M\) be nonempty affine subsets of a real vector space. Then \[A\subseteq B\iff a-b\in M\text{ and }L\subseteq M.\] Consequently, \[A=B\iff L=M\text{ and }a-b\in L.\] Thus two affine sets having the same direction space are either equal or disjoint.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\subseteq B\iff(a-b\in M\land L\subseteq M)\), and \(A=B\iff(L=M\land a-b\in L)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\leq V\) be a linear subspace and let \(q:V\to V/L\) be the quotient map. The nonempty affine subsets of \(V\) with direction space \(L\) are exactly the fibers \[q^{-1}(q(a))=a+L,\qquad a\in V.\] Hence they are in bijection with the elements of \(V/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine sets parallel to a fixed subspace are the fibers of the quotient map.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a linear subspace of a real vector space \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{A\subseteq V:A\text{ is nonempty affine and }\operatorname{dir}(A)=L\}=\{q^{-1}(\xi):\xi\in V/L\}.\)

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine hull and intrinsic affine dimension
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and choose \(s_0\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine dimension; dimension is intrinsic to the smallest affine ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine hull of \(S\) is the smallest affine set containing it: \[\operatorname{aff}S:=\bigcap\{A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:S\subseteq A,\ A\text{ affine}\}.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{aff}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i:m\geq1,\ s_i\in S,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\}=s_0+\operatorname{span}(S-s_0).\] The affine dimension of \(S\) is \[\dim_{m aff}S:=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)=\dim\operatorname{span}(S-s_0),\] which is independent of \(s_0\). Thus affine hull identifies the intrinsic affine ambient space, while its parallel linear subspace supplies the intrinsic dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull of a nonempty set S is the intersection of all affine sets containing S, equivalently the set of all finite affine combinations of points of S. After choosing any point s0 in S, it equals s0 plus the linear span of all differences s minus s0. The affine dimension of S is the linear dimension of this direction span and therefore does not depend on the selected base point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}S\) is the set of all finite affine combinations of elements of \(S\).
\(\dim_{m aff}S=d\) exactly when \(S\) contains \(d+1\) affinely independent points but no \(d+2\) affinely independent points.
special_cases_latex: A singleton has affine dimension \(0\).
If \(\operatorname{aff}S=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(S\) is full affine-dimensional and \(\dim_{m aff}S=n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{aff}S\).
If \(S\subseteq T\), then \(\operatorname{aff}S\subseteq\operatorname{aff}T\) and \(\dim_{m aff}S\leq\dim_{m aff}T\).
boundary_notes: Affine dimension differs from manifold or topological dimension for general nonconvex sets; for example, a circle has full affine hull in its plane.
The definition here excludes the empty set, whose affine dimension requires a separate convention.

notation.meaning: dimension of the affine hull of S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine sets, affine hulls, and intrinsic dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines affine structure and records the affine-hull identities and dimension convention for nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is affine if \(M=x+S\) for some \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and a uniquely determined linear subspace \(S\), called the subspace parallel to \(M\). Equivalently, \(M\) contains the entire line through every pair of distinct points in \(M\). For nonempty \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{aff}(X)=\bigcap\{M:M\text{ is affine and }X\subseteq M\}.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\subseteq\operatorname{aff}(X)\) and \[\operatorname{aff}(X)=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{conv}(X))=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{cl}X).\] The dimension of an affine set is the dimension of its parallel subspace; for a nonempty convex set \(C\), \(\dim C=\dim\operatorname{aff}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine set is a translate of a uniquely determined linear subspace, equivalently a set containing the full line through every two distinct points. The affine hull is the smallest affine set containing a nonempty set. It contains the convex hull and is unchanged by first taking either the convex hull or closure. Dimension is measured using the parallel subspace of the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Certificate for Effective Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generating-family formulation.

For a nonempty finite set \(S=\{x_0,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),

children.title: Dimension Loss Under Affine Containment
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional placement relative to the surrounding space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality Criterion for a Containing Affine Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite dimensionality is needed for the equal-dimension implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) lie in a finite-dimensional affine set \(M\). Then
\[
\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)=\dim M
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{aff}S=M.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{aff}S\subsetneq M\) is equivalent to strict dimension loss relative to \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a finite-dimensional affine carrier, a set has the carrier's full affine dimension exactly when its affine hull equals the carrier.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite-dimensional affine subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Criterion for a Containing Affine Space

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with \(\dim V=n\).
\(S\subseteq M\subseteq V\), where \(S\neq\varnothing\) and \(M\) is affine.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: monotonicity of affine hull and finite-dimensional subspace dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strict dimension loss is relative to a finite-dimensional ambient space and requires proper affine containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be an \(n\)-dimensional real vector space, let \(M\subseteq V\) be affine, and let \(\varnothing\neq S\subseteq M\). Then \(\operatorname{aff}(S)\subseteq M\), and consequently \[\dim_{\mathrm{eff}}(S)\leq\dim(M).\] In particular, if \(M\) is a proper affine subset of \(V\), then \[\dim_{\mathrm{eff}}(S)\leq\dim(M)\leq n-1<n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set contained in an affine set cannot have larger effective dimension than that affine set. Containment in a proper affine subset therefore forces dimension loss relative to the ambient finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Loss Under Affine Containment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional containment and strict dimension-loss claims are correct, and property is the appropriate kind, but no source reference is supplied.

children.title: Affine Independence
children.top_down_role: Independence structure underlying finite affine representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank and Augmented-Matrix Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinate tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), affine independence is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{rank}[x_1-x_0\ \cdots\ x_k-x_0]=k.
\]
Equivalently, the augmented vectors \((x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}\) are linearly independent. Hence an affinely independent family in \(\mathbb R^n\) has at most \(n+1\) points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine independence is certified by full column rank of a displacement matrix or linear independence of homogenized points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The points are affinely independent iff \(\operatorname{rank}[x_1-x_0\ \cdots\ x_k-x_0]=k\), equivalently iff \((x_i,1)\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank and Augmented-Matrix Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of Affine Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns affine coefficients, which need not be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The points \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\) are affinely independent if and only if every \(x\in\operatorname{aff}\{x_0,\ldots,x_k\}\) has a unique representation
\[
x=\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i x_i,
\qquad \sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i=1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family is affinely independent exactly when points of its affine hull have unique affine coordinates in that family.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\) lie in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\) are affinely independent iff their affine coordinates are unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of Affine Coordinates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Behavior Under Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Injectivity is required only on the family's direction span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\). If \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\) are affinely independent, then \(T(x_0),\ldots,T(x_k)\) are affinely independent exactly when
\[
\ker A\cap\operatorname{span}\{x_i-x_0:1\le i\le k\}=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map preserves a family's affine independence exactly when its linear part is injective on the family's direction span.
knowledge_statements.title: Behavior Under Affine Maps

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\) are affinely independent if and only if \(x_1-x_0,\ldots,x_k-x_0\) are linearly independent.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative integer determining the finite family size

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard equivalent definitions of affine independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is for a finite ordered family indexed by a nonnegative integer; repetition automatically violates affine independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\). Points \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\) in a real vector space \(V\) are affinely independent if the only scalars \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i x_i=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i=0\] are \(\lambda_0=\cdots=\lambda_k=0\). Equivalently, \(x_1-x_0,\ldots,x_k-x_0\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative integer k, a family of k+1 points is affinely independent when no nontrivial linear relation among the points has coefficients summing to zero; equivalently, their differences from the first point are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Independence

children.title: Simplex Geometry
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional affine building blocks for convex generation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barycentric-Coordinate Membership Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine independence makes the coordinate solution unique whenever the target lies in the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb R^d\) be affinely independent, set \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_k\}\), and let \(B=[v_1-v_0\ \cdots\ v_k-v_0]\). Solve \(B\alpha=x-v_0\). If it is unsolvable, then \(x\notin\operatorname{aff}(\Delta)\). Otherwise set \(\lambda_i=\alpha_i\) for \(1\leq i\leq k\) and \(\lambda_0=1-\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i\). Then \[x\in\Delta\iff\lambda_i\geq0\quad(0\leq i\leq k).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex membership is tested by solving for barycentric coordinates and checking nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.title: Barycentric-Coordinate Membership Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Equivalence with the Standard Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The affine bijection is between affine hulls, so embedded lower-dimensional simplices are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_k\}\) is a \(k\)-simplex, then \[T:\Delta_k\to\Delta,\qquad T(\lambda)=\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i v_i,\] where \(\Delta_k=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\), is an affine bijection. Its inverse assigns barycentric coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every k-simplex is affinely equivalent to the standard probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Equivalence with the Standard Simplex

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face and Relative-Interior Structure of a Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior and boundary are relative to the simplex's affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_k\}\), and write \(x\in\Delta\) uniquely as \(x=\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i v_i\). For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{0,\ldots,k\}\), \[F_I:=\operatorname{conv}\{v_i:i\in I\}=\{x\in\Delta:\lambda_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}\] is a face, and every nonempty face is uniquely of this form. Moreover, \[\operatorname{ri}(\Delta)=\{x\in\Delta:\lambda_i>0\ \forall i\},\qquad \operatorname{rbd}(\Delta)=\{x\in\Delta:\lambda_i=0\text{ for some }i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces correspond to vertex subsets; positive barycentric coordinates characterize relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_I\leftrightarrow I\neq\varnothing\) classifies nonempty faces, and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\Delta)\iff\lambda_i(x)>0\ \forall i\).

notation.meaning: Face generated by the indexed vertex subset

knowledge_statements.title: Face and Relative-Interior Structure of a Simplex

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_k\}\) is a \(k\)-simplex, and every \(x\in\Delta\) has unique barycentric coordinates.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative integer equal to the simplex dimension

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a simplex and uniqueness of barycentric coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record uses the vertex representation of a finite-dimensional simplex in an arbitrary real vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\). If \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\) are affinely independent points of a real vector space \(V\), their \(k\)-simplex is \[\Delta:=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_k\}=\left\{\sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\geq 0,\ \sum_{i=0}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Every \(x\in\Delta\) has a unique tuple \((\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_k)\) satisfying these conditions; these scalars are its barycentric coordinates. Moreover, \(\operatorname{aff}(\Delta)=\operatorname{aff}\{v_0,\ldots,v_k\}\) and \(\dim_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Delta)=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative integer k, a k-simplex is the convex hull of k+1 affinely independent vertices. Each point has unique nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one, and the simplex has effective dimension k.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex Definition, Barycentric Uniqueness, and Barycenter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex geometry and barycentric terminology, with the finite-hull definition of a polytope retained as its enclosing context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points. If b_0,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb{R}^n are affinely independent, then \operatorname{conv}\{b_0,\ldots,b_m\} is an m\text{-dimensional simplex} with vertices b_0,\ldots,b_m. Every x in this simplex has a unique representation x=\sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i b_i with \lambda_i\geq0 and \sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i=1. The equal-weight point \bar b=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{i=0}^m b_i is its barycenter, also called its midpoint in the source. For m=0,1,2,3, the simplex is respectively a point, a closed line segment, a triangle, or a tetrahedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points. The convex hull of m+1 affinely independent points is an m-dimensional simplex with those points as its vertices. Every point of the simplex has unique nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one, and equal coordinates give its barycenter. Simplices of dimensions zero through three are points, closed line segments, triangles, and tetrahedra.
assumptions_latex: b_0,\ldots,b_m\ \text{are affinely independent for the simplex assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{b_0,\ldots,b_m\}\text{ is an }m\text{-simplex with vertices }b_i;\quad \forall x\in\operatorname{conv}\{b_i\}\ \exists!\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0:\ \sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i=1,\ x=\sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i b_i;\quad \bar b=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=0}^m b_i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity-preserving set-construction calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E,E_i,F\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(C_i\subseteq E_i\) and \(C,D\subseteq E\) be convex, and let \(f:E\to F\) be affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic preservation of convexity; preservation of closedness is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The elementary convex-set construction calculus consists of the following operations: arbitrary intersections \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\) when all sets share an ambient space; finite Cartesian products \(\prod_{i=1}^kC_i\); affine images \(f(C)\); inverse images \(f^{-1}(Q)\) of convex \(Q\subseteq F\); scalar images \(\alpha C\); translations \(C+a\); and Minkowski sums \(C+D=\{c+d:c\in C,d\in D\}\). Each resulting set is convex whenever the input sets indicated above are convex. The empty intersection, if used, is interpreted as the full ambient space. These rules permit constraint aggregation by intersection, lifting by products, transport by affine maps, and additive composition by Minkowski sums within one common calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex sets remain convex under arbitrary intersections, finite Cartesian products, affine images and inverse images, scalar multiplication, translation, and Minkowski addition. These operations form the basic construction calculus for assembling new convex feasible regions from existing ones. The assertion concerns convexity only and does not automatically transfer closedness, boundedness, or compactness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_iC_i\), \(\prod_iC_i\), \(f(C)\), \(f^{-1}(Q)\), \(\alpha C\), \(C+a\), and \(C+D\) are convex under the stated convexity hypotheses.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Minkowski addition is the affine image of \(C\times D\) under \((c,d)\mapsto c+d\).
Coordinate projection is a special affine image, while a system of convex constraints is represented by an intersection.
special_cases_latex: Intersections of affine sets are affine, and intersections of convex cones are convex cones.
A translate \(C+a\) and a dilation \(\alpha C\) are affine images of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear projections of convex lifted formulations are convex.
Sets defined by any family of affine inequalities are convex because they are intersections of halfspaces.
boundary_notes: Unions of convex sets are generally not convex.
Affine images and Minkowski sums of closed convex sets need not be closed without additional hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of C and D

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{C_i\mid i\in I\}\) be a family of convex sets in a common real vector space. Then \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\) is convex. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite convex combinations and simplex coefficients
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a real vector space, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in E\), and let \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support convex generation; infinite barycenters are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The coefficient simplex is \[\Delta_m:=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m:\lambda_i\geq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] A finite convex combination of \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) is a point \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\) with \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\). For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq E\), its finite convex generation is \[\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(S):=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda\in\Delta_m\right\}.\] A set \(C\) is convex exactly when \(\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(C)=C\). Convex combinations are associative in the sense that a convex combination of points that are themselves finite convex combinations is again a finite convex combination of the underlying generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard simplex Delta_m contains the nonnegative coefficient vectors whose coordinates sum to one. Applying such a vector to m points gives a finite convex combination. The finite convex generation of S consists of every point obtainable this way using any positive finite number of generators. A set is convex exactly when it is closed under this operation, and nested finite mixtures can be flattened into a single finite mixture.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(S)\) is the closure of \(S\) under finite convex combinations, and \(C\) is convex iff \(\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(C)=C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For fixed \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), their finite convex combinations form the linear image \(\{\sum_i\lambda_i x_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m\}\).
Zero coefficients permit a combination using fewer than \(m\) active generators to be represented in \(\Delta_m\).
special_cases_latex: \(\Delta_1=\{1\}\), so a one-point convex combination returns that point.
For \(m=2\), finite convex combinations form the closed line segment \(\{\theta x_1+(1-\theta)x_2:0\leq\theta\leq1\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(S\subseteq\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(S)\).
Applying finite convex generation twice adds no points: \(\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(S))=\operatorname{co}_{\rm fin}(S)\).
boundary_notes: No uniform bound on the number of generators is built into this definition; dimensional bounds belong to Carathéodory regimes.
The coefficients need not be unique.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flattening Nested Finite Convex Combinations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This barycentric associativity law explains why finite mixtures may be grouped or ungrouped without changing the resulting point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha_j\geq0\) with \(\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j=1\), and for each \(j\) let \(\beta_{ji}\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}\beta_{ji}=1\). For points \(x_{ji}\) in a real vector space, \[\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}\beta_{ji}x_{ji}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}(\alpha_j\beta_{ji})x_{ji},\] where the coefficients \(\alpha_j\beta_{ji}\) are nonnegative and sum to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested finite convex combinations can be flattened by multiplying the outer and inner weights.
assumptions_latex: \(x_{ji}\) lie in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nested mixture is the convex combination with weights \(\gamma_{ji}=\alpha_j\beta_{ji}\).

notation.meaning: Inner convex weight in group j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of Finite Barycentric Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniqueness boundary for normalized coefficients over a fixed finite generating family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) lie in a real vector space. The family is affinely independent if and only if
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i x_i,\qquad
\sum_i\lambda_i=\sum_i\mu_i=1
\]
implies \(\lambda_i=\mu_i\) for every \(i\). Consequently, every point of \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\) has unique convex weights exactly when the generators are affinely independent; if they are affinely dependent, at least one point has two distinct convex-weight representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex weights are unique throughout a finite hull exactly when its listed generators are affinely independent.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) lie in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\) has unique convex coefficients if and only if \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) are affinely independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of Finite Barycentric Coordinates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Maps Preserve Finite Convex Combinations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Naturality of finite barycentric mixtures under affine transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V,W\) be real vector spaces, let \(T:V\to W\) be affine, and let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in V\). If \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), then
\[
T\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iT(x_i).
\]
Consequently,
\[
T\bigl(\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\bigr)=\operatorname{conv}\{T(x_1),\ldots,T(x_m)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine maps commute with finite convex combinations and carry a finite convex hull onto the hull of the images.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\sum_i\lambda_i x_i)=\sum_i\lambda_iT(x_i)\) for normalized nonnegative weights, and \(T(\operatorname{conv}\{x_i\})=\operatorname{conv}\{T(x_i)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Maps Preserve Finite Convex Combinations

notation.meaning: Convex hull of the finite point set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The representation concerns a finite generating family; repeated points are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) in a real vector space \(V\), a finite convex combination is a vector \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\) with \(\lambda_i\geq0\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of the points is exactly \[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex combination uses nonnegative weights summing to one, and all such combinations of a finite family form its convex hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and finite convex combinations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes convex sets and records the resulting finite-combination representation of a convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if and only if, for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\), and every \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge 0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), one has \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\in C\). Consequently, for \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i:m\ge1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is convex exactly when it contains every finite convex combination of its points. Consequently, the convex hull of a set consists of all finite convex combinations of its points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is convex}\iff C\text{ contains every finite convex combination of its points};\qquad \operatorname{conv}S\text{ is the set of all finite convex combinations of points of }S.

children.title: Iterated Segment Generation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Segment Parameters for Prescribed Convex Weights
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit conversion between a finite coefficient vector and an ordered sequence of binary interpolations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), set \(s_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\), and let \(r=\min\{i:\lambda_i>0\}\). Set \(y_r=x_r\). For \(k=r+1,\ldots,m\), define
\[
t_k=\frac{\lambda_k}{s_k},\qquad y_k=(1-t_k)y_{k-1}+t_kx_k.
\]
Then
\[
y_k=\frac1{s_k}\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i,
\qquad y_m=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.
\]
Conversely, starting with \(y_1=x_1\), parameters \(t_2,\ldots,t_m\in[0,1]\) in \(y_k=(1-t_k)y_{k-1}+t_kx_k\) produce the convex weights
\[
\lambda_1=\prod_{j=2}^m(1-t_j),\qquad
\lambda_i=t_i\prod_{j=i+1}^m(1-t_j)\quad(2\le i\le m).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite convex weights can be converted explicitly into sequential binary interpolation parameters, and every such parameter sequence induces normalized convex weights.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) lie in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed sequential interpolation produces \(\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\), and every parameter sequence in \([0,1]^{m-1}\) induces the displayed convex weights.

notation.meaning: binary interpolation parameter at stage k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recursive decomposition of finite convex combinations into binary segment operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The recursion depends on an ordering of the generators, but its final set is their order-independent convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\), and let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) lie in a real vector space \(V\). Define \(S_1:=\{x_1\}\) and, for \(k=2,\ldots,m\), define \[S_k:=\bigcup_{y\in S_{k-1}}[y,x_k]=\{(1-t)y+tx_k:y\in S_{k-1},\ t\in[0,1]\}.\] Then, for every \(k=1,\ldots,m\), \[S_k=\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}.\] Thus every finite convex combination can be generated by finitely many successive line-segment operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a positive integer m, starting from one point and repeatedly joining every previously generated point to the next generator produces exactly the convex hull of the generators processed so far.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection and Cartesian-product constructions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\) be an index set, let \(E\) be a real vector space, and let \(C_i\subseteq E\) be convex for \(i\in I\). For a finite product, let \(C_j\subseteq E_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary intersections and finite Cartesian products of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The intersection construction is \[C_{\cap}:=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\{x\in E:x\in C_i\ \text{for every }i\in I\}.\] It is convex, including when \(I\) is infinite; for \(I=\varnothing\), the conventional value is \(E\). The product construction is \[C_{\times}:=C_1\times\cdots\times C_k=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_k):x_j\in C_j\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,k\}\subseteq E_1\times\cdots\times E_k.\] It is convex exactly when every nonempty factor \(C_j\) is convex. Intersection aggregates simultaneous constraints in one space, whereas a product places independent component constraints in a product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection of a family of convex sets in the same vector space consists of the points satisfying every component constraint and is convex, even for an infinite family. The Cartesian product of finitely many convex sets consists of tuples whose coordinates belong to their respective factors and is convex in the product vector space. Intersections aggregate constraints; products lift separate constraints into a joint space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every \(C_i\) is convex, then \(\bigcap_iC_i\) is convex, and if every \(C_j\subseteq E_j\) is convex, then \(\prod_{j=1}^kC_j\) is convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in\prod_jC_j\iff x_j\in C_j\) for all \(j\).
For nonempty factors, \(\prod_jC_j\) is convex if and only if each coordinate projection \(C_j\) is convex.
special_cases_latex: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many affine halfspaces.
\(C\times\{0\}\) is a convex embedding of \(C\) in a larger space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any feasible set specified by an arbitrary family of convex-set membership constraints is convex.
Block-separable convex constraints define a convex feasible set in the product variable.
boundary_notes: A union of convex sets need not be convex.
An infinite Cartesian product requires a specified product vector space and topology; it is outside this finite-product definition.

children.title: Product-Space Constraint Structure
children.top_down_role: Interaction between component constraints and product geometry.

assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(X_i\) is a real vector space, \(J_i\) is an index set, and every \(f_{ij}:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
The factor constraint set is \(C_i=\bigcap_{j\in J_i}\{u\in X_i:f_{ij}(u)\leq 0\}\), and \(\pi_i:\prod_{k=1}^mX_k\to X_i\) is the coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \[\prod_{i=1}^m C_i=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\bigcap_{j\in J_i}\{x\in\prod_{k=1}^mX_k:(f_{ij}\circ\pi_i)(x)\leq0\},\] and this set is convex.

notation.meaning: Constraint function lifted to the product space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A separable product constraint is represented as the intersection of coordinate-lifted convex inequalities.

source_refs.locator: III.1.2 Convexity-Preserving Operations on Sets, p. 90
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(X_i\) be a real vector space, let \(J_i\) be an index set, and let \(f_{ij}:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex for every \(j\in J_i\). Set \(C_i:=\bigcap_{j\in J_i}\{u\in X_i:f_{ij}(u)\leq0\}\), and let \(\pi_i:\prod_{k=1}^mX_k\to X_i\) denote the coordinate projection. Then \[\prod_{i=1}^m C_i=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\bigcap_{j\in J_i}\left\{x\in\prod_{k=1}^mX_k:(f_{ij}\circ\pi_i)(x)\leq0\right\}.\] Every \(f_{ij}\circ\pi_i\) is convex, so the represented product-space constraint set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Cartesian product of coordinatewise convex inequality sets is exactly the intersection of those inequalities lifted by the coordinate projections, and is therefore convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Constraint Structure

source_witnesses.locator: III.1.2 Convexity-Preserving Operations on Sets, p. 90

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product Feasibility Decouples by Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite product feasibility; no shared variable couples the factor constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C_i\subseteq X_i\), \(\prod_{i=1}^mC_i\ne\varnothing\) if and only if \(C_i\ne\varnothing\) for every \(i\). A point \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) belongs to the product exactly when \(x_i\in C_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility of a finite product constraint is exactly coordinatewise feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Feasibility Decouples by Coordinates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersections as Diagonal Pullbacks of Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates common-variable aggregation to product geometry without duplicating sibling closure properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq X\) and define \(\Delta:X\to X^m\) by \(\Delta(x)=(x,\ldots,x)\). Then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i=\Delta^{-1}(\prod_{i=1}^mC_i)\). Thus, for convex factors, the intersection is the inverse image of a convex product under a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection of constraints on one variable is the inverse image of their Cartesian product under the diagonal map.

notation.meaning: Diagonal embedding into the product space

knowledge_statements.title: Intersections as Diagonal Pullbacks of Products

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine images and inverse images of convex sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine, \(f(x)=Ax+b\), with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine transport; no injectivity, surjectivity, or closedness assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its affine image is \[f(C):=\{Ax+b:x\in C\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m.\] For \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), its affine inverse image is \[f^{-1}(D):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax+b\in D\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n.\] If \(C\) is convex, then \(f(C)\) is convex; if \(D\) is convex, then \(f^{-1}(D)\) is convex. These operations satisfy \(f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)=\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)\) for every \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\), which is the defining compatibility between affine maps and affine combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map has the form f(x)=Ax+b. The image of a set C consists of all Ax+b with x in C, and the inverse image of D consists of all x whose image lies in D. Affine images of convex sets are convex, and inverse images of convex sets are convex. Neither conclusion requires the linear part A to be one-to-one or onto.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ convex}\Rightarrow f(C)\text{ convex}\) and \(D\text{ convex}\Rightarrow f^{-1}(D)\text{ convex}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Coordinate projection is an affine-image operation.
A constraint \(Ax+b\in D\) defines precisely the inverse image \(f^{-1}(D)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(A=I\), \(f(C)=C+b\) is a translation.
For \(b=0\) and \(A=\alpha I\), \(f(C)=\alpha C\) is scalar multiplication.
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear projections of convex lifted sets are convex.
Affine equality and inequality constraints preserve convexity through inverse images of affine subspaces and halfspaces.
boundary_notes: The image of a closed convex set under a linear map need not be closed.
The notation \(f^{-1}(D)\) denotes an inverse image and does not require an inverse function.

notation.meaning: set-theoretic inverse image of D under f

children.title: Injective, Surjective, or Degenerate Map Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric variation caused by rank and range behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, \(T:X\to Y\) has the affine form \(T(x)=Ax+b\), and \(C\subseteq X\), \(D\subseteq Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(T\) is injective, then \(T^{-1}(T(C))=C\). For every \(T\), \(T(T^{-1}(D))=D\cap T(X)\); hence surjectivity gives \(T(T^{-1}(D))=D\). If \(A=0\), then \(T(C)\subseteq\{b\}\) and \(T^{-1}(D)=X\) when \(b\in D\), while \(T^{-1}(D)=\varnothing\) when \(b\notin D\).

notation.meaning: Linear part of the affine map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: These identities distinguish information-preserving, range-filling, and constant affine maps; convexity of \(C\) or \(D\) is not needed for the identities.

source_refs.locator: III.1.2 Convexity-Preserving Operations on Sets, p. 90
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces, let \(T:X\to Y\) be given by \(T(x)=Ax+b\) with \(A:X\to Y\) linear, and let \(C\subseteq X\) and \(D\subseteq Y\). If \(T\) is injective, then \[T^{-1}(T(C))=C.\] For every affine \(T\), \[T(T^{-1}(D))=D\cap T(X),\] so if \(T\) is surjective, then \(T(T^{-1}(D))=D\). In the degenerate constant regime \(A=0\), one has \(T(C)\subseteq\{b\}\), with equality when \(C\neq\varnothing\), and \[T^{-1}(D)=\begin{cases}X,&b\in D,\\ \varnothing,&b\notin D.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Injectivity makes image followed by preimage recover the original set; surjectivity makes preimage followed by image recover the target set. A constant affine map collapses every nonempty image to one point, and its preimage of a set is either the whole domain or empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Injective, Surjective, or Degenerate Map Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kernel Saturation of Image–Preimage Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This gives the exact recovery law for noninjective affine maps and sharpens the injective case in the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) be affine and let \(C\subseteq X\). Then \[T^{-1}(T(C))=C+\ker A.\] Consequently, \(T^{-1}(T(C))=C\) exactly when \(C\) is saturated by the fibers of \(T\), and this equality holds for every \(C\subseteq X\) if and only if \(T\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Image followed by preimage enlarges a set by every direction in the kernel; exact recovery occurs precisely for fiber-saturated sets, and universally precisely for injective maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}(T(C))=C+\ker A\); hence universal exact recovery is equivalent to \(\ker A=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Kernel of the linear part of T
Minkowski sum of C with the kernel, equivalently the union of fibers meeting C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minkowski addition and scalar multiplication of sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\) be subsets of a real vector space \(E\), let \(a\in E\), and let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic set addition and scalar multiplication; convexity preservation is included, but closedness preservation is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski sum and scalar image are \[C+D:=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\},\qquad \alpha C:=\{\alpha c:c\in C\}.\] More generally, \[\alpha C+\beta D:=\{\alpha c+\beta d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}.\] Translation is the special case \(C+a=C+\{a\}\), and reflection is \(-C=(-1)C\). Minkowski addition is associative and commutative, with \(C+\{0\}=C\). If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, then \(\alpha C+\beta D\) is convex for all real \(\alpha,\beta\). For a convex \(C\) and nonnegative \(\alpha,\beta\), \[\alpha C+\beta C=(\alpha+\beta)C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski sum C+D contains every sum c+d with c in C and d in D. Scalar multiplication applies the scalar to every point of a set, and weighted set sums combine these operations. Translation, reflection, and dilation are special cases. Minkowski addition is associative and commutative, and weighted sums of convex sets are convex. For one convex set and nonnegative weights, alpha C plus beta C equals (alpha+beta)C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C,D\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \alpha C+\beta D\text{ convex}\), and for convex \(C\) with \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\), \(\alpha C+\beta C=(\alpha+\beta)C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C+D\) is the image of \(C\times D\) under the linear addition map \((c,d)\mapsto c+d\).
\(x\in C+D\iff C\cap(x-D)\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: \(C+\{a\}=C+a\) is translation by \(a\).
\(0C=\{0\}\) when \(C\neq\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite Minkowski sums of convex sets are convex.
For convex \(C\), \(\theta C+(1-\theta)C=C\) whenever \(0\leq\theta\leq1\).
boundary_notes: Minkowski subtraction is not generally an inverse to Minkowski addition.
The sum of two closed convex sets need not be closed unless additional hypotheses hold.

notation.meaning: reflection of C through the origin

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minkowski sums, translations, and scalar multiples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic additive and scalar operations on subsets of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $V$ be a real vector space, let $A,B,X\subseteq V$, let $b\in V$, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. The Minkowski sum is $A+B=\{x+y:x\in A,\ y\in B\}$. The set $A+b=\{x+b:x\in A\}$ is the translation of $A$ by $b$. The scalar multiple is $\alpha X=\{\alpha x:x\in X\}$; for $\alpha>0$, it is also called a dilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minkowski sum contains all pairwise sums from two sets. Adding a fixed vector translates a set. Multiplying every point by a real scalar gives a scalar multiple, called a dilation when the scalar is positive.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a real vector space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A+B=\{x+y:x\in A,\ y\in B\},\quad A+b=\{x+b:x\in A\},\quad \alpha X=\{\alpha x:x\in X\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional topological guarantee; two merely closed summands need not have a closed sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(C\) is closed and \(D\) is compact, then \(C+D\) is closed. If both sets are compact, then \(C+D\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a compact set to a closed set preserves closedness in finite dimensions, and a sum of compact sets is compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Laws of Minkowski Addition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure set-addition laws, including empty-set and singleton behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(A,B,C\) of a real vector space, \(A+B=B+A\), \((A+B)+C=A+(B+C)\), \(A+\{0\}=A\), and \(A+\varnothing=\varnothing\). For every \(a\), \(A+\{a\}=\{x+a:x\in A\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition is commutative and associative, has the zero singleton as identity and the empty set as an absorbing element, and addition of a singleton is translation.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B,C\) are subsets of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Laws of Minkowski Addition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composition and Invertibility of Set Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the exceptional zero and empty-set regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every subset \(C\) of a real vector space and scalars \(\lambda,\mu\), \(\lambda(\mu C)=(\lambda\mu)C\), \(1C=C\), and \((-1)C=-C\). If \(\lambda\ne0\), scaling by \(\lambda\) is bijective with inverse scaling by \(1/\lambda\). If \(\lambda=0\), then \(0C=\{0\}\) for \(C\ne\varnothing\), whereas \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set scaling composes multiplicatively; nonzero scaling is invertible, negative-one scaling reflects, and zero scaling distinguishes nonempty sets from the empty set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition and Invertibility of Set Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological Invariance Under Nonzero Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional topology; zero scaling is excluded because it collapses nonempty sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda\ne0\), then \(x\mapsto\lambda x\) is a homeomorphism. Hence \(C\) is closed, open, bounded, or compact if and only if \(\lambda C\) has the corresponding property. Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}(\lambda C)=\lambda\operatorname{cl}C\), and for convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{ri}(\lambda C)=\lambda\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonzero scalar multiplication preserves standard topological properties and commutes with closure and relative interior.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Invariance Under Nonzero Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\), let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be convex subsets of a real vector space \(X\), and let \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0\). Their weighted Minkowski combination has the representation \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i c_i:c_i\in C_i\text{ for every }i\right\}.\] This set is convex. If additionally \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), each represented point is a convex combination of selected points \(c_i\in C_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted Minkowski combination consists of weighted sums formed by selecting one point from each set. It is convex when all the component sets are convex; normalized weights make each such sum a convex combination.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Weights Do Not Suppress Empty Summands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the seed's literal point-selection definition and the convention \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i=\{\sum_i\lambda_ic_i:c_i\in C_i\text{ for every }i\}\), the combination is empty whenever any \(C_i\) is empty, even if its coefficient is zero. Deleting zero-weight indices is therefore valid only when their sets are nonempty, or under a different explicit zero-term convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the literal selection-based definition, an empty component makes the weighted combination empty even when its weight is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge1\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(C_i\) are subsets of a real vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex hull of a set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space \(E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic convex hull formed by finite convex combinations; closure is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex hull of \(S\) is the smallest convex subset of \(E\) containing \(S\): \[\operatorname{conv}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq E:S\subseteq C,\ C\text{ convex}\}.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i:m\geq1,\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Thus \(S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\), the set \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is convex, and for every convex \(C\) with \(S\subseteq C\), one has \(\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a nonempty set S is the intersection of all convex sets containing S. It is equivalently the set of all finite convex combinations of points of S. It contains S, is convex, and is contained in every convex set that contains S. The definition is algebraic and does not automatically take a topological closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is the unique smallest convex set containing \(S\), and it equals the set of all finite convex combinations from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) iff there exist finitely many \(s_i\in S\) and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i\).
\(S\) is convex iff \(S=\operatorname{conv}S\).
special_cases_latex: For two points, \(\operatorname{conv}\{x,y\}=\{\theta x+(1-\theta)y:0\leq\theta\leq1\}\).
For a finite set \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), its hull is \(\{\sum_i\lambda_i x_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull formation is monotone: \(S\subseteq T\Rightarrow\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}T\).
Convex-hull formation is idempotent: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{conv}S\).
boundary_notes: A convex hull need not be closed when the generating set is unbounded.
The closed convex hull is \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\), a distinct object.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Sets, Convex Combinations, and Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definitions and the finite-combination representation of a convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is convex if \(x,y\in\Omega\), \(\alpha,\beta\ge 0\), and \(\alpha+\beta=1\) imply \(\alpha x+\beta y\in\Omega\). A convex combination has the form \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\), where \(\alpha_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\). The convex hull \(\operatorname{co}\Omega\), defined as the intersection of all convex sets containing \(\Omega\), is exactly the set of all finite convex combinations of points of \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set contains each line-segment combination of two of its points. The convex hull is the smallest convex set containing a given set and consists exactly of its finite convex combinations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability-Simplex Representation of a Finite Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(X=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_m]\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and define \(\Delta_m:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\lambda\geq0,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generator lists in Euclidean space; repetitions and redundant generators are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite convex hull is
\[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m\right\}=X\Delta_m.\]
Consequently,
\[x\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\iff\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\ X\lambda=x,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1,\ \lambda\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) is the linear image \(X\Delta_m\) of the probability simplex. Thus membership is equivalent to feasibility of \(X\lambda=x\), \(\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\), and \(\lambda\geq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\{X\lambda:\lambda\in\Delta_m\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), \(x=\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\) with \(0\leq\lambda\leq1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite convex hull is a bounded polyhedron, hence a polytope.
boundary_notes: The coefficient vector need not be unique when the generators are affinely dependent.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the generators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex representation of a finite convex hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(m\geq1\), and let \(M=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hulls of a prescribed finite list; redundant or repeated generators are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite hull representation of \(X\) is \[\operatorname{conv}X=\left\{M\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\right\}=M\Delta_m.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{conv}X\) exactly when the linear system \[M\lambda=x,\qquad \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1,\qquad \lambda\geq0\] has a solution. Any feasible \(\lambda\) is a barycentric or convex-coordinate representation of \(x\) relative to the listed generators. Its support \(\{i:\lambda_i>0\}\) records the active generators, but neither the coefficients nor their support need be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many points collected as the columns of M, their convex hull is the image of the standard simplex under the map lambda to M lambda. A point x belongs to the hull exactly when there is a nonnegative coefficient vector lambda summing to one and satisfying M lambda=x. Such a coefficient vector gives convex coordinates; redundant generators can make this representation nonunique.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}X=M\Delta_m\).
The finite hull is the affine image of the coefficient simplex under \(\lambda\mapsto M\lambda\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), the coefficient simplex yields the line segment between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).
If \(x_1,,x_m\) are affinely independent, every point of their affine hull has unique affine coordinates and every point of their convex hull has unique convex coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite convex-hull membership is a linear feasibility problem in the coefficient vector.
The hull of finitely many points is compact because it is the continuous image of the compact simplex \(\Delta_m\).
boundary_notes: Uniqueness fails when the generators are affinely dependent.
This representation does not say that all listed points are necessary; zero coefficients may remove generators.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the hull generators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{co}S=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:C\text{ is convex and }S\subseteq C\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i x_i:k\in\mathbb{N}_{*},\ x_i\in S,\ \alpha\in\Delta_k\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of S, defined as the intersection of all convex sets containing S, is exactly the set of all finite convex combinations of points of S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The indexed family may be arbitrary, but every coefficient family in the representation has finite support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull and Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), equipped with its usual topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean closure; the distinction between algebraic convex hull and closed convex hull is explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The algebraic convex hull is
\[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\}.\]
The closed convex hull is
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^n:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\]
These regimes are related by
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S,\]
with equality exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary convex hull of \(S\) consists of its finite convex combinations. The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed convex sets containing \(S\). In Euclidean space it equals the closure of the ordinary convex hull. Thus the two regimes coincide precisely when the convex hull is already closed; otherwise the closed hull adds limit points.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{cl}S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
The closed convex hull is the unique smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is compact in \(\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and hence \(\operatorname{conv}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\).
For a finite set \(S\), its convex hull is a compact polytope and is closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Both hull operations are monotone and idempotent.
Closing first does not change the closed convex hull, although it can change the ordinary convex hull.
boundary_notes: A closed but unbounded set can have a nonclosed convex hull, so closedness of \(S\) alone is insufficient.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the closure depends on the chosen topology; this record uses the Euclidean topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic and closed convex hulls
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and let \(\operatorname{cl}\) denote Euclidean closure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean topology; algebraic convexification is distinguished from closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algebraic convex hull is \(\operatorname{conv}S\), the set of finite convex combinations from \(S\). The closed convex hull is \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:S\subseteq C,\ C\text{ closed and convex}\}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S).\] Hence \[S\subseteq\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S.\] The two hulls coincide exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed. In particular, if \(S\) is compact, then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and therefore closed, so no additional closure is needed. A closed but unbounded generating set may nevertheless have a nonclosed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algebraic convex hull consists of finite convex combinations. The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed convex sets containing S, equivalently the Euclidean closure of the algebraic convex hull. They coincide precisely when the algebraic hull is closed. Compact generating sets have compact, hence closed, convex hulls, while closed unbounded sets can fail to have closed convex hulls.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
\(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{cl}S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{conv}S)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is finite, then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and equals its closed convex hull.
If \(S\) is compact, \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed-convex-hull formation is monotone and idempotent.
Limits of sequences of finite convex combinations belong to \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\), even when they do not belong to \(\operatorname{conv}S\).
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(S\) alone does not guarantee closedness of \(\operatorname{conv}S\).
In infinite-dimensional spaces, compactness and closure behavior require additional care and are outside this scope.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull Operator Laws
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are the algebraic closure-operator laws for convex generation; no topology is involved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(A,B\) of a real vector space \(X\), \[A\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(A),\qquad A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow\operatorname{conv}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(B),\qquad \operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{conv}(A))=\operatorname{conv}(A).\] Moreover, \(A\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}(A)=A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex hull is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and its fixed points are exactly the convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(A\mapsto\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is a closure operator whose fixed points are precisely the convex subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull Operator Laws

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of any set is convex, and a set is convex exactly when it equals its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}S\text{ is convex},\qquad S\text{ is convex}\iff S=\operatorname{conv}S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are the closure-operator properties of closed convex generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(S,T\) of a Hausdorff topological real vector space, \[S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S),\qquad S\subseteq T\implies\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(T),\] and \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\bigr)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S).\] Moreover, \(S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\) exactly when \(S\) is closed and convex.
