knowledge_statements.statement_title: Net Representation of the Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequences suffice in first-countable spaces, including normed spaces; general topological vector spaces may require nets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\). A point \(x\in X\) belongs to \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\) if and only if there exists a net \((x_\alpha)\) in \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) converging to \(x\). Equivalently, every \(x_\alpha\) is a finite convex combination of points of \(S\). If \(X\) is first countable, the net may be replaced by a sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed convex hull exactly when it is a limit of finite convex combinations.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Hull with Prescribed Horizon Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs the least closed convex enlargement containing a set and prescribed horizon directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed closed cone and let \(\varnothing\ne C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed with \(C^\infty\subset K\). Set \(D=\operatorname{con}C+\operatorname{con}K\). Then \(D\) is closed and is the smallest closed convex set containing \(C\) whose horizon cone contains \(K\). Moreover, \(D^\infty=\operatorname{con}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a nonempty closed set C has all its horizon directions in a pointed closed cone K, then the sum of the convex hulls of C and K is closed. It is the smallest closed convex set containing C whose horizon cone contains K, and its horizon cone equals the convex hull of K.
assumptions_latex: K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a pointed closed cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is closed and is the smallest closed convex set containing }C\text{ with }K\subset D^\infty,\qquad D^\infty=\operatorname{con}K.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Closed Planar Set with Nonclosed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional example shows that closedness of an unbounded generating set does not ensure closedness of its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq x^{-1}\},\qquad S:=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(S\) is closed, while \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(u,v):u>0,\ v>0\}.\] Consequently \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed; for example, \((1,n^{-1})\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) converges to \((1,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed unbounded planar set can have a nonclosed convex hull: adjoining the origin to the epigraph of 1/x yields the open positive quadrant together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is closed but \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup(0,\infty)^2\) is not closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space example shows that finite convex-combination generation need not produce a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2\) with its norm topology, let \((e_n)_{n\geq1}\) be its standard orthonormal basis, and set \(S:=\{e_n:n\geq1\}\). For \(N\geq1\), define \[x_N:=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N e_n.\] Then \(x_N\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) and \(\|x_N\|_2=N^{-1/2}\to0\), so \(0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))\). Every element of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is a finite nonnegative combination of the \(e_n\) whose coefficients sum to \(1\), so it is nonzero. Thus \[0\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{conv}(S)\neq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences, the convex hull of the standard unit vectors is not closed. Uniform averages of the first N unit vectors lie in the hull and converge to zero, but zero itself is not a finite convex combination of those vectors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex and Conic Carathéodory Witnesses
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. Define \(\operatorname{cone}S\) as the set of finite nonnegative combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional convex and conic representation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex Carathéodory witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) is a representation
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n+1,\quad x_i\in S,\quad \lambda_i\geq0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1.\]
For nonzero \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\), a conic Carathéodory witness is a representation
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i x_i,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n,\quad x_i\in S,\quad \mu_i>0,\]
where the selected vectors may be chosen linearly independent. Carathéodory's theorem asserts that every point in the respective hull possesses such a witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) has a convex representation using at most \(n+1\) points of \(S\). Every nonzero point of \(\operatorname{cone}S\) has a positive representation using at most \(n\) linearly independent vectors of \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\1\leq |T|\leq n+1}}\operatorname{conv}T.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull and nonzero conic-hull membership in finite dimensions admit exact certificates whose support is bounded by dimension.
boundary_notes: The conic statement treats \(x=0\) separately; the zero vector is represented by the empty sum or by zero coefficients.
These are exact representation results, not approximation bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Carathéodory witness number and its principal regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. For \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\), a convex witness is a finite tuple \((x_i,\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m\) with \(x_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex and conic support bounds; the record defines the family of witness regimes rather than supplying a proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Carathéodory number of \(S\) is \[c(S):=\min\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}:\text{every }x\in\operatorname{conv}S\text{ has a convex witness using at most }k\text{ points of }S\right\}.\] The classical ambient-dimensional regime asserts \(c(S)\leq n+1\). If \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\), the intrinsic affine-dimensional regime asserts \(c(S)\leq d+1\). For conic generation, a conic witness for \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\) is \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i x_i\) with \(\mu_i\geq0\); the corresponding finite-dimensional regime permits at most \(n\) linearly independent active generators for nonzero \(x\). These are the principal convex, intrinsic, and homogeneous members of the Carathéodory family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex witness represents a hull point using finitely many generators and nonnegative coefficients summing to one. The Carathéodory number is the smallest uniform bound on the number of generators needed for all hull points. In n-dimensional space the classical bound is n+1; if the generating set has affine dimension d, the intrinsic bound is d+1. The conic analogue drops normalization and bounds a nonzero conic representation by n linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family consists of the bounds \(c(S)\leq n+1\), \(c(S)\leq\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)+1\), and the conic bound of at most \(n\) linearly independent generators.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(c(S)\leq k\) iff every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) lies in the convex hull of some subset of \(S\) having at most \(k\) elements.
The intrinsic bound is the ambient theorem applied within the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}S\), whose dimension is \(d\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) lies on an affine line, then \(c(S)\leq2\).
If \(S\) is a singleton, then \(c(S)=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex-hull membership assertion in finite dimension has a uniformly sparse finite witness.
The supporting generators may depend on the represented point; the definition does not require one fixed generating subset for the whole hull.
boundary_notes: The coefficients and supporting points need not be unique.
For \(x=0\) in a conic hull, the empty or all-zero representation depends on convention; the stated conic independence form concerns nonzero \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An ambient-dimension Carathéodory witness for \(x\) is a tuple
\[(m;x_1,\ldots,x_m;\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m)\]
such that
\[1\leq m\leq n+1,\qquad x_i\in S,\qquad \lambda_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1,\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambient-dimension Carathéodory witness represents a point \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) as a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) points of \(S\). Every hull point has such a witness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x\in\operatorname{conv}S\ \exists m\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\},\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0:\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i.\]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional regime indexed by the surrounding dimension n, whether or not S is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ambient-dimensional Carathéodory regime is the hull-membership witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq n+1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in S,\ \exists\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0:\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Zero coefficients may be deleted, so the active generators can be taken to have positive coefficients. Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{F\subseteq S\\1\leq |F|\leq n+1}}\operatorname{conv}F.\] The bound is uniform over all points of the hull but the witnessing subset \(F\) may vary with \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the ambient-dimensional Carathéodory regime, every point in the convex hull of a nonempty subset of R^n can be represented as a convex combination of at most n+1 points from that subset. Equivalently, the full convex hull is the union of the hulls of all subsets with at most n+1 elements. The supporting subset may depend on the point being represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) admits a convex-combination witness using at most \(n+1\) generators from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{F\subseteq S,\ 1\leq|F|\leq n+1}\operatorname{conv}F\).
Any initially finite convex representation can be replaced by one with support cardinality at most \(n+1\).
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}\), at most two generators are required.
In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), at most three generators are required.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull membership in fixed dimension has a bounded-size certificate independent of the cardinality of \(S\).
For compact \(S\), sequences in \(\operatorname{conv}S\) may be represented using a fixed maximum of \(n+1\) coefficient-generator pairs.
boundary_notes: The ambient bound can be reduced to \(d+1\) when \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S<n\).
The theorem does not provide one common subset of \(n+1\) generators for every point of the hull.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(d:=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic regime indexed by effective affine dimension d rather than ambient dimension n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-dimensional Carathéodory regime is the witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq d+1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in S,\ \exists\lambda_i\geq0:\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{F\subseteq S\\1\leq|F|\leq d+1}}\operatorname{conv}F.\] The dimension \(d\) is the dimension of the direction space parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}S\), so this formulation is invariant under affine embeddings and removes unused ambient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the affine hull of S has dimension d, every point in the convex hull of S is a convex combination of at most d+1 points of S. Equivalently, the hull is the union of the hulls of all subsets of size at most d+1. This intrinsic form can be sharper than the ambient n+1 bound and is unchanged by placing the same affine geometry in a larger surrounding space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) has a convex witness supported on at most \(d+1\) points, where \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{F\subseteq S,\ 1\leq|F|\leq d+1}\operatorname{conv}F\).
The bound is the ambient-dimensional Carathéodory bound computed in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(d=0\), \(S\) is contained in a singleton affine space and one generator suffices.
For \(d=1\), every hull point lies on a segment joining at most two points of \(S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Embedding \(S\) affinely into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space does not enlarge the intrinsic witness bound.
Any convex representation with more than \(d+1\) active generators can be replaced by a representation with at most \(d+1\) active generators.
boundary_notes: The number \(d+1\) is a universal upper bound and need not be the smallest possible bound for a particular set.
Affine dimension, not topological dimension of a nonconvex generating set, controls this regime.

children.title: Conic Caratheodory Regime
children.top_down_role: Finite generator reduction for conic hulls.

assumptions_latex: The active generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update preserves \(x\), keeps all coefficients nonnegative, removes at least one active generator, and finite repetition yields linearly independent positive support.

notation.meaning: A nonzero coefficient vector witnessing linear dependence among the active generators.
The maximal dependence step preserving coefficient nonnegativity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the constructive finite-support reduction underlying conic Caratheodory; it specifies the coefficient update without duplicating the theorem statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\) with \(s_i\in S\) and \(\lambda_i>0\). If the active generators are linearly dependent, choose \(\beta\neq0\) with \(\sum_i\beta_i s_i=0\), changing its sign if necessary so that some \(\beta_i>0\). Set \[t=\min_{\beta_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\beta_i},\qquad \lambda_i'=\lambda_i-t\beta_i.\] Delete generators whose updated coefficient is zero and repeat while the active generators remain dependent. Every update preserves \(x\) and coefficient nonnegativity and removes at least one active generator; the procedure terminates with linearly independent positive support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear dependence determines a maximal coefficient step that preserves the represented vector and nonnegativity while deleting at least one generator; repetition produces independent support.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Dependence-Elimination Algorithm
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Dependence-Elimination Algorithm

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every conic representation of \(x\) using generators from \(S\) has support size \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The coordinate-ray family establishes that the intrinsic generator bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\ge1\), let \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^r\) and \(x=e_1+\cdots+e_r\). Then \(\dim(\operatorname{span}S)=r\), and every representation \(x=\sum_{s\in S}\mu_s s\) with \(\mu_s\ge0\) has \(\mu_{e_i}=1\) for every \(i\). Thus every such representation has support size exactly \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the coordinate vectors requires all \(r\) coordinate rays, so the span-dimension bound is sharp.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic Carathéodory generator-reduction regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\setminus\{0\}\), where \(\operatorname{cone}S\) consists of finite nonnegative combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonzero conic representations; coefficients are nonnegative and are not normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic Carathéodory regime is the witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{cone}S\setminus\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq n,\ \exists s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S,\ \exists\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m>0:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i s_i,\] where the active generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) may be chosen linearly independent. More intrinsically, if \(r=\dim\operatorname{span}S\), then \(m\leq r\). Thus conic normalization removes the additional affine coordinate responsible for the \(n+1\) convex-hull bound: a nonzero conic point needs at most the dimension of the relevant linear span many active rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero point in the conic hull of a subset of R^n can be expressed as a positive combination of at most n generators from the set, and the active generators can be chosen linearly independent. If the generators span only an r-dimensional linear subspace, at most r are needed. Unlike a convex combination, the conic coefficients are not required to sum to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonzero \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\) has a positive representation using at most \(\dim\operatorname{span}S\leq n\) linearly independent generators from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}S=\bigcup\{\operatorname{cone}F:F\subseteq S,\ F\text{ linearly independent}\}\), with the origin included by convention.
Any conic representation with linearly dependent active generators can be replaced by one with fewer active generators.
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), every nonzero conic-hull point needs at most two linearly independent generators.
If \(S\) lies in a one-dimensional subspace, every nonzero conic-hull point uses one active generator whenever it is representable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonzero conic-hull membership has a certificate supported on at most \(n\) generators.
The selected positive generators determine a simplicial cone containing the represented point.
boundary_notes: The zero vector may be represented by all-zero coefficients; requiring strictly positive coefficients is therefore restricted to nonzero points.
The conic hull need not be closed, even when the generating set is compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Verification Cost of a Sparse Hull Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This counts exact real-arithmetic operations; bit complexity depends additionally on numeric encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and suppose a certificate lists indices \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and coefficients \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\). The conditions \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i s_i\) can be verified in \(O(d|I|)\) arithmetic operations. If \(|I|\leq r+1\leq d+1\), the cost is \(O(d(r+1))\), hence at most \(O(d^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse convex-combination certificate is verifiable in time linear in dimension times support size.
assumptions_latex: The points, target, indices, and coefficients use an exact-arithmetic representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Carathéodory-Sparse Convex-Hull Witness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). A finite family may repeat points, although zero coefficients and repetitions may always be removed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convex hulls; the bound used here is the ambient-dimension bound \(n+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sparse hull-membership witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}X\) is a tuple \(W=((x_i)_{i=1}^m,(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m)\) such that \[1\le m\le n+1,\qquad x_i\in X,\qquad \lambda_i>0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Its support is \(\operatorname{supp}W=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), and its support size is \(m\). Thus the witness is an explicitly checkable certificate consisting of at most \(n+1\) generating points and their convex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a sparse witness certifying that \(x\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}X\) consists of at most \(n+1\) points of \(X\) and positive coefficients summing to one whose weighted sum is \(x\). The number of positive coefficients is the witness support size.
equivalent_formulations_latex: After removing zero coefficients, the certificate is equivalently a finitely supported probability vector \(\lambda:X\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(|\operatorname{supp}\lambda|\le n+1\) and \(x=\sum_{u\in X}\lambda(u)u\).
The lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}\) may be chosen linearly independent; consequently, the selected points are affinely independent.
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), every hull point has a witness supported on at most two points.
If \(x\in X\), the singleton witness \(m=1\), \(x_1=x\), and \(\lambda_1=1\) is valid.
immediate_consequences_latex: Hull membership in \(\mathbb R^n\) always has a certificate whose support cardinality is bounded independently of the cardinality of \(X\).
boundary_notes: The definition is finite-dimensional; no uniform finite support bound follows in a general infinite-dimensional space.
The sharper affine-dimension bound is a neighboring regime and is not asserted as the defining bound in this record.
The representation need not be unique.

notation.meaning: selected generating points with positive weight

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology Relative to the Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, put \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and equip \(A\) with the subspace topology inherited from \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(B(x,r)=\{y:\|y-x\|<r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative topology in the effective affine ambient space \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative topology of \(C\) is the topology induced on \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\). Its intrinsic topological objects are \[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists r>0,\ B(x,r)\cap A\subseteq C\},\] \[\operatorname{cl}_A C=\{x\in A:\forall r>0,\ B(x,r)\cap C\ne\varnothing\},\qquad \operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_A C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] A set \(U\subseteq A\) is relatively open when \(U=A\cap O\) for some open \(O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relevant ambient space for a nonempty convex set \(C\) is its affine hull \(A\). Relative interior, closure, and boundary are respectively the interior, closure, and boundary computed in the subspace topology of \(A\). A relative neighborhood of \(x\) is obtained by intersecting an ordinary open ball about \(x\) with \(A\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if \(x\in C\) and some neighborhood of \(x\) in \(A\) is contained in \(C\).
Because \(A\) is closed in finite dimensions and contains \(C\), the relative closure \(\operatorname{cl}_A C\) equals the ordinary Euclidean closure \(\operatorname{cl}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=A\) is affine, then \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\) and \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\varnothing\).
If \(C\) is a nondegenerate line segment, its relative interior is the open segment and its relative boundary consists of its endpoints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative topological notions do not become degenerate merely because \(C\) lies in a proper affine subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: Ambient interior and ambient boundary are different objects when \(A\ne\mathbb R^n\).
The finite-dimensional equality between relative and ambient closures can fail in nonclosed affine subspaces of more general topological vector spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative interior, relative openness, and relative boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic topological notions for a nonempty convex set within its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A point \(x\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\) if and only if \(x\in C\) and there exists an open sphere \(S\) centered at \(x\) such that \(S\cap\operatorname{aff}(C)\subseteq C\). The set \(C\) is relatively open if \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=C\), and its relative boundary is \(\operatorname{cl}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative interior point has a neighborhood within the affine hull that lies in the set. The set is relatively open when all its points are relative interior points, and its relative boundary consists of closure points outside the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ri}(C)=\{x\in C:\exists\text{ an open sphere }S\text{ centered at }x,\ S\cap\operatorname{aff}(C)\subseteq C\},\quad C\text{ relatively open}\iff\operatorname{ri}(C)=C,\quad\operatorname{rbd}(C)=\operatorname{cl}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set, let \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and let \(L=A-A\) be the linear space parallel to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, including lower-dimensional and nonclosed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative interior of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ x+(B(0,\varepsilon)\cap L)\subseteq C\}.\] Thus \(x\) is a relative interior point precisely when \(C\) contains an open neighborhood of \(x\) in its own affine hull. The relative dimension of \(C\) is \(\dim C=\dim A=\dim L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point \(x\) lies in the relative interior of a nonempty convex set \(C\) when a sufficiently small ball around \(x\), restricted to directions parallel to the affine hull of \(C\), remains inside \(C\). This definition measures interior intrinsically and therefore remains meaningful for lower-dimensional convex sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is the ordinary interior of \(C\) in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
Using any norm on \(\mathbb R^n\) gives the same relative interior because all finite-dimensional norms induce the same topology.
special_cases_latex: For a singleton \(C=\{x\}\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).
For an affine set \(C\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).
For a nonempty full-dimensional convex set, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is nonempty and convex, and \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{aff}C\).
boundary_notes: Convexity is not needed to write the subspace-interior definition, but it is essential for the listed structural consequences.
Relative interior does not require \(C\) to be closed.
Ambient interior may be empty even when relative interior is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative interior and relative boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-hull-relative interior and boundary, including nonemptiness of the relative interior for nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a point \(x\in S\) is a relative interior point if there is an open neighborhood \(N\) of \(x\) such that \(N\cap\operatorname{aff}S\subseteq S\). The relative interior \(\operatorname{ri}S\) is the set of all such points, and the relative boundary is \(\operatorname{cl}S\setminus\operatorname{ri}S\). If \(S\) is nonempty and convex, then \(\operatorname{ri}S\neq\varnothing\), although its ambient interior may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior is interior measured within the affine hull. Relative boundary is the closure minus the relative interior. Every nonempty convex set has a nonempty relative interior, even if its ordinary interior is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{ri}S\iff\exists N\text{ open neighborhood of }x:\ N\cap\operatorname{aff}S\subseteq S;\quad \operatorname{relbd}S=\operatorname{cl}S\setminus\operatorname{ri}S;\quad S\neq\varnothing,\ S\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\operatorname{ri}S\neq\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and relative-interior invariance for convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations among a nonempty convex set, its closure, and its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\), \(\operatorname{cl}(C)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}(C))\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}(C))\). Moreover, for nonempty convex sets \(C\) and \(\bar C\), the following are equivalent: \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=\operatorname{ri}(\bar C)\); \(\operatorname{cl}(C)=\operatorname{cl}(\bar C)\); and \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\subseteq\bar C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set and its relative interior have the same closure, while the set and its closure have the same relative interior. Two nonempty convex sets have the same relative interior exactly when they have the same closure, equivalently when one lies between the other's relative interior and closure.

\bar C\text{ is a nonempty convex set for the equivalence statement}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure–relative-interior invariance and equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutual determination of the closure and relative interior of nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Then \(\operatorname{cl}(C)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}(C))\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}(C))\). If \(\bar C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is another nonempty convex set, the following are equivalent: \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=\operatorname{ri}(\bar C)\); \(\operatorname{cl}(C)=\operatorname{cl}(\bar C)\); and \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\subseteq\bar C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking relative interior does not change a nonempty convex set's closure, and taking closure does not change its relative interior. Two nonempty convex sets have the same relative interior exactly when they have the same closure, equivalently when one lies between the other's relative interior and closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior, Relative Openness, and Relative Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic topology of a nonempty convex subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A point \(x\in C\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\) if there exists an open Euclidean ball \(S\) centered at \(x\) such that \(S\cap\operatorname{aff}(C)\subseteq C\). The set \(C\) is relatively open if \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=C\), and its relative boundary is \(\operatorname{cl}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a relative-interior point has a neighborhood in the affine hull lying inside the convex set. The set is relatively open when all its points are relative-interior points, and its relative boundary is its closure minus its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ri}(C)=\{x\in C:\exists\text{ an open ball }S\text{ centered at }x,\ S\cap\operatorname{aff}(C)\subseteq C\},\quad C\text{ is relatively open}\iff\operatorname{ri}(C)=C,\quad\operatorname{rbd}(C)=\operatorname{cl}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ri}(C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Intrinsic Interior and Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. The definition uses only segments inside \(C\), while the equivalent relative-interior formulation uses the topology of \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine geometry; the stated equivalence is for nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the intrinsic algebraic interior of \(C\) by \[\operatorname{aint}C=\{x\in C:\forall y\in C\ \exists\gamma>0\text{ such that }x+\gamma(x-y)\in C\}.\] A point in \(\operatorname{aint}C\) is therefore an endpoint from which every segment \([y,x]\subseteq C\) can be prolonged a positive distance beyond \(x\) without leaving \(C\). In finite-dimensional convex geometry, \[\operatorname{aint}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic algebraic interior consists of those points \(x\in C\) for which every segment joining another point \(y\in C\) to \(x\) can be extended beyond \(x\) while staying in \(C\). For a nonempty convex subset of finite-dimensional space, this segment-based notion is exactly the relative interior.
assumptions_latex: All quantifiers over directions are restricted to the effective affine space of \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(z=x+\gamma(x-y)\), the condition says that \(x\) lies in the open segment \((y,z)\) for some \(z\in C\), for every \(y\in C\).
The same points are characterized by the existence of an affine-hull neighborhood \(B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is affine, every point satisfies the prolongation condition.
If \(C=[a,b]\) with \(a\ne b\), exactly the points of \((a,b)\) satisfy it.
immediate_consequences_latex: The intrinsic-interior notion is affine invariant: for an affine bijection \(T\), \(T(\operatorname{aint}C)=\operatorname{aint}(T(C))\).
boundary_notes: The parameter \(\gamma\) may depend on \(y\); no uniform positive prolongation length is required.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, algebraic interior and topological relative interior need not coincide.
Convexity is part of the equivalence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative interior defined using the closed generated linear space appearing in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior and Dimension of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines relative interior in the affine-hull topology and records the associated dimension convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), its relative interior is its interior in the topology relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\). Equivalently, \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff x\in\operatorname{aff}C\ \text{and}\ \exists\delta>0\text{ such that }(\operatorname{aff}C)\cap B(x,\delta)\subset C.\] The dimension of \(C\) is \(\dim C:=\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\), equivalently the dimension of the linear subspace parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a convex set is its interior relative to its affine hull. A point is relatively interior exactly when an affine-hull neighborhood of it lies in the set. The set's dimension is the dimension of its affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonemptiness, Affine Hull, and Segment Stability of Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior geometry of finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set. Then \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\neq\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{ri}(C))=\operatorname{aff}(C)\). Moreover, if \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(C)\) and \(\bar{x}\in C\), then \(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)\bar{x}\in\operatorname{ri}(C)\) for every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). Thus only the endpoint \(\bar{x}\) may fail to belong to \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty convex set has a nonempty relative interior with the same affine hull. Starting at a relative-interior point and moving toward any point of the set, every segment point except possibly the destination remains in the relative interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative interior of a finite-dimensional convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative interior measured in the affine hull, including its basic containment and full-dimensional specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Its relative interior is
\[
\operatorname{ri}C=\left\{x\in\operatorname{aff}C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ (x+\varepsilon B)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C\right\},
\]
where \(B=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\|z\|\le 1\}\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\), and if \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a convex set is its interior when the set is viewed inside its affine hull. It lies in the set, and for a full-dimensional convex set it equals the ordinary interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Access from a Relative-Interior Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, choose \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the target may be a missing limit point of a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\) is radially accessible from \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) when every point before \(y\) on the segment from \(x\) to \(y\) remains in the relative interior: \[x_t=(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\qquad(0\le t<1).\] The radial-access set from \(x\) is \[\operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\{y\in\operatorname{cl}C:\forall t\in[0,1),\ (1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\}.\] For a nonempty convex \(C\), every closure point is accessible, so \(\operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix a relative-interior point \(x\) of a convex set \(C\). A closure point \(y\) is radially accessible from \(x\) if the half-open segment from \(x\) to \(y\) is contained in the relative interior of \(C\). Convexity implies that every point of the closure is accessible in this sense, even when the endpoint itself is absent from \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the point \(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
The half-open segment \([x,y)\) is contained in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(y\in C\), accessibility holds along an ordinary segment contained in \(C\).
If \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), every point before the missing endpoint still lies in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every closure point is the limit of a one-dimensional path lying entirely in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
Consequently, \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C\).
boundary_notes: No assertion is made that the endpoint \(y\) itself belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) or even to \(C\).
The starting point must lie in the relative interior; an arbitrary boundary starting point need not provide this access.

notation.meaning: point at parameter t on the segment from x to y
closure points radially accessible from x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Dimensional and Lower-Dimensional Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Ambient interior is computed in \(\mathbb R^n\), whereas relative interior is computed in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ambient-relative interior regime of \(C\) is determined by \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\). It is full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\), and lower-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\). Precisely, \[\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\iff\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n,\] and in the full-dimensional regime \[\operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\] In the lower-dimensional regime, \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set is in the full-dimensional regime when its affine hull is all of the ambient space. Exactly in that regime its ambient interior is nonempty and equals its relative interior. If the affine hull is proper, the ambient interior is empty, but the relative interior remains nonempty because it is measured inside the affine hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The full-dimensional regime is equivalently \(\dim C=n\).
The lower-dimensional regime is equivalently \(\dim C<n\), in which case every point of \(C\) is an ambient boundary point.
special_cases_latex: A line segment in \(\mathbb R^2\) has empty ambient interior but a nonempty relative interior.
An affine space \(A\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(\operatorname{ri}A=A\) and \(\operatorname{int}A=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For lower-dimensional convex sets, statements requiring an interior point must be formulated with \(\operatorname{ri}C\), not \(\operatorname{int}C\).
boundary_notes: Nonemptiness is essential: conventions for the affine hull and relative interior of the empty set vary.
The equivalence uses convexity for the implication from full affine hull to nonempty interior.

notation.meaning: interior relative to the affine hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior-Compatible Set Operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be an operation taking one or more nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-set operations; qualifications are part of compatibility where required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) is relative-interior compatible on inputs \((C_1,\ldots,C_m)\) when \[\operatorname{ri}\Phi(C_1,\ldots,C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{ri}C_1,\ldots,\operatorname{ri}C_m),\] with the right side interpreted using the same set operation. Cartesian products, Minkowski sums, and affine images are compatible without a constraint qualification. Finite intersections are compatible under \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\); affine preimages are compatible when the preimage meets the target relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior calculus records when taking relative interiors commutes with a convex-set construction. Products, sums, and affine images commute unconditionally. Intersections and affine preimages require a nonempty relative-interior feasibility condition. The qualification is part of the operation's declared domain of compatibility.
assumptions_latex: All participating sets are nonempty and convex in finite-dimensional spaces.
Any intersection or affine-preimage identity is invoked only under its stated relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ri}\Phi(C_1,\ldots,C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{ri}C_1,\ldots,\operatorname{ri}C_m)\] for each operation on its qualified domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Compatibility means that intrinsic neighborhoods are transported exactly by the set operation, rather than yielding merely one-sided inclusion.
For an affine map \(T\), image compatibility reads \(T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C))\).
special_cases_latex: For products, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1\times\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
For sums, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A compound construction may be evaluated by propagating relative interiors through successive compatible operations while retaining every necessary qualification.
boundary_notes: Closure does not share all of these unconditional commutation properties.
Without a common relative-interior point, the intersection identity can fail.
The definition concerns exact equality, not merely inclusion.

If at least one of \(C_1,C_2\) is bounded, then \(\operatorname{cl}(C_1)+\operatorname{cl}(C_2)=\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2)\).

Then \(\operatorname{ri}C_1=\{y>0\}\), \(\operatorname{ri}C_2=\{y<0\}\), and \(C_1\cap C_2=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior-Regular Intersection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets, where \(m\ge1\), and put \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections of finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((C_i)_{i=1}^m\) is relative-interior regular when \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing.\] For such a family, the intersection calculus is exact: \[\operatorname{ri}\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{cl}\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}C_i.\] Relative-interior regularity is therefore a geometric constraint qualification for commuting both intrinsic interior and closure with intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of convex sets is relative-interior regular when all sets share a point that lies in each of their relative interiors. Under this qualification, the relative interior of the intersection is the intersection of the relative interiors, and closure also commutes with the intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regularity means that there exists \(\bar x\) and radii \(r_i>0\) such that \(B(\bar x,r_i)\cap\operatorname{aff}C_i\subseteq C_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=1\), regularity is automatic because a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set has nonempty relative interior.
For two sets, the qualification is \(\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2\ne\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The qualified intersection is nonempty, and its relative interior contains every common relative-interior point.
boundary_notes: Without the qualification, equality may fail even when the intersection is nonempty; for example, opposite closed half-lines can meet at one point while their relative interiors are disjoint.
For arbitrary infinite families, finite-family induction does not establish the same identities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product and Minkowski-Sum Relative-Interior Rules
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be nonempty convex sets. When forming a Minkowski sum, assume all summands lie in a common vector space \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products and finite Minkowski sums in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cartesian product and Minkowski sum are \[\prod_{i=1}^m C_i=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):x_i\in C_i\},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m C_i=\{x_1+\cdots+x_m:x_i\in C_i\}.\] Their relative-interior calculus is \[\operatorname{ri}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\] No common-interior qualification is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a finite Cartesian product is the product of the relative interiors. For convex sets in a common vector space, the relative interior of their Minkowski sum is the sum of their relative interiors. Both identities hold without an intersection-type constraint qualification.
assumptions_latex: For the sum identity, \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) for all \(i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The sum identity is the affine-image rule applied to the addition map \(A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i x_i\) on \(\prod_i C_i\).
special_cases_latex: For two sets, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
For a scalar \(\alpha>0\), \(\operatorname{ri}(\alpha C)=\alpha\operatorname{ri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vector \(z\in\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)\) admits a decomposition \(z=x_1+x_2\) with \(x_i\in\operatorname{ri}C_i\).
boundary_notes: For multiplication by \(\alpha=0\), the image is the singleton \(\{0\}\), whose relative interior is itself.
Analogous closure equality for sums can fail when both summands are unbounded, even if they are closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Image and Qualified Preimage Calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine, \(T(x)=Ax+b\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine images and preimages; preimages require relative-interior feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine images transport relative interiors exactly: \[T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C)).\] For a target set \(D\), define \(T^{-1}(D)=\{x:T(x)\in D\}\). If \[T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\ne\varnothing,\] then the affine preimage is relative-interior regular and \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D),\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map sends the relative interior of a nonempty convex set onto the relative interior of its image. A preimage obeys the corresponding relative-interior and closure identities provided at least one point maps into the relative interior of the target set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The preimage qualification says \(T(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing\).
Translations do not affect the rule, so the linear-map statements apply to affine maps after translating the image.
special_cases_latex: If \(T\) is an affine bijection, both image and preimage formulas hold without an additional qualification.
Coordinate projection satisfies the unconditional image formula.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fiberwise Characterization of Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space specialization of relative-interior calculus for a coordinate projection and its fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subset\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) be convex, let \(X=\operatorname{proj}_xG\), and for each \(x\in X\) define \(S(x)=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m\mid(x,u)\in G\}\). A pair is relatively interior exactly when its projected coordinate is relatively interior to the projection and its second coordinate is relatively interior to the corresponding fiber.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, with the Euclidean topology on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, possibly nonclosed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closure of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{cl}C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\forall\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap C\ne\varnothing\}.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\) exactly when there is a sequence \((x_k)\subseteq C\) with \(x_k\to x\). For convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{cl}C\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(C\), and \[\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{aff}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of \(C\) consists of all points whose every neighborhood meets \(C\), equivalently all limits of sequences from \(C\). If \(C\) is convex, its closure remains convex and is the smallest closed convex superset of \(C\). Closing a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set does not change its affine hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}C\) is the intersection of all closed subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) containing \(C\).
Because closure preserves convexity, it is also the intersection of all closed convex sets containing \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}C=C\).
For an open segment \((a,b)\), \(\operatorname{cl}C=[a,b]\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point missing solely because of nonclosedness belongs to \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\).
The relative topology of \(C\) and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) uses the same affine ambient space.
boundary_notes: Closure does not imply boundedness or compactness.
Affine images of closed unbounded convex sets need not be closed.
The empty-set convention is excluded by the stated nonemptiness assumption.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure–Relative-Interior Equivalence Class
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, without a closedness assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\) when \(C\) and \(D\) have the same closure-relative-interior data. For nonempty convex sets, the following equivalent conditions define this relation: \[\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{cl}D,\qquad \operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{ri}D,\] or, after possibly exchanging \(C\) and \(D\), \[\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C.\] Each set satisfies the canonical pairing identities \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C,\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty finite-dimensional convex sets, closure and relative interior determine one another. Two such sets have the same closure exactly when they have the same relative interior. Any convex set lying between the relative interior of \(C\) and the closure of \(C\) belongs to the same closure–relative-interior equivalence class.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\) if and only if both sets lie between their common relative interior and common closure.
For a convex \(D\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\) implies \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\).
special_cases_latex: \(C\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) all belong to the same equivalence class.
An open convex set relative to its affine hull and its closure have the same relative interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Adding or deleting only non-interior boundary points while remaining convex does not change either canonical datum.
boundary_notes: Convexity is essential; arbitrary sets with the same closure need not have the same interior.
Nonemptiness avoids exceptional conventions for relative interior.
Equality of closures does not imply equality of the underlying sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-Exact Convex-Set Operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be an operation on nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional spaces. Write \(\overline C=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian products and Minkowski addition, with explicit boundedness conditions for exact closure of sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) is closure exact at \((C_1,	ext{\ldots},C_m)\) when \[\operatorname{cl}\Phi(C_1,	ext{\ldots},C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{cl}C_1,	ext{\ldots},\operatorname{cl}C_m).\] Cartesian product is always closure exact: \[\operatorname{cl}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1\times\operatorname{cl}C_2.\] Minkowski addition always satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}C_1+	ext{\operatorname{cl}}C_2\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2),\] and it is closure exact when at least one summand is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-set operation is closure exact when closing its inputs before applying the operation gives the same set as closing its output. Cartesian products are always closure exact. Minkowski sums have a general one-sided inclusion and become closure exact when at least one of the two convex summands is bounded.
assumptions_latex: For exactness of Minkowski addition, at least one of \(C_1,C_2\) is bounded.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For Minkowski addition, closure exactness means every limit of sums can be written as a sum of one point from each input closure.
special_cases_latex: If both summands are compact, their sum is compact and hence closed.
If \(C_1\) is bounded and \(C_2\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1+C_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closure calculus for a product followed by addition is exact whenever the boundedness condition is retained at the addition stage.
boundary_notes: The boundedness condition cannot simply be discarded: sums of closed unbounded convex sets may be nonclosed.
Closure exactness is operation- and input-dependent; it is not implied merely by convexity.
The inserted null markers in the displayed tuple notation carry no mathematical meaning and should be removed during normalization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its closed convex hull satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\bigcap\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:S\subseteq K,\ K\text{ is closed and convex}\}.\] Thus \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) is the unique smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of the convex hull of a set is exactly the intersection of all closed convex sets containing it, hence its smallest closed convex superset.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Invariance of Convex Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closing the generators before convexification does not alter the resulting closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cl}S)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is unchanged if the generating set is first replaced by its closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Invariance of Convex Generation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Carathéodory Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional sequential membership form of the closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) if and only if, for every \(m\), there are \(s_{m,0},\ldots,s_{m,n}\in S\) and \(\lambda_{m,i}\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_{m,i}=1\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_{m,i}s_{m,i}\longrightarrow x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed convex hull exactly when it is a limit of convex combinations using at most n+1 generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\iff x\text{ is a limit of convex combinations of at most }n+1\text{ points of }S.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Carathéodory Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and Horizon Cone of a Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides the convex-hull closure formula and its horizon cone under a pointedness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and suppose that \(C^\infty\) is pointed. Then \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{con}C)=\operatorname{con}C+\operatorname{con}C^\infty,\qquad \bigl(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{con}C)\bigr)^\infty=\operatorname{con}C^\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed set C with a pointed horizon cone, the closure of its convex hull equals its convex hull plus the convex hull of its horizon cone. The resulting closed convex hull has exactly that convexified horizon cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of Finite Unions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equality is restricted to finite unions; infinite unions may acquire additional limit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) in a Euclidean space, \[\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i\right)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}A_i.\] For an arbitrary family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\), only \[\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{cl}A_i\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\right)\] is automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure commutes with finite unions, while infinite unions may have additional limit points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(A+B)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}A+\operatorname{cl}B).\] If one summand is compact and the other is closed, then \(A+B\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the summands does not change the closure of their Minkowski sum; compact-plus-closed sums are closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Sets Can Have a Nonclosed Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional failure of closedness under Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\},\qquad V=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.\] Both \(C\) and \(V\) are closed and convex, but \[C+V=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\] is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets can have a nonclosed Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Sets Can Have a Nonclosed Sum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull of a Closed Set Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This demonstrates why the outer closure in the definition of the closed convex hull cannot generally be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\},\qquad S=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(S\) is closed, but for every \(r>0\), \[(r,0)\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\setminus\operatorname{conv}S.\] Hence \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the origin to the closed epigraph of 1/x produces a closed set whose convex hull approaches but does not contain the positive horizontal axis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is closed but }\operatorname{conv}S\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull of a Closed Set Need Not Be Closed

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Images Need Not Preserve Closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional closed-convex counterexample; compactness of the domain set would restore closedness of the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\}\) and let \(L(x,y)=x\). Then \(C\) is closed and convex, whereas \[L(C)=(0,\infty)\] is not closed. Thus \(L(\operatorname{cl}C)\neq\operatorname{cl}(L(C))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Images Need Not Preserve Closedness

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An elementary one-dimensional counterexample showing that closure need not commute with intersection when the compatibility condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(0,1)\) and \(B=(1,2)\). Then \[A\cap B=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{cl}A\cap\operatorname{cl}B=\{1\},\] and consequently \[\operatorname{cl}(A\cap B)=\varnothing\neq\{1\}=\operatorname{cl}A\cap\operatorname{cl}B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure does not generally commute with intersection: the disjoint intervals (0,1) and (1,2) have closures meeting at 1.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncommuting Closure Operations

children.title: Nonclosed Convex-Set Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Attainment, representation, and separation failures caused by missing limit points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Separation Detects Only Points Outside the Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the separation obstruction at an omitted boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle<\alpha\le\langle a,c\rangle\) for every \(c\in C\) if and only if \(x\notin\operatorname{cl}C\). Thus every \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) is a nonmember admitting no strong separator from \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is strongly separable from a convex set exactly when it lies outside the closure; omitted boundary points cannot be strongly separated.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Separation Detects Only Points Outside the Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Attainment Is Determined by Missing Closure Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the exact mechanism by which omitted limit points can destroy attainment without changing an optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+\beta\). Then \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{cl}C}f(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f=C\cap\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{cl}C}f.\] Consequently, if the infimum is attained on \(\operatorname{cl}C\) only at points omitted from \(C\), it is not attained on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a set does not change the infimum of a continuous linear objective, but it can add all of the minimizers and thereby restore attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Attainment Is Determined by Missing Closure Minimizers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Halfspace Hull of a Nonclosed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional representation loss caused by omitted limit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing \(C\) is \(\operatorname{cl}C\). Hence \(C\) is representable exactly as an intersection of closed halfspaces if and only if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-halfspace inequalities cannot distinguish a convex set from its closure and represent the original set exactly precisely when it is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap\{H:H\text{ is a closed halfspace and }C\subseteq H\}=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Halfspace Hull of a Nonclosed Convex Set

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0\) is unattained, and the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing \(C\) equals \([0,1]\neq C\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional example simultaneously exhibiting loss of attainment, loss of exact closed-halfspace representation, and failure of strict separation from a missing boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be given by \(f(x)=x\). Then \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing.\] Moreover, the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing \(C\) is \(\operatorname{cl}C=[0,1]\neq C\). The missing boundary point \(0\) cannot be strictly separated from \(C\), because \(0\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the nonclosed convex interval (0,1), minimizing the linear function x has unattained infimum 0. Closed-halfspace descriptions recover [0,1], not the original set, and the missing endpoint 0 cannot be strictly separated from the interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex-Set Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Missing Boundary and Attained Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, not necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonclosed convex sets and their relative boundary decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative boundary is \[\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Its missing-boundary part and attained-boundary part are respectively \[\operatorname{mbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C,\qquad \operatorname{abd}C=C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Since \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\), these sets form the disjoint decomposition \[\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{abd}C\mathbin{\dot\cup}\operatorname{mbd}C.\] The set is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary of a possibly nonclosed convex set splits into boundary points that belong to the set and missing limit points that do not. The missing boundary is \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\); it is empty exactly when \(C\) is closed. Both types lie outside the relative interior.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in\operatorname{mbd}C\) if and only if \(y\notin C\) and some sequence in \(C\) converges to \(y\).
special_cases_latex: For a relatively open convex set, \(\operatorname{abd}C=\varnothing\), so all relative-boundary points are missing.
For a closed convex set, \(\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing\), so every relative-boundary point is attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: An optimization value approached only through a point of \(\operatorname{mbd}C\) need not be attained over \(C\).
Affine images and sums can create missing boundary points even from closed unbounded convex inputs.
boundary_notes: The decomposition classifies topological membership only; it does not by itself assert existence or nonexistence of an optimizer.
Ambient boundary can be larger than relative boundary for lower-dimensional sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Cone and Lineality Data
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global asymptotic geometry of closed finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic cone geometry of \(C\) is the pair \((C^\infty,\operatorname{lin}_\infty C)\), where \[C^\infty=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\forall x\in C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x+td\in C\}\] and \[\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=C^\infty\cap(-C^\infty).\] The cone \(C^\infty\) records directions retained indefinitely by \(C\), while \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty C\) records two-sided directions along which every point of \(C\) lies on a complete line contained in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global asymptotic geometry of a nonempty closed convex set consists of its recession cone and the lineality subspace inside that cone. A recession direction can be followed indefinitely from every point of the set. A lineality direction and its negative are both recession directions, so entire parallel lines remain in the set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\infty\text{ is a closed convex cone},\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty C=C^\infty\cap(-C^\infty)\text{ is a linear subspace}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{lin}_\infty C\) if and only if \(x+td\in C\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(t\in\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(C^\infty=\{0\}\).
If \(C\) is an affine space \(x_0+L\), then \(C^\infty=\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=L\).
If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^\infty=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(C\) is unbounded exactly when \(C^\infty\) contains a nonzero vector.
The asymptotic cone is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=\{0\}\).
boundary_notes: Closedness is required for the stated closed-cone and unboundedness characterizations.
For nonclosed convex sets, the recession cone may fail to be closed and may fail to detect unboundedness.
This record treats set asymptotics, not recession functions of convex functions.

notation.meaning: asymptotic or recession cone of C
lineality subspace of the asymptotic cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizon cones and half-lines of convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes horizon directions of a nonempty convex set and the half-line geometry of closed convex unbounded sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(\bar x\in C\). Then \(C^\infty\) is convex and
\[
C^\infty=\{w\in\mathbb R^n\mid \bar x+\tau w\in\operatorname{cl}C\text{ for every }\tau\ge 0\}.
\]
If \(C\) is also closed, then \(C\) is unbounded if and only if it contains a half-line \(\bar x+\mathbb R_+w\) for some \(w\ne0\). For every such horizon direction \(w\), one has \(x+\tau w\in C\) for all \(x\in C\) and \(\tau\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon cone of a convex set is convex and consists of the directions whose rays from any point of the set remain in its closure. A closed convex set is unbounded exactly when it contains a nonconstant half-line, and each horizon direction generates a parallel half-line from every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^\infty=\{w\mid \bar x+\tau w\in\operatorname{cl}C\ \forall\tau\ge0\};\quad C\text{ closed}\Rightarrow\left(C\text{ unbounded}\iff\exists w\ne0:\bar x+\mathbb R_+w\subset C\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession cone of a closed convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and boundedness properties for nonempty closed convex sets in finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed. Define \[S_\infty:=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\exists x\in S\text{ such that }x+\tau v\in S\ \forall\tau\ge0\}.\] If \(S\) is convex, then equivalently \[S_\infty=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:x+\tau v\in S\ \forall x\in S,\ \forall\tau\ge0\}.\] In this case \(S_\infty\) is a closed convex cone, every nonzero \(v\in S_\infty\) generates an unbounded ray in \(S\), and \(S\) is bounded if and only if \(S_\infty=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed set, the recession cone consists of directions generating an infinite ray from some point. If the set is convex, the same directions generate rays from every point; the recession cone is then a closed convex cone and is trivial exactly when the set is bounded.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is convex for the all-base-points formula and structural properties}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ closed and convex}\implies S_\infty\text{ is a closed convex cone and }\bigl(S\text{ bounded}\iff S_\infty=\{0\}\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Direction and Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. The basic definition applies without closedness; the one-base-point characterization requires \(C\) to be closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, with closedness explicitly separated from the general definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) is a recession direction of \(C\) when \[x+td\in C\qquad\text{for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\ge0.\] The recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:\forall x\in C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x+td\in C\}.\] If \(C\) is also closed, membership can be tested from one base point: \[d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff\exists x_0	ext{\in}C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x_0+td\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction of a convex set is a direction that can be followed indefinitely from every point without leaving the set. All such directions form the recession cone. For a nonempty closed convex set, it is enough to exhibit one complete ray with base point in the set; the same direction then works from every point.
assumptions_latex: For the one-base-point equivalence and closed-cone conclusions, \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:x+td\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ t\ge0\},\quad d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff\exists x_0\in C\ \forall t\ge0:\ x_0+td\in C\] when \(C\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For closed convex \(C\), any single ray \(x_0+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\) certifies \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\).
The defining condition is equivalently \(C+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\).
special_cases_latex: The zero vector always belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
For a closed halfspace \(C=\{x:a^Tx\le b\}\), \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:a^Td\le0\}\).
For bounded closed convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a closed convex cone.
Such a set is unbounded if and only if its recession cone contains a nonzero direction.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed convex set, one ray from one base point need not certify recession from every point.
An unbounded nonclosed convex set may have no nonzero recession direction.
Recession directions describe infinite rays, not merely feasible infinitesimal directions.
