knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nested closed-convex intersection regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_k\}_{k\geq 0}\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(C_{k+1}\subseteq C_k\). Write \(R_k=\operatorname{rec}(C_k)\), \(L_k=R_k\cap(-R_k)\), \(R=\bigcap_{k\geq0}R_k\), and \(L=\bigcap_{k\geq0}L_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nested sequences are classified by compactness, common recession geometry, and retractiveness. These are sufficient-regime definitions, not an assertion that every nonempty intersection satisfies one of them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence is in the compact regime if some \(C_j\) is bounded. It is in the lineality-balanced regime if \(R=L\). An asymptotic sequence is a sequence \(x_k\in C_k\setminus\{0\}\) for which \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) and \(x_k/\|x_k\|\to d/\|d\|\) for some \(d\in R\setminus\{0\}\). Such a sequence is retractive if \(x_k-d\in C_k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\); the nested family is retractive when every asymptotic sequence is retractive. These conditions define the principal nested closed-set intersection regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing sequence of nonempty closed convex sets is in the compact regime when one member is bounded, and in the lineality-balanced regime when its common recession cone equals its common lineality space. An unbounded selection is asymptotic when its normalized vectors converge to a nonzero common recession direction. It is retractive when subtraction of that direction eventually leaves every selected vector in its corresponding set; the family is retractive if this holds for every asymptotic selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{compact regime: }\exists j\ C_j\text{ bounded};\qquad \text{balanced regime: }R=L;\qquad \text{retractive regime: }\forall\{x_k\}\text{ asymptotic},\ \exists k_0\ \forall k\geq k_0,\ x_k-d\in C_k.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), boundedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{0\}\).
The equality \(R=L\) says that every common recession direction is reversible in every \(C_k\).
special_cases_latex: If some \(C_j\) is compact, then every later \(C_k\) lies in the compact set \(C_j\).
A constant sequence \(C_k=C\) is retractive exactly when the closed convex set \(C\) is retractive in the corresponding single-set sense.
immediate_consequences_latex: A retractive nested sequence has nonempty intersection.
If \(R=L\), then the intersection is nonempty and has the form \(L+K\) for some nonempty compact convex set \(K\).
boundary_notes: Nestedness and closedness are essential to the stated regime terminology.
Retractiveness is sufficient for nonemptiness but is not necessary.
The definition is finite-dimensional; compactness and subsequence arguments require modification in general topological vector spaces.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set.
Lineality space of the kth set.
Common recession cone and common lineality space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Recession-Lineality Conditions for Nested Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes retractivity, intersection existence, compactness modulo common lineality, and the auxiliary-set extension. The accompanying counterexample indicates that retractivity of the auxiliary set cannot generally be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \{C_k\} be a nested sequence of nonempty closed convex sets, and define
\[
R=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}R_{C_k},\qquad L=\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}L_{C_k}.
\]
(a) If R=L, then \{C_k\} is retractive, \(\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}C_k\neq\varnothing\), and there is a nonempty compact set \(\widetilde C\) such that
\[
\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}C_k=L+\widetilde C.
\]
(b) Let X be a retractive closed convex set. If \(\bar C_k=X\cap C_k\neq\varnothing\) for every k and \(R_X\cap R\subset L\), then \(\{\bar C_k\}\) is retractive and
\[
\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}\bar C_k\neq\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the common recession cone of a nested family equals its common lineality space, the family is retractive and its nonempty intersection is compact modulo that lineality space. Intersecting the family with a retractive closed convex set preserves retractivity and nonempty intersection when every component intersection is nonempty and the compatible recession directions lie in the common lineality space. The accompanying construction shows that the retractivity assumption on the auxiliary set is essential in general.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trivial Recession Kernel Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of the seed criterion, not an example of a nonclosed image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness of \(A(C)\) does not imply \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\). For \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and the zero map \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\), \(A(C)=\{0\}\) is closed, while \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The seed's recession-kernel test is sufficient but not necessary: the zero map sends the whole line to a closed singleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Trivial Recession Kernel Is Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality-Relaxed Recession Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A broader finite-dimensional sufficient condition than the seed's trivial-intersection criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, with \(E,F\) finite-dimensional. If \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace, then \(A(C)\) is closed. The seed condition \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) is the zero-subspace special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image is closed when the recession directions annihilated by the map form only reversible lineality; requiring that intersection to be zero is a stronger special case.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Relaxed Recession Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trivial Recession Kernel as Properness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent compact-preimage formulation of the seed's stronger sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear. Then \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) if and only if \(C\cap A^{-1}(K)\) is compact for every compact \(K\subseteq F\). Equivalently, \(A|_C:C\to F\) is proper; consequently \(A(C)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absence of a nonzero kernel recession direction is equivalent to properness of the restricted map and therefore guarantees a closed image.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\iff \forall K\subseteq F\text{ compact},\ C\cap A^{-1}(K)\text{ is compact};\quad A(C)\text{ is closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-regular closedness under a linear map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Put \(R_C=\operatorname{rec}(C)\), \(L_C=R_C\cap(-R_C)\), and \(N(A)=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition isolates a standard finite-dimensional sufficient regime for preservation of closedness. It does not claim that the recession condition is necessary whenever the image happens to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((C,A)\) is recession-regular for closed images if \(R_C\cap N(A)\subseteq L_C\). It is strongly recession-regular if \(R_C\cap N(A)=\{0\}\). The set \(C\) is closed-image stable under \(A\) when \(A(C)\) is closed, equivalently when every convergent sequence \(Ax_j\to y\) with \(x_j\in C\) has a point \(x\in C\) satisfying \(Ax=y\). Recession regularity is the asymptotic criterion defining the canonical guaranteed-closedness regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set and a linear map form a recession-regular pair when every recession direction annihilated by the map is a lineality direction of the set. Strong regularity requires the only annihilated recession direction to be zero. Closed-image stability means that the linear image is closed, or equivalently that every limit of image points has a preimage in the set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(A(C)\text{ is closed}\iff \forall (x_j)\subset C,\ Ax_j\to y\Rightarrow \exists x\in C:\ Ax=y.\)
The condition \(R_C\cap\ker A\subseteq L_C\) means that no irreversible escape direction of \(C\) is collapsed to zero by \(A\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(R_C=\{0\}\), so \(A(C)\) is compact and closed.
If \(A\) is injective, then \(\ker A=\{0\}\), so strong recession regularity holds.
The image of a polyhedral convex set under any linear map is polyhedral and hence closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under recession regularity, \(\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(R_C)\).
The stronger condition \(R_C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) is an immediately checkable sufficient criterion.
boundary_notes: A continuous linear image of an arbitrary closed set need not be closed.
For nonclosed or nonconvex domains, the recession criterion in this form does not apply.
Failure of recession regularity signals possible degeneracy but does not by itself force nonclosedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness of a Linear Image Under a Recession-Lineality Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional closedness and recession-cone criterion for a linear image of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty and convex, and let A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be linear. Suppose every nonzero z\in 0^+(\operatorname{cl}C) satisfying Az=0 belongs to \operatorname{lin}(\operatorname{cl}C). Then \operatorname{cl}(AC)=A(\operatorname{cl}C) and 0^+\!\left(A(\operatorname{cl}C)\right)=A\left(0^+(\operatorname{cl}C)\right). In particular, if C is closed and 0^+C\cap\ker A=\{0\}, then AC is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty convex set, closure commutes with a linear image and the recession cone of the image is the image of the original recession cone when every nonzero recession direction annihilated by the map is a lineality direction. If the set is closed and its recession cone meets the kernel only at zero, its image is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(AC)=A(\operatorname{cl}C),\qquad 0^+\!\left(A(\operatorname{cl}C)\right)=A\left(0^+(\operatorname{cl}C)\right);\qquad C\text{ closed and }0^+C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\implies AC\text{ closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Witnesses of Nonclosed Linear Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary escape behavior of preimages approaching a missing image point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, where \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. If \(x_k\in C\), \(Ax_k\to z\), and \(z\notin A(C)\), then \((x_k)\) is unbounded. For any \(c\in C\), every convergent subsequence of \((x_k-c)/\|x_k-c\|\) has a unit limit \(d\in C^\infty\cap\ker A\). Conversely, nonclosedness of \(A(C)\) supplies such a sequence for some \(z\in\overline{A(C)}\setminus A(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing image limit can only be approached through unbounded preimages, whose normalized escape directions yield nonzero recession directions annihilated by the map.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Missing image limits have unbounded preimage witnesses with unit cluster directions in \(C^\infty\cap\ker A\).

Define
\[A\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{smallmatrix}\right)=(a,b).\]

\[A(\mathbb S_+^2)=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\]
This image is not closed because \((1/j,1)\) belongs to it for every positive integer \(j\), whereas its limit \((0,1)\) does not.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial-extremal representation hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A segment is written \([x,y]=\{(1-t)x+ty:0\leq t\leq1\}\), and its relative interior is obtained by requiring \(0<t<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hierarchy combines the standard finite-dimensional notions of faces, exposed faces, extreme points and directions, and their internal representation roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex subset \(F\subseteq C\) is a face if \((1-t)x+ty\in F\), with \(x,y\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(x,y\in F\). It is exposed if \(F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\) for some nonzero \(a\), whenever the maximum is attained. A singleton face is an extreme point; a half-line face determines an extreme direction. Thus exposed points and directions lie within the corresponding extreme classes, and the extremal classes form the minimal generators used in finite-dimensional representation theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is a convex subset that contains both endpoints of every segment of the ambient convex set whose relative interior meets it. An exposed face is the maximizer set of a nonzero linear functional. Singleton faces are extreme points, while half-line faces define extreme directions. Exposed points and directions are therefore special extreme structures, and extreme structures provide the canonical internal generators of closed convex sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in C\) is extreme iff \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), \(y,z\in C\), and \(0<t<1\) imply \(y=z=x\).
A proper exposed face has the form \(C\cap H\), where \(H\) is a nontrivial supporting hyperplane of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed and bounded, then \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{Ext}(C))\).
If \(C\) is closed and contains no lines, it is generated by its extreme points and extreme directions.
For a pointed closed convex cone, the directional extremal objects are its extreme rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed point is extreme, but an extreme point need not be exposed.
Every face inherits its own facial-extremal hierarchy, and its extreme points and directions remain extreme in \(C\).
boundary_notes: The empty set and \(C\) are included as improper faces.
An exposing functional may define an empty maximizer set when its supremum is not attained.
Lineality can eliminate extreme points and extreme directions from an unbounded convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces and facial depth
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set, and let \(\mathcal F(C)\) denote all faces of \(C\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats the facial hierarchy as the inclusion-ordered boundary structure of a finite-dimensional convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\) is a convex subset \(F\subseteq C\) such that \((1-t)x+ty\in F\), where \(x,y\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(x,y\in F\). A proper face satisfies \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(F\neq C\). A facial chain is a strictly increasing sequence \(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r\) in \(\mathcal F(C)\). Its length and the dimensions of its members measure facial depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is a convex subset that cannot contain an interior point of a segment from the ambient set without also containing both endpoints. The empty face and the entire convex set are improper faces; every other nonempty face is proper. Faces ordered by inclusion form the facial hierarchy, and a facial chain records successively larger boundary strata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\iff F\subseteq C,\ F\text{ convex},\ \forall x,y\in C\ \forall t\in(0,1),\ (1-t)x+ty\in F\Rightarrow x,y\in F.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex subset \(F\subseteq C\) is a face iff every closed segment in \(C\) whose relative interior meets \(F\) has both endpoints in \(F\).
For every proper face \(F\), one has \(F\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}(C)\) and \(\dim F<\dim C\).
special_cases_latex: A zero-dimensional nonempty face is an extreme point.
A codimension-one proper face is commonly called a facet.
A half-line face determines an extreme direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(G\) is a face of \(F\) and \(F\) is a face of \(C\), then \(G\) is a face of \(C\).
Every strictly decreasing chain of faces is finite in finite dimensions.
boundary_notes: Faces need not be exposed by a single supporting functional.
For a nonclosed convex set, a face need not be closed in the ambient space, though it is relatively closed in the stated sense \(F=C\cap\operatorname{cl}F\).
The codimension-one term facet is relative to the affine dimension of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Family of all faces of the convex set.
Relative boundary of the convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial classes and the minimal face of a set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set and \(S\subseteq C\). Let \(\mathcal F(C)\) be its family of faces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition organizes standard facial classes by dimension and defines the smallest facial container of a point or subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimal face of \(C\) containing \(S\) is \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\bigcap\{F\in\mathcal F(C):S\subseteq F\}\). For a point \(x\in C\), write \(F_C(x)=\operatorname{face}_C(\{x\})\). The facial classes comprise the improper faces \(\varnothing,C\), proper faces, extreme-point faces \(\{x\}\), half-line faces defining extreme directions, and facets satisfying \(\dim F=\dim C-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest face containing a subset is the intersection of all faces that contain it. For one point this is its minimal face. Faces are classified as improper, proper, singleton extreme-point faces, half-line faces giving extreme directions, or facets of relative codimension one. These classes locate a point or constraint set at its smallest facial level.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_C(x)\) is the unique face \(F\) whose relative interior contains \(x\).
A point \(x\) is extreme iff \(F_C(x)=\{x\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(C)\), then \(F_C(x)=C\).
If \(x\) lies in the relative interior of a facet \(F\), then \(F_C(x)=F\).
For \(S=\varnothing\), the intersection definition gives the least face \(\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(S\subseteq T\subseteq C\), then \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_C(T)\).
A face \(F\) contains \(S\) iff it contains \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\).
boundary_notes: A facet need not be exposed for an arbitrary convex set, although facets of polyhedral convex sets are exposed.
Half-line faces concern unbounded convex sets; extreme rays are the conic specialization.
The affine dimension of \(C\), not the dimension of the containing Euclidean space, determines facets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\subseteq F.\] Hence \(S\subseteq T\) implies \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_C(T)\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the ambient convex set containing the specified subset.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal containment property and monotonicity of the minimal-face operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every face \(F\) of \(C\),
\[\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\subseteq F.\]
Consequently, the minimal-face operator is monotone:
\[S\subseteq T\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{face}_C(S)\subseteq\operatorname{face}_C(T).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face generated by S lies in a face F exactly when S lies in F. In particular, enlarging the generating subset can only enlarge its minimal face.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Containment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The containment equivalence and monotonicity are correct properties of the minimal-face operator and match the leaf, but they lack source support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Hull Invariance of Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an algebraic containment property of the minimal-face operator, not a redefinition of minimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and \(S\subseteq C\). Since every face of \(C\) is convex, a face contains \(S\) if and only if it contains \(\operatorname{conv}S\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\operatorname{face}_C(\operatorname{conv}S).\] More generally, for \(S,T\subseteq C\), \[\operatorname{face}_C(S\cup T)=\operatorname{face}_C\bigl(\operatorname{face}_C(S)\cup\operatorname{face}_C(T)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generating a minimal face is unchanged by first taking the convex hull. The minimal face generated jointly by two subsets is also the minimal face generated by their individual minimal faces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension Growth Along Face Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension means affine dimension. Strict inclusion and nonemptiness are essential; no dimension convention for the empty face is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\subsetneq G\) are nonempty faces of a finite-dimensional convex set \(C\), then \[\operatorname{aff}F\subsetneq\operatorname{aff}G\quad\text{and hence}\quad \dim F<\dim G.\] Consequently, every strictly increasing chain of nonempty faces contains at most \(\dim C+1\) faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper inclusion of nonempty faces strictly increases affine dimension, so a chain has at most one face of each possible dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(F\) and \(G\) are nonempty faces of \(C\) with \(F\subsetneq G\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces of a Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This includes the empty face when that convention is adopted and identifies the lower interval below \(G\) with the face family of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a face of a convex set \(C\). For every \(F\subseteq G\), \[F\text{ is a face of }G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\text{ is a face of }C.\] Thus the faces below \(G\) in the inclusion order are exactly the faces of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of a face G is a face of G exactly when it is a face of the ambient convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(G\) is a face of \(C\), and \(F\subseteq G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is a face of }G\Longleftrightarrow F\text{ is a face of }C\).

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(\mathcal F(C)\) denotes all faces of \(C\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(C\).

notation.meaning: Family of all faces of the convex set.
Meet and join in the face-inclusion order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The face family is ordered by inclusion; the stated formulas include arbitrary indexed families with the usual empty-family conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Ordered by inclusion, \(\mathcal F(C)\) is a complete lattice. For every family \((F_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq\mathcal F(C)\),
\[\bigwedge_{i\in I}F_i=\bigcap_{i\in I}F_i,\qquad \bigvee_{i\in I}F_i=\operatorname{face}_C\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}F_i\right).\]
In particular, \(\varnothing\) is the least face and \(C\) is the greatest face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces ordered by inclusion form a complete lattice. The meet is intersection, and the join is the minimal face containing the union. The empty face is least and the whole set is greatest.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Inclusion Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The face family forms a complete lattice with the stated meet and join formulas when the declared empty-face and empty-family conventions are used. The property content kind fits, but an exact source is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete lattice of faces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and order \(\mathcal F(C)\) by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition captures incidence and containment among faces through their finite-dimensional complete-lattice structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any family \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal F(C)\), its meet is \(\bigwedge\mathcal A=\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal A}F\). Its join is the least face containing their union, \(\bigvee\mathcal A=\operatorname{face}_C(\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal A}F)\). With least element \(\varnothing\) and greatest element \(C\), these operations make \((\mathcal F(C),\subseteq)\) the face-inclusion lattice. Incidence means simply \(F\subseteq G\) for two faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces are ordered by inclusion. The greatest lower bound of any family is its intersection, while the least upper bound is the smallest face containing its union. The empty face and the whole set are respectively the least and greatest elements. This complete lattice is the canonical face-incidence structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigwedge\mathcal A=\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal A}F,\qquad \bigvee\mathcal A=\bigcap\{G\in\mathcal F(C):\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal A}F\subseteq G\}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\subseteq G\) is equivalent to saying that \(F\) is a face of the intermediate convex set \(G\).
For two faces, \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\) and \(F\vee G=\operatorname{face}_C(F\cup G)\).
special_cases_latex: The meet of the empty family is \(C\), and the join of the empty family is \(\varnothing\).
If \(F\subseteq G\), then \(F\wedge G=F\) and \(F\vee G=G\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Arbitrary intersections of faces are faces.
If \(H\) is a face of \(F\) and \(F\) is a face of \(C\), then \(H\in\mathcal F(C)\).
Every inclusion chain has well-defined infimum and supremum in \(\mathcal F(C)\).
boundary_notes: The face lattice need not be distributive.
The join is generally larger than the set-theoretic union, which need not be convex.
Strict face inclusion forces a dimension increase between nonempty faces in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: Meet and join in the inclusion-ordered face lattice.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\ne\varnothing}(C)\) be the family of nonempty faces of \(C\). For \(x\in C\), define the minimal face \[F_C(x):=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a face of }C\text{ and }x\in F\}.\] Then \(F_C(x)\) is a face, \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_C(x)\), and it is the unique face whose relative interior contains \(x\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-interior facial stratification
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set. For each nonempty face \(F\), take its relative interior \(\operatorname{ri}(F)\) in \(\operatorname{aff}(F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strata are relative interiors of all nonempty faces; no smooth-manifold or Whitney regularity is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial relative-interior stratification of \(C\) is \(\mathscr S(C)=\{\operatorname{ri}(F):F\in\mathcal F(C),\ F\neq\varnothing\}\). It is a partition: \(C=\bigsqcup_{F\neq\varnothing}\operatorname{ri}(F)\). Equivalently, every \(x\in C\) belongs to the relative interior of a unique face, namely its minimal face \(F_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The facial strata of a convex set are the relative interiors of its nonempty faces. These sets are pairwise disjoint and cover the convex set. Thus every point lies in exactly one stratum, which is the relative interior of its minimal face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Define \(x\sim y\) when \(x=y\) or some segment in \(C\) contains both \(x\) and \(y\) in its relative interior; the equivalence classes are precisely the sets \(\operatorname{ri}(F)\).
The strata are the maximal relatively open convex subsets of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: The top stratum is \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\).
Each extreme point forms a zero-dimensional stratum \(\{x\}\).
For a polytope, the strata are the relative interiors of all vertices, edges, higher-dimensional proper faces, and the polytope itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two faces with intersecting relative interiors are equal.
For every \(x\in C\), the closure of its stratum relative to \(C\) is the minimal face \(F_C(x)\) when that face is closed.
A relatively open convex subset of \(C\) lies in a single facial stratum.
boundary_notes: Different faces may intersect along lower-dimensional faces, but their relative interiors do not intersect.
This partition is finite only when \(C\) has finitely many faces.
Relative interior is taken in each face's own affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partition by relative interiors of faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial relative-interior stratification and the characterization of its strata as maximal relatively open convex subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C be a nonempty convex set and let \mathcal U=\{\operatorname{ri}F:F\text{ is a nonempty face of }C\}. Then the members of \mathcal U are pairwise disjoint and their union is C. Every relatively open convex subset D\subseteq C is contained in a member of \mathcal U, and the members of \mathcal U are precisely the maximal relatively open convex subsets of C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interiors of the nonempty faces of a nonempty convex set form a partition of the set. Every relatively open convex subset lies in one such stratum, and these strata are exactly the maximal relatively open convex subsets.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a nonempty convex set.}
\mathcal U=\{\operatorname{ri}F:F\text{ is a nonempty face of }C\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=\bigsqcup_{U\in\mathcal U}U,\qquad \forall D\subseteq C\;\bigl(D\text{ is convex and relatively open}\Rightarrow\exists U\in\mathcal U\;D\subseteq U\bigr),\qquad \mathcal U\text{ is the family of maximal relatively open convex subsets of }C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary facial construction calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(\mathcal F(C)\) be its faces, and let \(h_a(x)=\langle a,x\rangle\) be a linear functional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The calculus consists of source-supported operations that construct faces from intersections, nested faces, intermediate convex sets, and supporting functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The elementary facial construction operations are: \(\bigcap_iF_i\in\mathcal F(C)\) for any family \(F_i\in\mathcal F(C)\); transitivity, whereby \(G\in\mathcal F(F)\) and \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\) imply \(G\in\mathcal F(C)\); restriction, whereby \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\) and \(F\subseteq D\subseteq C\) with \(D\) convex imply \(F\in\mathcal F(D)\); and exposure, whereby a nonempty maximizer set \(F_a=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\) is an exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces may be constructed by arbitrary intersections, by taking faces of existing faces, by restricting an existing face to an intermediate convex set, and by maximizing a linear functional. These operations form the elementary facial construction calculus and preserve the endpoint property that defines a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_i\unlhd C\Rightarrow\bigcap_iF_i\unlhd C;\quad G\unlhd F\unlhd C\Rightarrow G\unlhd C;\quad F\unlhd C,\ F\subseteq D\subseteq C\Rightarrow F\unlhd D;\quad F_a\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow F_a\unlhd C.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The smallest face containing \(S\subseteq C\) is produced by intersection: \(\operatorname{face}_C(S)=\bigcap\{F\unlhd C:S\subseteq F\}\).
A proper exposed face is the intersection of \(C\) with a nontrivial supporting hyperplane.
special_cases_latex: If \(F\) is exposed in \(C\) and \(F\subseteq D\subseteq C\), then \(F\) is exposed in \(D\).
An extreme point of a face is an extreme point of the ambient convex set.
For finitely many faces, their intersection may be empty, which is still a face.
immediate_consequences_latex: The face family is closed under arbitrary meets.
Facial chains can be built recursively without losing facial status in the original set.
Linear optimization supplies a direct construction of exposed faces.
boundary_notes: An exposed face of a face need not be exposed in the original set.
Set unions and Minkowski sums do not generally preserve faces without additional hypotheses.
The symbol \(\unlhd\) is local shorthand for the face relation, not an order on arbitrary subsets.

notation.meaning: The set is a face of the ambient convex set.
Maximizer set of the functional indexed by the vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial Reflection and Invariants Under Affine Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This supplements forward face preservation with reflection, exposed-face correspondence, and dimension preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine with \(A|_C\) injective. For every \(G\subseteq A(C)\), \[G\text{ is a face of }A(C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (A|_C)^{-1}(G)\text{ is a face of }C.\] Together with forward image preservation, \(F\mapsto A(F)\) is an inclusion-preserving bijection between the face lattices of \(C\) and \(A(C)\). It preserves and reflects exposed faces, and for every face \(F\) of \(C\), \[\dim A(F)=\dim F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine embedding induces an order isomorphism of face lattices. It preserves and reflects exposed faces and preserves every face's relative dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is affine and injective on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto A(F)\) is a face-lattice isomorphism from \(C\) to \(A(C)\), preserving exposedness and dimension.

notation.meaning: Inverse image of G under the bijection from C onto A(C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed Faces Under Affine Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This supplements the deferred face-preservation statement with preservation and reflection of exposedness and relative dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine with \(A|_C\) injective. Then a subset \(F\subseteq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\) if and only if \(A(F)\) is an exposed face of \(A(C)\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}A(C)\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine embedding preserves and reflects exposed faces, and it preserves the relative dimension of every face.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed Faces Pull Back to Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-preimage preservation of exposed facial structure relative to the original convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(A(x)=Lx+b\) be affine, and let
\[
G=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in A(C)}\langle u,y\rangle
\]
be a nonempty exposed face of \(A(C)\). Then
\[
C\cap A^{-1}(G)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle L^*u,x\rangle,
\]
so the relative preimage is an exposed face of \(C\). It equals \(C\) if and only if \(x\mapsto\langle L^*u,x\rangle\) is constant on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preimage inside C of an exposed face of its affine image is exposed by the adjoint-pulled functional.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the nonempty face of \(A(C)\) exposed by \(u\).

notation.meaning: adjoint of the linear part of A
exposed face of the affine image

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face-Lattice Correspondence for Affine Preimages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-preserving correspondence between image faces and affine-fiber-saturated faces of the original convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine. Call a face \(F\unlhd C\) \(A\)-saturated when
\[
F=C\cap A^{-1}(A(F)).
\]
Then
\[
G\longmapsto C\cap A^{-1}(G)
\]
is an inclusion-preserving bijection from the nonempty faces of \(A(C)\) onto the nonempty \(A\)-saturated faces of \(C\). Its inverse is \(F\mapsto A(F)\). Consequently, for every nonempty face \(G\unlhd A(C)\),
\[
A\bigl(C\cap A^{-1}(G)\bigr)=G.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of an affine image correspond exactly to faces of the original set that contain every feasible point in each affine fiber they meet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maps \(G\mapsto C\cap A^{-1}(G)\) and \(F\mapsto A(F)\) are inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between nonempty faces of \(A(C)\) and nonempty \(A\)-saturated faces of \(C\).

notation.meaning: F is a face of C

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Correspondence for Affine Preimages

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a face of \(A(C)\), and \(C\cap A^{-1}(G)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: A face of the image A(C).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The relative preimage is taken inside the original convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine. If \(G\) is a face of \(A(C)\) and \(C\cap A^{-1}(G)\neq\varnothing\), then \[C\cap A^{-1}(G)\] is a face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preimage inside a convex set of a face of its affine image is itself a face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=[-1,1]^2,\qquad T(x,y)=x.\] The distinct singleton faces \(F_+=\{(1,1)\}\) and \(F_-=\{(1,-1)\}\) satisfy \[T(F_+)=T(F_-)=\{1\}.\] Thus a noninjective affine map can merge distinct faces, even though their common image remains a face of \(T(C)=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of a square onto one coordinate sends two distinct vertex faces to the same endpoint face, merging their facial identities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distinct faces \(F_+\) and \(F_-\) have the same image \(\{1\}\).

notation.meaning: The upper-right and lower-right vertex faces of the square.

knowledge_statements.title: Merger of Distinct Faces Under Projection

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face \(F=\{(0,1)\}\) satisfies \(A(F)=\{0\}\), but \(\{0\}\) is not a face of \(A(C)=[-1,1]\).

notation.meaning: The top vertex, which is a face of C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional example isolates the loss of facial structure caused by a noninjective affine projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \[C:=\operatorname{conv}\{(-1,0),(0,1),(1,0)\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2,\qquad A(x,y):=x.\] The singleton \(F:=\{(0,1)\}\) is an exposed face of \(C\), while \[A(C)=[-1,1]\qquad\text{and}\qquad A(F)=\{0\}.\] Since \(0=\tfrac12(-1)+\tfrac12(1)\) but neither endpoint belongs to \(\{0\}\), the set \(A(F)\) is not a face of \(A(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a triangle onto its horizontal axis sends its top-vertex face to the interior point zero of an interval. Thus a noninjective affine map need not preserve faces.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial Collapse Under Noninjective Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit projection example is correct, and counterexample is the exact mathematical role for this failure leaf. Nevertheless, no evidence accompanies the record.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Saturation Criterion for Preservation of a Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This valid criterion is deferred because its canonical home is the positive forward-image calculus sibling, not this failure-boundary leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine, and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(C\). Define \(\operatorname{sat}_T(F):=C\cap T^{-1}(T(F))\). Then \[T(F)\text{ is a face of }T(C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{sat}_T(F)\text{ is a face of }C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face has a facial image exactly when the union within C of all affine fibers meeting that face is itself a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(F)\) is a face of \(T(C)\) if and only if \(C\cap T^{-1}(T(F))\) is a face of \(C\).

notation.meaning: The portion of C in all affine fibers whose images meet F.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Saturation Criterion for Preservation of a Face

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory consists of examples of the two rank-deficient failure modes: a face may map to a nonface, and distinct faces may merge. The proposed saturation equivalence is mathematically sound but deferred as canonically belonging to Faces Under Affine Images; positive image and inverse-image calculus are excluded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed faces, points, and directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Its support function is \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\), possibly taking the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposure is defined by attainment of a finite supporting value of a nonzero linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\neq0\) with \(\sigma_C(a)<+\infty\) and attained, the exposed face selected by \(a\) is \(F_C(a)=\{x\in C:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\). An exposed point is a point \(x\) for which \(F_C(a)=\{x\}\) for some \(a\neq0\). An exposed direction is the direction of an exposed half-line face; for a cone, such a half-line face is an exposed ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero linear functional exposes the set of points where it attains its finite maximum over a convex set. That maximizer set is an exposed face. If it consists of one point, that point is exposed; if it is a half-line face, its direction is exposed. For cones, exposed half-lines are exposed rays.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper nonempty subset \(F\) is an exposed face iff \(F=C\cap H\) for a nontrivial supporting hyperplane \(H\) of \(C\).
A point \(x\) is exposed iff some supporting hyperplane through \(x\) contains no other point of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: For a compact convex set, \(F_C(a)\) is nonempty for every \(a\neq0\).
For a polytope, every nonempty face is exposed.
For a closed pointed cone, exposed rays are exposed directional faces.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is a face.
Every exposed point is an extreme point, and every exposed direction is an extreme direction.
Positive rescaling of the exposing vector does not change the exposed face: \(F_C(\lambda a)=F_C(a)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
boundary_notes: A supremum that is infinite or unattained does not define a nonempty exposed face.
Different functionals may expose the same face.
Not every face or extreme point is exposed.

notation.meaning: Support function of the convex set.
Face exposed by the linear functional with normal vector a.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Intersection Closure of Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The intersection must be nonempty; a proper intersection is exposed by the sum of the exposing directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \[F_i=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u_i,x\rangle\] be nonempty contact sets with \(\sigma_C(u_i)<+\infty\). If \(F:=\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i\neq\varnothing\), then \[F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^m u_i,x\right\rangle.\] Thus every nonempty proper finite intersection of exposed faces is exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite intersection of exposed faces is exposed by the sum of their exposing directions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is a nonempty contact set with finite support value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle\sum_i u_i,x\rangle\); a proper such intersection is exposed.

notation.meaning: Contact set exposed by direction u_i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additivity of maximizing faces in a fixed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty convex compact sets. For every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the maximizing face of their Minkowski sum satisfies $G_x(U+V)=G_x(U)+G_x(V)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The face of a Minkowski sum exposed by a direction equals the Minkowski sum of the faces of the summands exposed by that same direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed Face of a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the face exposed by a direction, including the zero-direction convention and possible emptiness for unbounded sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, with support function \(\sigma_S\). For \(d\neq0\), define \[F_S(d):=\{s\in S:\langle s,d\rangle=\sigma_S(d)\}.\] This is the face of \(S\) exposed by \(d\). By convention, \(F_S(0):=S\). When \(S\) is unbounded, a direction may expose no face, so \(F_S(d)\) may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The face exposed by a nonzero direction consists of the points attaining the support value in that direction. The zero direction conventionally exposes the whole set. For an unbounded set, some directions may expose no face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_S(d)=\{s\in S:\langle s,d\rangle=\sigma_S(d)\}\) for \(d\neq0\), with \(F_S(0)=S\), and \(F_S(d)\) may be empty in the unbounded-set regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed Faces and Exposed Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty contact sets of supporting hyperplanes and their singleton specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty subset \(F\subseteq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if there exists a supporting hyperplane \(H_{s,r}\) of \(C\) such that \(F=C\cap H_{s,r}\). An exposed point is a point \(x\in C\) for which some supporting hyperplane satisfies \(C\cap H_{s,r}=\{x\}\); equivalently, \(\{x\}\) is a zero-dimensional exposed face. In the source's terminology, an exposed point is also called a vertex. Every exposed face is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed face is a nonempty contact set of a supporting hyperplane. An exposed point is a singleton contact set, hence a zero-dimensional exposed face; the source also calls it a vertex. Exposed faces are convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is exposed}\iff\exists H_{s,r}\text{ supporting }C:\ F=C\cap H_{s,r};\qquad x\text{ is exposed}\iff\exists H_{s,r}\text{ supporting }C:\ C\cap H_{s,r}=\{x\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support, exposure, and extremality hierarchy for points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(x\in C\). For \(a\neq0\), write \(F_C(a)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle\) when the maximum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hierarchy distinguishes boundary points touched by a supporting hyperplane from points uniquely selected by one and from segment-indecomposable points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The point \(x\) is a support point if \(x\in F_C(a)\) for some \(a\neq0\); it is an exposed point if \(F_C(a)=\{x\}\) for some \(a\neq0\); and it is an extreme point if \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), with \(y,z\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(y=z=x\). Hence \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C)\subseteq C\), while support points need not be extreme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support point lies on a supporting hyperplane. An exposed point is the unique point of the set on some supporting hyperplane. An extreme point cannot be expressed as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points of the set. Every exposed point is extreme and supported, whereas a supported point may lie in a positive-dimensional face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ exposed}\Rightarrow x\text{ extreme and supported};\qquad x\text{ supported}\iff\exists a\neq0:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)<+\infty.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\) is exposed iff a nontrivial supporting hyperplane intersects \(C\) exactly in \(\{x\}\).
\(x\) is extreme iff \(\{x\}\) is a face of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: Every relative-boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set admits a supporting hyperplane, although it need not be exposed.
Every vertex of a polytope is exposed.
A point in \(\operatorname{ri}(C)\) is not a support point unless \(C\) lies in a proper affine hyperplane and the functional is constant on \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An exposing functional supplies a strict linear preference for \(x\) over every other point of \(C\).
A support point belongs to the exposed face determined by its supporting functional.
The set of exposed points may be strictly smaller than the set of extreme points.
boundary_notes: Support is understood relative to a nonzero functional and a finite attained support value.
A supporting hyperplane may contain an entire edge or higher-dimensional face.
For nonclosed sets, boundary support and attainment require separate verification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Points Are Exactly Included Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary means ambient Euclidean boundary. Under the seed's convention, a supporting hyperplane may contain an entire lower-dimensional convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Then \[\{x\in C:x\text{ is a support point of }C\}=C\cap\operatorname{bd}C.\] In particular, if \(\operatorname{aff}C\neq\mathbb{R}^n\), then every point of \(C\) is a support point in the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Point and Supporting Hyperplane
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines support points and their nonzero normal vectors for arbitrary nonempty subsets of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, let \(x\in C\), and let \(u\in\mathcal H\setminus\{0\}\). If \(\sup_{y\in C}\langle y,u\rangle\leq\langle x,u\rangle\), then \(\{y\in\mathcal H\mid\langle y,u\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(C\) at \(x\), and \(x\) is a support point of \(C\) with normal vector \(u\). The support-point set is denoted by \(\operatorname{spts}C\), and its closure by \(\overline{\operatorname{spts}C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point x in a nonempty set C is a support point with nonzero normal u when the linear functional defined by u is maximized over C at x. Its equality level set is a supporting hyperplane at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{y\in\mathcal H\mid\langle y,u\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle\}\text{ supports }C\text{ at }x,\quad x\in\operatorname{spts}C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonexposed faces and extreme points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\), and let \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposure failure is defined relative to selection by one supporting functional; it does not mean that the face lacks supporting hyperplanes altogether.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face \(F\) is nonexposed if there is no \(a\neq0\) such that \(F=\{x\in C:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\). An extreme point \(x\) is nonexposed if \(\{x\}\) is a face but no nonzero linear functional has \(x\) as its unique maximizer on \(C\). The exposure-failure boundary is the class \(\mathcal F(C)\setminus\mathcal F_{\mathrm{exp}}(C)\), particularly \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\) at the point level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is nonexposed when no single nonzero linear functional selects exactly that face as its maximizer set. An extreme point is nonexposed when it is a singleton face but is never the unique maximizer of a linear functional. These objects form the boundary between facial extremality and functional exposure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ nonexposed}\iff F\in\mathcal F(C)\ \text{and}\ \forall a\neq0,\ F\neq\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in C}\langle a,z\rangle;\quad x\text{ nonexposed extreme}\iff x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\setminus\operatorname{ExpPt}(C).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: An extreme point \(x\) is nonexposed iff every supporting hyperplane through \(x\) contains another point of \(C\).
A face is exposed exactly when it is the intersection of \(C\) with a single nontrivial supporting hyperplane; failure of every such representation is nonexposure.
special_cases_latex: Every face of a polyhedral convex set is exposed, so its exposure-failure class is empty.
A positive-dimensional exposed face may contain extreme points of \(C\) that are not exposed in \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonexposed extreme point remains extreme despite the failure of unique linear selection.
For a closed convex set in finite dimensions, nonexposed extreme points can be approximated by exposed points.
Exposure of a face does not imply that all faces contained in it are exposed in the ambient set.
boundary_notes: The whole set and empty face require conventions and are excluded from the usual proper-face exposure comparison.
Nonuniqueness of an exposing functional is not exposure failure; only nonexistence matters.
Nonexposure is ambient-set dependent: a point may be exposed in a face but not in the whole set.

notation.meaning: Family of exposed faces of the convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme points, directions, and rays
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. When \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a convex cone, write \(\mathbb R_+d=\{\lambda d:\lambda\geq0\}\) for \(d\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point extremality concerns indecomposable locations, while ray extremality concerns indecomposable conic directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in C\) is extreme if \(x=(1-t)y+tz\), with \(y,z\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), implies \(y=z=x\). A half-line face of \(C\) determines an extreme direction. For a convex cone \(K\), the ray \(\mathbb R_+d\) is extreme if it is a face of \(K\); equivalently, \(u,v\in K\) and \(u+v\in\mathbb R_+d\) imply \(u,v\in\mathbb R_+d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point cannot be split as a nontrivial convex combination of distinct points. An extreme direction is the direction of a half-line face. In a convex cone, an extreme ray is a one-dimensional face; equivalently, any two cone vectors whose sum lies on that ray must themselves lie on the ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\iff \{x\}\unlhd C;\qquad \mathbb R_+d\text{ extreme in }K\iff \mathbb R_+d\unlhd K\iff [u,v\in K,\ u+v\in\mathbb R_+d\Rightarrow u,v\in\mathbb R_+d].\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\) is extreme iff it lies in no open segment joining two distinct points of \(C\).
A nonzero \(d\in K\) generates an extreme ray iff every decomposition \(d=u+v\) with \(u,v\in K\) has \(u\) and \(v\) nonnegative scalar multiples of \(d\).
special_cases_latex: The origin is the only possible extreme point of a nontrivial convex cone.
For a pointed polyhedral cone, its one-dimensional faces are exactly its extreme rays.
A closed bounded convex set has extreme points but no extreme directions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Extreme points are precisely the zero-dimensional nonempty faces.
Extreme rays are invariant under positive rescaling of their generators.
Extreme directions of a closed convex set are also extreme directions of its recession cone, though the converse may fail.
boundary_notes: A cone containing a line has no extreme rays along that line in the pointed sense.
A recession direction need not determine a half-line face and hence need not be extreme.
Ray extremality concerns the ray, not a particular normalized generator.

notation.meaning: Closed ray generated by a nonzero vector.

Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\). A point \(x\in C\) is an extreme point of \(C\) when, for all \(y,z\in C\) and \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[
x=(1-t)y+tz\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=z=x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Tests for an Extreme Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These algebraic equivalences require neither topology nor finite dimensionality. The empty set is convex in the deletion formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space and let \(x\in C\). The following are equivalent: \[x\in\operatorname{ext}C;\] \[x=\frac{y+z}{2},\quad y,z\in C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=z=x;\] \[\{x\}\text{ is a face of }C;\] and \[C\setminus\{x\}\text{ is convex}.\] They are also equivalent to finite-combination rigidity: if \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\), where \(x_i\in C\), \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\), then \(x_i=x\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is extreme exactly when it passes the midpoint test, its singleton is a face, deleting it leaves a convex set, or each positive finite convex representation of it is trivial.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{ext}C\iff\{x\}\text{ is a face of }C\iff C\setminus\{x\}\text{ is convex}, with equivalent midpoint and finite-combination tests.

notation.meaning: set of extreme points of C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dubins theorem for hyperplane sections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point representation for a compact convex set intersected with finitely many hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}_0\), let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be closed, bounded, and convex, and let \(L=K\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^n H_j\), where each \(H_j\) is a hyperplane. Every extreme point of \(L\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) extreme points of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of a section of a compact convex set by n hyperplanes is a convex combination of at most n plus one extreme points of the original set.
assumptions_latex: K\subset\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is closed, bounded, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\operatorname{ext}(L),\ \exists m\leq n+1,\ e_i\in\operatorname{ext}(K),\ \lambda_i\geq0:\quad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i e_i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generator-Relative Criterion for an Extreme Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the extract's finite-generator formulation. The unit-vector condition is stronger than the standard formulation when the indexed family contains repeated copies of a generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{\mathbf{s}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{s}_N\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^L\) and \(\mathbf{x}\in\operatorname{conv}S\). The extract calls \(\mathbf{x}\) an extreme point when, for every \(\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb{R}_+^N\), \(\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i\mathbf{s}_i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i=1\) imply \(\boldsymbol\theta\in\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_N\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the extract's generator-relative formulation, an extreme point has no convex representation using the listed generators except a unit-vector representation. Repeated copies of a generator are a failure boundary for this formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The source defines extremality by the midpoint condition for an arbitrary subset of a vector space, without assuming convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a vector space, let \(A\subset V\), and let \(a\in A\). The point \(a\) is an extreme point of \(A\) if, for all \(b,c\in A\), \[\frac{b+c}{2}=a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c=a.\] The set of all extreme points of \(A\) is denoted \(\operatorname{ex}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point a in A is an extreme point of A when every representation of a as the midpoint of two points b and c in A forces b and c both to equal a. The set of extreme points is denoted ex(A).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Points from Attained Linear Extrema
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique linear optimizers are extreme points, and extreme points of an attained maximum or minimum level set remain extreme in the ambient set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a vector space, let \(\varnothing\ne A\subset V\), and let \(f:V\to\mathbb R\) be linear. If \(u\in A\) is the unique maximizer or the unique minimizer of \(f\) over \(A\), then \(u\in\operatorname{ex}(A)\). Moreover, suppose \(f\) attains its maximum or minimum value \(\alpha\) on \(A\), and define \[B=\{x\in A:f(x)=\alpha\}.\] Then every \(u\in\operatorname{ex}(B)\) also belongs to \(\operatorname{ex}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unique maximizer or minimizer of a linear functional over a nonempty set is an extreme point of that set. More generally, an extreme point of the set on which an attained linear maximum or minimum occurs is also extreme in the original set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(u\text{ uniquely maximizes or minimizes }f\text{ on }A\bigr)\Rightarrow u\in\operatorname{ex}(A),\qquad \operatorname{ex}(B)\subseteq\operatorname{ex}(A)

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ray \(R=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\) is extreme exactly when \(u,v\in K\) and \(u+v\in R\) imply \(u,v\in R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a real vector space \(X\), let \(r\in K\setminus\{0\}\), and set \(R=\mathbb{R}_{+}r=\{\lambda r:\lambda\geq0\}\). The ray \(R\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) if
\[
u,v\in K\ \text{ and }\ u+v\in R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u,v\in R.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero ray in a convex cone is extreme when any two cone elements whose sum lies on that ray must themselves lie on the ray.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality Obstructs Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness is necessary, but without additional hypotheses it is not asserted to be sufficient for existence of extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If a convex cone \(K\) has nontrivial lineality,
\[
\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\ne\{0\},
\]
then \(K\) has no extreme rays. Consequently, existence of an extreme ray implies that \(K\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone containing a nonzero line has no extreme rays; hence a cone with an extreme ray must be pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Obstructs Extreme Rays

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Rays as One-Dimensional Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The zero face is excluded. No topology, closedness, or finite-dimensional assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a convex cone and let \(R=\mathbb{R}_+r\subset K\) with \(r\ne0\). Then
\[
R\text{ is an extreme ray of }K
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R\text{ is a one-dimensional face of }K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero ray of a convex cone is extreme exactly when it is a one-dimensional face.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is extreme if and only if it is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).

notation.meaning: The feasible intersection of the family.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be convex subsets of a real vector space, and suppose \(C=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). If there is an index \(j\in I\) such that \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{ext}C_j\), then
\[
x\in\operatorname{ext}C.
\]
The converse need not hold: for example, two closed half-planes in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\) may have no extreme points individually while their intersection is a pointed wedge with an extreme vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point of any one constraint set remains extreme after imposing further convex constraints, provided it remains feasible. The intersection may also acquire extreme points absent from every individual constraint set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inherited and created extreme points under intersection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex with nonempty intersection \(E=C\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates extreme points inherited from either operand from new extreme points produced by simultaneous constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extreme point \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(E)\) is inherited from \(C\) if \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C)\), inherited from \(D\) if \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(D)\), and intersection-created if \(x\notin\operatorname{Ext}(C)\cup\operatorname{Ext}(D)\). Extremality is preserved upon restriction: \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\cap D\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C\cap D)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}(D)\cap C\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C\cap D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point of an intersection is inherited when it was already extreme in one of the intersected sets. It is intersection-created when it is extreme only after both constraint systems are imposed. Any extreme point of one set that remains feasible for the other remains extreme in the intersection.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{Ext}(C\cap D)\) iff \((1-t)y+tz=x\), with \(y,z\in C\cap D\) and \(0<t<1\), forces \(y=z=x\).
If \(F\) is a face of \(C\) and \(F\subseteq D\subseteq C\), then \(F\) remains a face of \(D\); singleton faces give the preservation inclusion.
special_cases_latex: If \(D\) is a supporting hyperplane section of \(C\), then \(C\cap D\) is an exposed face and its extreme points are extreme in \(C\).
Intersecting a strictly convex body with affine constraints can create endpoints that were not extreme points of the uncut affine space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Restriction cannot destroy an extreme point that remains feasible.
The reverse inclusion generally fails because active constraints can create new extreme points.
If \(C\cap D\) is a face of \(C\), every extreme point of the intersection is extreme in \(C\).
boundary_notes: An extreme point of \(C\) outside \(D\) is irrelevant to the intersection.
Created extremality depends on both operands and is not intrinsic to either set alone.
The definition concerns binary intersections; finite families are handled by iteration.

notation.meaning: Intersection of the two convex sets.

children.title: Extremality Under Affine Maps
children.top_down_role: Preservation, collapse, and lifting of extremal structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fiber \(F=C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})\) is a nonempty compact face of \(C\), and some \(x\in\operatorname{ext}C\) satisfies \(T(x)=y\). If \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then \(T(\operatorname{ext}C)=\operatorname{ext}T(C)\).

notation.meaning: Fiber over the image point y.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The compact finite-dimensional lifting form is stated. Without injectivity, an extreme point of the domain may map to a nonextreme point or collapse with other points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\) be affine, with \(T(x)=Ax+b\). If \(y\in\operatorname{ext}T(C)\), then
\[
F=C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})
\]
is a nonempty compact face of \(C\). Consequently, there exists \(x\in\operatorname{ext}C\) with \(T(x)=y\). If, in addition, \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then
\[
T(\operatorname{ext}C)=\operatorname{ext}T(C).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of the affine image of a compact convex set lifts to an extreme point of the original set. An affine map that is injective on the set preserves and reflects all extreme points; a noninjective map may collapse extremal structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremality Under Affine Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Extreme-Point Lifting Without a Compact Fiber
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example isolates the extremal-existence requirement for the fiber in the lifting portion of the accepted theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2,\qquad T(s,t)=s.\] Then \(T(C)=[0,\infty)\), so \(0\in\operatorname{ext}T(C)\). Its fiber is \(C\cap T^{-1}(\{0\})=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\), which is a face of \(C\) but has no extreme point. Indeed, \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\). Consequently, the extreme image point \(0\) has no extreme preimage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of a half-plane containing a line gives an extreme endpoint in the image, but its fiber has no extreme point, so extreme-point lifting fails.

notation.meaning: The closed convex half-plane used in the counterexample.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Extreme-Point Lifting Without a Compact Fiber

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Assumption-Free Fiber and Injective-Map Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness is unnecessary for faciality of an extreme image fiber or for preservation and reflection under an affine map injective on the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine. If \(y\in\operatorname{ext}T(C)\), then \[C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})\] is a face of \(C\). Moreover, if \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then for every \(x\in C\), \[x\in\operatorname{ext}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(x)\in\operatorname{ext}T(C),\] and hence \(T(\operatorname{ext}C)=\operatorname{ext}T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fibers above extreme image points are faces without compactness, and affine maps injective on the convex set preserve and reflect extreme points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme image fibers are faces; if \(T|_C\) is injective, then \(x\) is extreme in \(C\) exactly when \(T(x)\) is extreme in \(T(C)\).

notation.meaning: The restriction of T to C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-image extremality and facial fibers
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine, \(T(x)=Ax+b\). For \(y\in T(C)\), define the fiber \(C_y=C\cap T^{-1}(\{y\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The fiber criterion exactly distinguishes preservation and collapse under arbitrary affine maps; injective maps form the preservation-only regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(y\in T(C)\) is extreme in \(T(C)\) exactly when its fiber \(C_y\) is a face of \(C\). An extreme point \(x\in C\) is preserved when \(T(x)\in\operatorname{Ext}(T(C))\), collapsed when another point of \(C\) has the same image, and lifted over an extreme image point when \(x\in C_y\). If \(T\) is injective on \(C\), then \(x\mapsto T(x)\) bijects \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}(T(C))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An image point is extreme precisely when all of its preimages in the convex set form a face. This facial-fiber condition captures both lifting and collapse. Under an injective affine map, no fiber contains more than one point, so extreme points are preserved in both directions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\) is extreme iff whenever \((1-t)x_1+tx_2\in C_y\), with \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and \(0<t<1\), one has \(x_1,x_2\in C_y\).
For injective \(T|_C\), \(x\) is extreme in \(C\) iff \(T(x)\) is extreme in \(T(C)\).
special_cases_latex: An affine isomorphism preserves the entire face lattice by \(F\mapsto T(F)\).
A projection may send several extreme points to one image point or send an extreme point into a nonextreme image point.
If \(C_y\) is a singleton face, the extreme image point has a unique extreme lift.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every preimage fiber of an extreme image point contains only facially compatible decompositions.
Noninjective affine maps may collapse extremal distinctions.
The preimage of an extreme image point is never an arbitrary convex slice; it is a face.
boundary_notes: The image of an extreme point need not be extreme when the map is noninjective.
An extreme image point may have a positive-dimensional facial fiber.
Affine maps preserve convex combinations but need not preserve closedness of unbounded closed convex sets.

notation.meaning: Fiber of the affine map over an image point, restricted to the convex set.
Restriction of the affine map to the convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-exposure correspondence package
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex set. Write \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\) and \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\) for its extreme and exposed points, and use analogous notation for directions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The correspondence is finite-dimensional and combines inclusion, density, and representation. Closure is required in the density statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extreme-exposure correspondence consists of: \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(C)\); \(\operatorname{ExpDir}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{ExtDir}(C)\); and the density identity \(\operatorname{Ext}(C)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C))\). Thus every extreme point is a limit of exposed points. When \(C\) contains no lines, its exposed points and exposed directions generate it after convexification and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exposed points and directions are always extreme. Conversely, for a closed finite-dimensional convex set, exposed points are dense among extreme points: every extreme point can be approximated by exposed points. For a closed convex set without lines, exposed points and exposed directions recover the entire set after taking the convex hull and closure.

The closure of the exposed-point set and the closure of the extreme-point set coincide.

If every extreme point is exposed, then \(\operatorname{ExpPt}(C)=\operatorname{Ext}(C)\).
For a pointed closed convex cone, exposed rays generate the cone after conic hull and closure.

Nonexposed extreme points do not obstruct approximation by uniquely supported points.
Exposure-based representations may require closure even when extreme-point representations do not.
boundary_notes: Density does not assert that every extreme point is exposed.
The finite-dimensional result differs from general infinite-dimensional Krein–Milman-type statements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolation by an Affine Hyperplane
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space, let \(A\subseteq V\), and write an affine hyperplane as \(H=\{x\in V:f(x)=\alpha\}\), where \(f:V\to\mathbb R\) is a nonzero linear functional and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic isolation is defined without topology. The accompanying existence regimes distinguish algebraically open convex sets in general vector spaces from arbitrary nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hyperplane \(H\) isolates \(A\) if either \(f(x)\leq\alpha\) for every \(x\in A\), or \(f(x)\geq\alpha\) for every \(x\in A\). It strictly isolates \(A\) if the corresponding inequality is strict for every \(x\in A\). For \(u\notin A\), an isolation certificate through \(u\) is a pair \((f,\alpha)\) with \(f\neq0\), \(f(u)=\alpha\), and one of these uniform inequalities on \(A\). The isolation-theorem family asserts existence of a strict certificate when \(A\) is algebraically open and convex, and existence of a non-strict certificate when \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine hyperplane isolates a set when the entire set lies in one of its closed halfspaces, and strictly isolates it when the set lies in one open halfspace. A certificate through an exterior point is a nonzero linear functional whose level hyperplane contains that point and whose values on the set all lie strictly or non-strictly on one side. Strict existence holds for algebraically open convex sets in a real vector space; ordinary isolation exists for every nonempty convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ isolates }A\iff [\sup_{x\in A}f(x)\leq\alpha]\lor[\inf_{x\in A}f(x)\geq\alpha]\), with strict isolation obtained by replacing \(\leq,\geq\) by \(<,>\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: After replacing \(f\) by \(-f\) if necessary, isolation through \(u\) can be normalized as \(f(u)=\alpha\) and \(f(x)\leq\alpha\) for all \(x\in A\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and convex and \(u\notin A\), some affine hyperplane through \(u\) isolates \(A\).
If \(A\) is algebraically open and convex, the isolating inequality may be chosen strict.
immediate_consequences_latex: An isolating hyperplane meeting a closed convex set determines an exposed face.
The definition supplies a functional certificate that the set does not cross the hyperplane.
boundary_notes: Strict isolation is stronger than ordinary isolation and is not guaranteed for an arbitrary convex set containing boundary points on the hyperplane.
In infinite-dimensional algebraic settings, convexity alone does not guarantee an isolation certificate through every exterior point.

notation.meaning: Affine hyperplane represented by a nonzero functional level set.
