knowledge_statements.statement_title: Straszewski Exposed-Point Approximation Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact convex set. Write \(\operatorname{ext}K\) for its extreme points and \(\operatorname{exp}K\) for the points uniquely maximizing some nonzero linear functional on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compact convex geometry. The definition packages the two standard forms of Straszewski’s theorem: density of exposed points among extreme points and exposed-point generation of the whole set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in K\) is exposed if there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(\langle c,x\rangle>\langle c,y\rangle\) for every \(y\in K\setminus\{x\}\). The set \(K\) has the Straszewski property when \(\operatorname{ext}K\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{exp}K}\). For compact convex \(K\), the associated generation form is \(K=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{exp}K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed point is the unique maximizer of a nonzero linear functional over the set. The Straszewski approximation property says that every extreme point of a finite-dimensional compact convex set can be approximated by exposed points. Equivalently at the level of set generation, the compact convex set is the closure of the convex hull of its exposed points.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{exp}K\) if and only if there is a supporting hyperplane whose intersection with \(K\) is exactly \(\{x\}\).
The density form means that for every \(x\in\operatorname{ext}K\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(z\in\operatorname{exp}K\) with \(\|z-x\|<\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: Every exposed point is extreme, so \(\operatorname{exp}K\subseteq\operatorname{ext}K\).
The set \(\operatorname{exp}K\) need not itself be closed, even when \(K\) is compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: Continuous affine optimization over \(K\) can be studied through exposed and extreme boundary structure.
Combining density with finite-dimensional extreme-point generation recovers \(K\) from exposed points after closure.
boundary_notes: An extreme point need not itself be exposed.
The closure in the convex-hull formulation cannot generally be removed.
This record does not assert the corresponding statement in arbitrary infinite-dimensional locally convex spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Krein–Milman Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact convex set. A point \(e\in K\) is extreme when it cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean formulation, also called Minkowski’s theorem in the cited source. Unlike the general locally convex Krein–Milman theorem, no closure is needed around the convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{ext}K=\{e\in K:(e=(1-t)x+ty,\ x,y\in K,\ 0<t<1)\Rightarrow x=y=e\}\). The finite-dimensional Krein–Milman property is the identity \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\). Thus the compact convex set is generated exactly by its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme points of a compact convex subset of Euclidean space are those points that do not lie in any open segment contained in the set. The finite-dimensional Krein–Milman property states that the whole set equals the convex hull of these points. In finite dimensions the convex hull is already the required set, so the closure appearing in the infinite-dimensional version is unnecessary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x\in K\), there are \(m\geq1\), points \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\in\operatorname{ext}K\), and coefficients \(\lambda_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) such that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i e_i\).
The midpoint definition of extremality is equivalent, for convex \(K\), to the formulation using every \(t\in(0,1)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a singleton, its unique point is extreme and the identity is immediate.
For a polytope, \(\operatorname{ext}K\) is its vertex set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty compact convex set in \(\mathbb R^d\) has an extreme point.
A linear functional attaining a maximum on \(K\) attains a maximum at some extreme point.
boundary_notes: Compactness is essential for this exact family statement.
The infinite-dimensional theorem generally uses the closed convex hull and an appropriate locally convex topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-Point Existence Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(\operatorname{ext}K\) denote the set of points not lying in a nondegenerate open segment contained in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty compact convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The record isolates the existence component from the stronger generation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extreme-point existence property for \(K\) is \(\operatorname{ext}K\neq\varnothing\), where \(e\in\operatorname{ext}K\) precisely when, for all \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), the equality \(e=(1-t)x+ty\) forces \(x=y=e\). Every nonempty compact convex \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) has this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact convex set has the extreme-point existence property when it contains at least one point that cannot be placed strictly between two different points of the set. Every nonempty compact convex subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space has such a point. This is only an existence assertion; it does not by itself say that all points of the set are generated by extreme points.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(e\in K\) such that \(e=(x+y)/2\) with \(x,y\in K\) implies \(x=y=e\).
special_cases_latex: Every singleton has its sole point as an extreme point.
More generally, a nonempty closed convex set in \(\mathbb R^d\) containing no straight line has an extreme point.
immediate_consequences_latex: The extreme-point generating set in the finite-dimensional Krein–Milman identity is nonempty.
Every compact convex face has an extreme point, since the face is again compact and convex.
boundary_notes: Nonemptiness is necessary.
Compactness cannot simply be omitted: an open convex set of positive dimension has no extreme points.
For closed noncompact sets, absence of lines is a useful sufficient condition, but it is not part of this compact-set definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generation by Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(\operatorname{conv}S\) denotes all finite convex combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional compact generation, not merely density or closed-convex-hull generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(K\) is extreme-point generated when \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\). Explicitly, this means that every \(x\in K\) belongs to some finite simplex whose vertices are extreme points of \(K\): there exist \(m\geq1\), \(e_i\in\operatorname{ext}K\), and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i e_i\). Every nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb R^d\) is extreme-point generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extreme-point generation means that each point of the compact convex set is a finite convex combination of extreme points of that same set. Equivalently, every point lies in a finite simplex whose vertices are extreme. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space every nonempty compact convex set has this exact generation property.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\).
Every point of \(K\) lies in the convex hull of a finite subset of \(\operatorname{ext}K\).
special_cases_latex: For a compact polytope, this is generation by its vertices.
For a line segment, the two endpoints generate every point of the segment.
immediate_consequences_latex: A convex subset containing every extreme point of \(K\) must equal \(K\) if it is closed under finite convex combinations.
The values of an affine map on \(K\) are generated by its values on \(\operatorname{ext}K\).
boundary_notes: The generating points must be extreme points of the same set \(K\).
For noncompact convex sets the equality may fail, even when the set is closed.
Infinite-dimensional variants generally require closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and set \(r:=\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\). Every \(x\in C\) admits a representation \[x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i v_i,\qquad v_i\in\operatorname{ext}C,\quad \lambda_i>0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1,\quad k\le r+1,\] in which \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) are affinely independent. The bound is sharp: if \(C\) is an \(r\)-simplex, every point of \(\operatorname{ri}C\) requires all \(r+1\) vertices in any extreme-point representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point is a convex combination of at most affine-dimension plus one affinely independent extreme points, and relative-interior points of a simplex show the bound is sharp.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Compactness cannot simply be deleted from finite-dimensional extreme-point generation. The open convex set \(C_1=(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{ext}C_1=\varnothing.
\]
The closed unbounded convex set \(C_2=[0,\infty)\subset\mathbb{R}\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{ext}C_2=\{0\},
\qquad
\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C_2)=\{0\}\neq C_2.
\]
Likewise, any nonempty affine subspace of positive dimension has no extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without compactness, extreme points may not exist, and even when they do exist they need not generate the set. An open interval has no extreme points, while the closed unbounded ray has only its endpoint as an extreme point.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty convex set, not assumed compact, and let \(\operatorname{ext}C\) denote its extreme points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundary class marking where compact extreme-point generation can fail. It includes open, lineal, and many unbounded convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the noncompact extremal-failure class by \(\mathcal F_d=\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^d:C
eq\varnothing,\ C	ext{ convex and noncompact},\ C
eq\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C)\}\). A sufficient failure condition is \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\), since then \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C)=\varnothing
eq C\). Every nonempty open convex set of positive dimension and every affine subspace of positive dimension has no extreme points and therefore belongs to \(\mathcal F_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The noncompact extremal-failure class consists of nonempty, noncompact convex sets that are not generated by their extreme points. The most direct failure occurs when there are no extreme points at all. Positive-dimensional open convex sets and positive-dimensional affine subspaces have this defect. Noncompactness permits failure but does not force it: some closed unbounded convex sets still possess extreme points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\in\mathcal F_d\iff C\neq\varnothing,\ C\text{ convex and noncompact},\ C\neq\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}C).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\in\mathcal F_d\) precisely when some \(x\in C\) has no finite convex representation by points of \(\operatorname{ext}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a nonempty open convex set with \(\dim C>0\), then \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\).
If \(C\) is an affine line or a higher-dimensional affine subspace, then \(\operatorname{ext}C=\varnothing\).
A nonempty closed convex set containing no straight line does have an extreme point, although generation may still require additional recession data.
immediate_consequences_latex: The compactness hypothesis in the finite-dimensional Krein–Milman equality cannot be deleted without replacement.
Extreme points alone are generally insufficient to represent unbounded convex geometry.
boundary_notes: Noncompactness alone is not equivalent to failure.
A set containing a line need not be classified solely from that fact without checking its complete extreme-point structure.
This record defines a boundary class; it does not claim a full characterization of all noncompact convex sets generated by extreme points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance and Projection Data of a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space metric geometry. The inner product is essential for the normal and firm-nonexpansiveness structures recorded here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal H\), define \(d_C(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\) and \(\Pi_C(x)=\{p\in C:\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\}\). The metric geometry of \(C\) is governed by the fact that \(\Pi_C(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\); its unique element is denoted \(P_Cx\). It satisfies \(P_Cx\in C\), \(\|x-P_Cx\|=d_C(x)\), and \(\langle y-P_Cx,x-P_Cx\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance to a nonempty closed convex set is the infimum of the distances to its points. The metric projection set consists of all points attaining that infimum. In a real Hilbert space, every nonempty closed convex set has exactly one nearest point to each ambient point, defining the projector. The displacement from the projected point to the original point forms a right or obtuse angle with every feasible direction in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_C(x)=\{P_Cx\}\quad\text{and}\quad p=P_Cx\iff p\in C\ \land\ \forall y\in C,\ \langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_Cx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\frac12\|x-y\|^2\).
\(x-P_Cx\in N_C(P_Cx)\), where \(N_C(p)=\{u:\langle u,y-p\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in C\), then \(P_Cx=x\) and \(d_C(x)=0\).
If \(C\) is a closed affine subspace, the variational inequality strengthens to orthogonality to its parallel subspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: The projector is everywhere defined and single-valued.
Projection connects metric approximation with the normal cone of convex analysis.
boundary_notes: A closed nonconvex set need not have a unique nearest point.
In a general Banach space, existence and uniqueness require additional geometric hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best Approximation, Proximinality, and Chebyshev Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, and let \(x\in\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General nearest-point terminology for subsets of Hilbert space, followed by the closed-convex regime guaranteeing existence and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(p\in C\) is a best approximation to \(x\) from \(C\) if \(\|x-p\|=d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\). The set \(C\) is proximinal if every \(x\in\mathcal H\) has at least one best approximation, and Chebyshev if every \(x\in\mathcal H\) has exactly one. When \(C\) is Chebyshev, \(P_Cx\) denotes that unique point. Every nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathcal H\) is Chebyshev.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A best approximation is a point of the set that realizes the smallest possible distance from a prescribed ambient point. A set is proximinal when at least one nearest point exists for every ambient point, and Chebyshev when that nearest point is always unique. For a nonempty closed convex set in a Hilbert space, both existence and uniqueness hold, so the nearest-point assignment is a well-defined projector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\Pi_C(x)\iff p\in C\ \land\ \|x-p\|=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|;\quad C\text{ Chebyshev}\iff\forall x,\ |\Pi_C(x)|=1.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Best approximations are minimizers of \(y\mapsto\frac12\|x-y\|^2\) over \(C\).
For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(p\) is the best approximation precisely when \(p\in C\) and \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
special_cases_latex: Every closed affine subspace is Chebyshev.
In finite-dimensional Hilbert space, every nonempty closed set is proximinal, although it need not be Chebyshev.
immediate_consequences_latex: For closed convex \(C\), the symbol \(P_Cx\) is defined for every \(x\in\mathcal H\).
Every proximinal set is necessarily nonempty and closed.
boundary_notes: Closedness alone does not ensure proximinality in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
Convexity is used for uniqueness; nonconvex proximinal sets can admit several nearest points.

notation.meaning: Set of all best approximations to \(x\) from \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in H\). There exists exactly one \(p\in C\) such that
\[
\|x-p\|=d_C(x).
\]
Thus the metric projection is the single-valued map \(P_C:H\to C\) defined by \(P_Cx=p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every point in a real Hilbert space, the nearest point in a nonempty closed convex set is unique, so metric projection onto that set is a well-defined function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Nearest-Point Property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global uniqueness property for all ambient points. The guaranteed regime is nonempty closed convex subsets of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) has the unique nearest-point property, or is Chebyshev, if for every \(x\in\mathcal H\) there exists a unique \(p\in C\) such that \(\|x-p\|=d_C(x)\). Equivalently, \(\Pi_C(x)=\{p\}\) for every \(x\). For nonempty closed convex \(C\), the unique point is characterized by \(p\in C\) and \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set has unique nearest points when every point of the ambient Hilbert space has exactly one distance-minimizing point in the set. Such a set is called Chebyshev, and its unique nearest-point map is the projector. Every nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space has this property; without convexity, two or more nearest points may occur.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\) is Chebyshev if and only if the set-valued map \(\Pi_C:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows C\) is everywhere singleton-valued.
For closed convex \(C\), uniqueness accompanies the variational inequality \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in C\), the unique nearest point is \(x\) itself.
Every nonempty closed affine subspace is Chebyshev.
immediate_consequences_latex: The projector \(P_C:\mathcal H\to C\) is a genuine function.
For closed convex \(C\), \(P_C\) is continuous and in fact firmly nonexpansive.
boundary_notes: Proximinality asserts existence but not uniqueness.
A nonempty closed nonconvex subset can fail uniqueness.
Whether every Chebyshev subset of an arbitrary infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is convex is not asserted here.

For \(x\in H\) and \(p\in C\), \[p=P_Cx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-p\in N_C(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle x-p,y-p\rangle\leq 0\ \text{for every }y\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point p in C is the nearest point to x exactly when the residual x−p is a normal to C at p, equivalently when it makes a nonpositive inner product with every displacement from p into C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Pythagorean Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This metric certificate is equivalent to the normal residual inequality for a specified candidate point; two-point firm nonexpansiveness belongs to projection regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the hypotheses of the pointwise projection-normal characterization, \(p\) is a nearest point to \(x\) in \(C\) if and only if, for every \(y\in C\), \[\|x-y\|^2\geq\|x-p\|^2+\|y-p\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate is the projection exactly when it yields the Pythagorean lower bound for every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Pythagorean Inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is Essential for Normal Necessity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The global normal inequality remains sufficient for nearest-point status for an arbitrary set, but without convexity it need not be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R\), \(x=0\), and \(p=1\). Then \(p\) is a nearest point in \(C\) to \(x\), but for \(y=-1\), \[\langle x-p,y-p\rangle=(-1)(-2)=2>0.\] Thus a nearest point of a nonconvex set need not satisfy the global projection-normal inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonconvex set, a genuine nearest point can fail the global normal inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}|x-y|\), but \(\langle x-p,y-p\rangle>0\) for some \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for Normal Necessity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projector as the Normal-Cone Resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the operator form of the seeded projection-normal characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then \[P_C=(I+N_C)^{-1}.\] Equivalently, for every \(p\in C\), \[P_C^{-1}(p)=p+N_C(p).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection is the resolvent of the normal-cone operator, and the points projecting to p are exactly p plus its normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: The identity operator on the Hilbert space.
The inverse relation of the identity plus the normal-cone operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Projector as the Normal-Cone Resolvent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Projection-Normal Characterization Without Closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness is needed to guarantee existence for every external point, but not for the characterization of a specified candidate nearest point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(x\in H\) and \(p\in C\). Then \[p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle x-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Thus the pointwise equivalence does not require \(C\) to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified point in a convex set, the normal inequality characterizes nearest-point status even when the set is not closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Characterized by the Convex Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(p\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hilbert-space characterization for convex metric projections and convex-analytic normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the normal cone to \(C\) at \(p\) by \(N_C(p)=\{u\in\mathcal H:\langle u,y-p\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}\), and set \(N_C(p)=\varnothing\) when \(p\notin C\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathcal H\), \(p=P_Cx\) if and only if \(x-p\in N_C(p)\). Thus the projection residual is precisely a supporting normal direction at the projected point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex normal cone at a feasible point consists of all vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every feasible displacement from that point. A point is the metric projection of an ambient point exactly when the residual vector from the projected point to the ambient point lies in this normal cone. This identifies best approximation with a supporting-normal condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=P_Cx\iff p\in C\ \land\ \forall y\in C,\ \langle x-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\iff x-p\in N_C(p).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in p+N_C(p)\iff p=P_Cx\).
\(P_C=(\operatorname{Id}+N_C)^{-1}\) as a single-valued mapping on \(\mathcal H\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a closed affine subspace with parallel subspace \(V\), then \(N_C(p)=V^\perp\) for every \(p\in C\).
If \(x\in C\), then \(P_Cx=x\) and the residual is \(0\in N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every projection point is a support point whenever its residual is nonzero.
The inverse image of \(p\) under \(P_C\) is \(p+N_C(p)\).
boundary_notes: The stated normal cone is the convex-analytic normal cone; nonconvex normal constructions are not covered.
Closedness and convexity ensure that \(P_Cx\) exists uniquely for every \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Projector and Residual Geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric structure of the nearest-point map in Hilbert space, including its variational angle condition and invariance along outward normal rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex projector is the mapping \(P_C:\mathcal H\to C\) defined by \(P_Cx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\). Its residual is \(R_C=\operatorname{Id}-P_C\). For every \(x\in\mathcal H\), \(p=P_Cx\) is characterized by \(\langle y-p,R_Cx\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\). Moreover, the entire ray \(p+\lambda R_Cx\), \(\lambda\geq0\), projects back to \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projector sends each ambient point to its unique nearest point in the closed convex set, while the residual records the displacement left after projection. The residual forms a right or obtuse angle with every feasible displacement from the projected point. Moving from the projected point any nonnegative distance along that same residual direction leaves the projection unchanged.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(R_Cx\in N_C(P_Cx)\).
\(P_C^{-1}(p)=p+N_C(p)\) for each \(p\in C\).
special_cases_latex: On \(C\), the projector is the identity and the residual vanishes.
For a closed linear subspace, \(P_Cx\) and \(R_Cx\) are orthogonal linear components.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(P_C\circ P_C=P_C\).
\(\operatorname{Fix}P_C=C\).
Normal rays describe the full fibers of the projector.
boundary_notes: The projector need not be affine unless \(C\) is affine.
For nonconvex sets, the projection may be set-valued and normal-ray invariance can fail.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal Projection onto a Closed Affine Subspace
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C=a+V\), where \(a\in\mathcal H\) and \(V\subseteq\mathcal H\) is a closed linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed affine subspaces of a Hilbert space. Their projectors are affine and satisfy exact orthogonality rather than only a variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal H\), the projection onto \(C=a+V\) is \(P_Cx=a+P_V(x-a)\). Equivalently, \(p=P_Cx\) if and only if \(p\in C\) and \(x-p\in V^\perp\). The map \(P_C\) is affine: for all \(x,y\in\mathcal H\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\), \(P_C((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)P_Cx+tP_Cy\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed affine subspace is a translate of a closed linear subspace. To project onto it, translate the point back to the parallel linear subspace, apply the orthogonal projector, and translate forward. The projection residual is orthogonal to every direction parallel to the affine set, and the resulting projector is an affine mapping.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p=P_Cx\iff p\in C\) and \(\langle y-z,x-p\rangle=0\) for every \(y,z\in C\).
The decomposition \(x-a=P_V(x-a)+P_{V^\perp}(x-a)\) yields the projected and residual components.
special_cases_latex: If \(a=0\), then \(C=V\) and \(P_C=P_V\) is linear.
For a hyperplane \(C=\{z:\langle z,u\rangle=\eta\}\) with \(u\neq0\), \(P_Cx=x+\frac{\eta-\langle x,u\rangle}{\|u\|^2}u\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The affine projector preserves arbitrary affine combinations.
boundary_notes: The parallel subspace must be closed for an everywhere-defined orthogonal projector.
Projection onto a general closed convex set is typically nonlinear and only satisfies an inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection onto the closed span of an orthonormal family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fourier-series representation of metric projection onto a closed linear span, including projection onto a one-dimensional subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((e_i)_{i\in I}\) be a countable orthonormal family in a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and set \(C=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_i\mid i\in I\}\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathcal H\), \[P_Cx=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i.\] In particular, if \(u\in\mathcal H\), \(\|u\|=1\), and \(U=\mathbb Ru\), then \(P_Ux=\langle x,u\rangle u\) for every \(x\in\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the closed span of a countable orthonormal family is given by the associated Fourier series. In particular, projection onto the line generated by a unit vector equals the vector's scalar component in that direction multiplied by the unit vector.

\((e_i)_{i\in I}\) is a countable orthonormal family.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong convergence to a metric projection from cluster-point and distance conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convergence criterion for projection onto a nonempty closed convex set in a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and variational characterization of Euclidean projection onto a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean projection onto a nonempty closed convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and variational characterization of Euclidean projection. The cited non-Euclidean failure boundary is specifically projection onto a polyhedron using the $\ell_\infty$ norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric projection onto a closed convex set in a Hilbert space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, variational characterization, nonexpansiveness, monotonicity, and radial scaling of the Hilbert metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $W$ be a Hilbert space and let $\varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W$ be closed and convex. For every $w\in W$ there is a unique nearest point $P(w)\in\mathcal C$. Moreover, $z=P(w)$ if and only if $z\in\mathcal C$ and $(w-z,v-z)_W\le 0$ for all $v\in\mathcal C$. For all $v,w\in W$, $\|P(v)-P(w)\|_W\le\|v-w\|_W$ and $(P(v)-P(w),v-w)_W\ge0$, with equality in the latter inequality if and only if $P(v)=P(w)$. Finally, for $w\in\mathcal C$ and $d\in W$, $t\mapsto t^{-1}\|P(w+td)-w\|_W$ is nonincreasing on $(0,\infty)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty closed convex set in a Hilbert space has a unique metric projection. The projection has the standard variational characterization, is nonexpansive and monotone, and its radial difference quotient from a feasible point is nonincreasing.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall w\in W\ \exists!\,P(w)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in\mathcal C}\|v-w\|_W,\quad z=P(w)\iff\bigl[z\in\mathcal C\ \land\ (w-z,v-z)_W\le0\ \forall v\in\mathcal C\bigr],\quad \|P(v)-P(w)\|_W\le\|v-w\|_W,\quad (P(v)-P(w),v-w)_W\ge0,\quad t\mapsto\frac{\|P(w+td)-w\|_W}{t}\text{ is nonincreasing}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection onto an intersection of closed convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract does not state that the intersection is nonempty. Nonemptiness is the necessary well-posedness condition; if the intersection is empty, the displayed problem has no solution and the projection is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb E\) be closed and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), let \(d\in\mathbb E\), and write \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^p C_i\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Firm Nonexpansiveness of Convex Projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global metric regularity of the Hilbert-space projector. Firm nonexpansiveness is stronger than ordinary nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projector \(P_C:\mathcal H\to C\) is firmly nonexpansive: for all \(x,y\in\mathcal H\), \(\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2+\|(x-P_Cx)-(y-P_Cy)\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2\). Equivalently, \(\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2\leq\langle x-y,P_Cx-P_Cy\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set is firmly nonexpansive. The squared change in the projected points plus the squared change in the residuals never exceeds the squared change in the original points. Equivalently, the projected displacement has squared norm no larger than its inner product with the original displacement. In particular, the projector is one-Lipschitz and continuous.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2\leq\langle x-y,P_Cx-P_Cy\rangle\).
\(2P_C-\operatorname{Id}\) is nonexpansive.
\(\operatorname{Id}-P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive.
special_cases_latex: For a closed affine subspace, \(\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2=\langle x-y,P_Cx-P_Cy\rangle\).
Ordinary nonexpansiveness follows as \(\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|\leq\|x-y\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(P_C\) is globally continuous.
Both the projection and residual maps are monotone and one-Lipschitz.
The reflected projector \(2P_C-\operatorname{Id}\) is nonexpansive.
boundary_notes: A general nearest-point selection for a nonconvex set need not be continuous or nonexpansive.
Firm nonexpansiveness is a Hilbert-space inner-product property.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative of convex projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional differentiability of metric projection at a base point belonging to the closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For every \(x\in C\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\mathrm{p}_C(x+td)-x}{t}=\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{T}_C(x)}(d).
\]
Equivalently, \(\mathrm{p}_C'(x;d)=\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{T}_C(x)}(d)\). If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), then \(\mathrm{T}_C(x)\) is the subspace parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}C\), so the derivative is projection onto that subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point belonging to a nonempty closed convex set, the directional derivative of the metric projection is the projection of the direction onto the tangent cone. At a relative-interior point, this is projection onto the subspace parallel to the affine hull.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau Decomposition for a Closed Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and define its polar cone by \(K^{\ominus}=\{u\in\mathcal H:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal metric decomposition associated with a closed convex cone and its negative polar. The sign convention is the polar \(K^{\ominus}\), not the positive dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Moreau polar decomposition of \(x\in\mathcal H\) is the pair \((P_Kx,P_{K^{\ominus}}x)\). It satisfies \(x=P_Kx+P_{K^{\ominus}}x\) and \(\langle P_Kx,P_{K^{\ominus}}x\rangle=0\). Equivalently, \(p=P_Kx\) exactly when \(p\in K\), \(x-p\in K^{\ominus}\), and \(\langle p,x-p\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone consists of vectors having nonpositive inner product with every vector in the original cone. Moreau decomposition splits every Hilbert-space vector into its projection onto a nonempty closed convex cone and its projection onto the polar cone. The two components sum to the original vector and are orthogonal. This projected orthogonal pair is uniquely determined.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p=P_Kx\iff p\in K,\ x-p\in K^{\ominus},\ \langle p,x-p\rangle=0\).
\(P_K+P_{K^{\ominus}}=\operatorname{Id}\) and \(\langle P_Kx,P_{K^{\ominus}}x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K=V\) is a closed linear subspace, then \(K^{\ominus}=V^\perp\) and the formula is the usual orthogonal decomposition.
For the nonnegative orthant, the two projections are the coordinatewise positive and negative parts under the stated polar convention.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(P_{K^{\ominus}}x=x-P_Kx\).
The distance to either cone is the norm of the projection onto the other cone.
The Moreau pair supplies complementary feasibility and orthogonality conditions.
boundary_notes: The cone must be closed and convex for the stated metric projections and identity.
Using the positive dual cone \(K^{\oplus}=-K^{\ominus}\) changes the sign in the decomposition.
An arbitrary decomposition into one vector from each cone need not be orthogonal or equal to the Moreau pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[P_K(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in K}\|x-z\|,\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Equivalently, \(y=P_K(x)\) exactly when \[y\in K,\qquad x-y\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle x-y,y\rangle=0.\] Thus projection onto \(K\) assigns to every \(x\) the unique cone point whose residual is polar to, and orthogonal to, that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection of a vector onto a nonempty closed convex cone is its unique nearest point in the cone. A cone point is this projection exactly when the residual lies in the polar cone and is orthogonal to the cone point.

\[P_K(\alpha x)=\alpha P_K(x)\qquad(\alpha\ge0).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(K\subset H\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(K^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle u,k\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\). Every \(x\in H\) has the orthogonal decomposition \[x=P_Kx+P_{K^\circ}x,\qquad \langle P_Kx,P_{K^\circ}x\rangle=0.\] Consequently, \[\|x\|^2=\|P_Kx\|^2+\|P_{K^\circ}x\|^2,\qquad d_K(x)=\|P_{K^\circ}x\|,\] where \(d_K(x)=\inf_{k\in K}\|x-k\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vector decomposes uniquely into mutually orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its polar. The norm obeys the corresponding Pythagorean identity, and the polar component has length equal to the distance to the cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Metric Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance to either member of a polar-cone pair is the norm of the projection onto the other, and the squared distances sum to the squared ambient norm.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau polar-cone metric decomposition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(K^\circ\) be its polar, and let \(P_K\) and \(P_{K^\circ}\) denote the corresponding metric projectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean space with the negative-polar convention \(\langle s,z\rangle\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar-cone metric decomposition of \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is the unique ordered pair \((x_K,x_{K^\circ})\) satisfying \[x=x_K+x_{K^\circ},\qquad x_K\in K,\qquad x_{K^\circ}\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle x_K,x_{K^\circ}\rangle=0.\] It is given by \[x_K=P_K(x),\qquad x_{K^\circ}=P_{K^\circ}(x),\qquad x=P_K(x)+P_{K^\circ}(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vector has a unique orthogonal decomposition into one component in a closed convex cone and one component in its polar cone. The two components are precisely the metric projections onto the two cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb R^n\), \[x=x_1+x_2,\ x_1\in K,\ x_2\in K^\circ,\ \langle x_1,x_2\rangle=0\iff x_1=P_K(x),\ x_2=P_{K^\circ}(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(K=V\) is a subspace, then \(K^\circ=V^\perp\) and the decomposition is the ordinary orthogonal decomposition.
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), the components are the coordinatewise positive and negative parts.
immediate_consequences_latex: The orthogonality condition distinguishes the unique metric decomposition from arbitrary, generally nonunique, sums of an element of \(K\) and an element of \(K^\circ\).
boundary_notes: The displayed signs use the negative polar; conventions based on the dual cone replace the polar component by a signed projection.
Closedness is essential for the projector formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local tangent-normal cone geometry of a convex set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set and \(x\in C\). Local geometry is represented at the origin by cones and at the base point by their translates through \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets; the construction is first-order and attached to one base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local cone geometry of \(C\) at \(x\) is the ordered primal-dual pair \[T_C(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x),\qquad N_C(x):=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\langle s,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}.\] The translated cone \(x+T_C(x)\) is the first-order feasible model containing \(C\), while \(N_C(x)\) is the cone of directions defining supporting homogeneous half-spaces at \(x\). These cones satisfy \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,\qquad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local cone geometry at a point consists of the closed cone generated by displacements from that point and the cone of all supporting normal directions. Translating the tangent cone back to the point gives the primal local model, while the normal cone gives its dual half-space description.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[T_C(x)=\{d:\langle s,d\rangle\le0\ \forall s\in N_C(x)\}.\]
\[x+T_C(x)=\bigcap_{s\in N_C(x)}\{x+d:\langle s,d\rangle\le0\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(T_C(x)=\mathbb R^n\) and \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone and \(x=0\), then \(T_K(0)=K\) and \(N_K(0)=K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both \(T_C(x)\) and \(N_C(x)\) are closed convex cones.
\[C\subseteq x+T_C(x).\]
boundary_notes: For nonconvex sets, several inequivalent tangent and normal constructions coexist.
The tangent cone records first-order directions and need not reproduce curvature near the base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand tangent-cone field
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in S\). For convex specialization, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The sequential definition applies to arbitrary subsets; the closed conical-hull formula is the convex specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in S\), the Bouligand tangent cone is \[T_S(x):=\left\{d:\exists x_k\in S,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ x_k\to x,\ \frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to d\right\}.\] The tangent-cone family is the set-valued field \(x\mapsto T_S(x)\) on \(S\). If \(S=C\) is closed and convex, then every member of the family has the global representation \[T_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\operatorname{cl}\bigcup_{t>0}\frac{C-x}{t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent-cone family assigns to every point all limits of rescaled feasible displacements approaching that point. For a closed convex set, each tangent cone is exactly the closure of the cone generated by all displacements from the base point.
assumptions_latex: For the conical-hull formula, \(S=C\) is closed and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in T_S(x)\iff \exists d_k\to d,\ t_k\downarrow0:\ x+t_kd_k\in S\quad\forall k.\]
\[d\in T_S(x)\iff \liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x+td,S)}{t}=0.\]
special_cases_latex: \(0\in T_S(x)\) for every \(x\in S\).
If \(x\in\operatorname{int}S\), then \(T_S(x)=\mathbb R^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every Bouligand tangent cone is closed and positively homogeneous.
For convex \(C\), \(C-x\subseteq T_C(x)\).
boundary_notes: For a nonconvex set, the tangent cone need not be convex.
The unclosed feasible-direction cone and the closed tangent cone can differ even when the set is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Tangent Cone and Its Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential tangent cone of an arbitrary Euclidean subset at a closure point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x\in\overline S\), define
\[
T_xS:=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\exists x_k\in S,\ x_k\to x,\ \exists t_k>0,\ t_k\to0,\ \frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to v\right\}.
\]
Its dimension is defined by \(\dim T_xS:=\dim(\operatorname{span}T_xS)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any subset S of Euclidean space and any point x in its closure, the tangent cone consists of limits of scaled displacements (x_k−x)/t_k, where x_k belongs to S and approaches x while positive t_k approaches zero. Its dimension is the dimension of its linear span.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_xS=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\exists x_k\in S,\ x_k\to x,\ \exists t_k>0,\ t_k\to0,\ \frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to v\right\},\qquad \dim T_xS:=\dim(\operatorname{span}T_xS).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial and feasible-direction cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(x\in C\). No closedness is needed for the unclosed local cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the pair distinguishes immediately realizable directions from their limiting closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The radial cone and feasible-direction cone of \(C\) at \(x\) are respectively \[R_C(x):=\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\{\alpha(y-x):\alpha\ge0,\ y\in C\},\] \[F_C(x):=\{d:\exists\delta>0\ \text{such that}\ x+td\in C\ \forall t\in[0,\delta]\}.\] Convexity gives the exact identification \[R_C(x)=F_C(x),\] and the associated closed tangent cone is their common closure: \[T_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}R_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}F_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial cone contains all nonnegative multiples of displacements from the base point. The feasible-direction cone contains directions along which a short segment remains in the convex set. For a convex set these two cones coincide, and their closure is the tangent cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in R_C(x)\iff \exists t>0:\ x+td\in C.\]
By convexity, the existence of one such \(t>0\) implies \(x+\tau d\in C\) for every \(0\le\tau\le t\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), then \(R_C(x)=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)\), hence it is already closed.
If \(C=K\) is a convex cone and \(x=0\), then \(R_K(0)=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(R_C(x)\subseteq T_C(x)\), with equality exactly when the radial cone is closed.
The gap between radial and tangent directions consists solely of limiting directions.
boundary_notes: Without convexity, the one-step radial cone and the short-segment feasible cone need not coincide.
Some authors use “feasible-direction cone” for its closure; under that convention it equals the tangent cone rather than the radial cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Direction Cone of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-constraint representation of the feasible-direction cone at a point of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge b\}\), let \(\bar x\in X\), and define \(\alpha(\bar x)=\{i:A_i\bar x=b_i\}\). Then \(\mathcal F(\bar x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:A_i v\ge0\text{ for every }i\in\alpha(\bar x)\}\) is the polyhedral cone of feasible directions at \(\bar x\); strictly, its nonzero members are the directions. If \(\alpha(\bar x)=\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal F(\bar x)=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron, feasible directions satisfy the homogeneous inequalities corresponding to the active constraints. Together with zero they form a polyhedral cone, which is the whole space when no constraint is active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F(\bar x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:(\forall i\in\alpha(\bar x))\ A_i v\ge0\},\qquad \alpha(\bar x)=\varnothing\Rightarrow\mathcal F(\bar x)=\mathbb R^n

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:Ay\leq b\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(x\in C\), and define \(I(x):=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\), where \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) is row \(i\) of \(A\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in C\). Then \(R_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}(C-x)\) is a convex cone containing \(C-x\), and it is the smallest cone containing \(C-x\). Equivalently, for \(d_1,d_2\in R_C(x)\) and \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\), one has \(\alpha d_1+\beta d_2\in R_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set, the radial cone is a convex cone and is the smallest cone containing all displacements from the base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_C(x)\text{ is a convex cone and }R_C(x)=\bigcap\{K:K\text{ is a cone and }C-x\subseteq K\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in C\). The feasible-direction cone is \[F_C(x):=\{d\in X:\exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall t\in[0,\varepsilon],\ x+td\in C\}.\] Convexity gives \[F_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=R_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is feasible at x if sufficiently small nonnegative steps along it remain in C. For a convex set, the feasible-direction cone equals the radial cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This closed nonconvex one-dimensional set shows that convexity cannot simply be dropped from the feasible-direction/radial-cone equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{0\}\cup[1,2]\subset\mathbb R\) and \(x=0\). For the small-step convention, \[F_C(0)=\{d:\exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall t\in[0,\varepsilon],\ td\in C\}=\{0\},\] whereas \[R_C(0)=\operatorname{cone}(C)=[0,\infty).\] Thus \(F_C(0)\ne R_C(0)\) when convexity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the nonconvex set consisting of zero and the interval from one to two, no nonzero direction permits all sufficiently small steps, although every nonnegative direction is radial. Thus feasible and radial directions need not coincide without convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|_2\leq1\}\) and \(x=(1,0)\). Then \[R_C(x)=\{0\}\cup\{d=(d_1,d_2)\in\mathbb R^2:d_1<0\},\] which is not closed, whereas \[\overline{R_C(x)}=\{d=(d_1,d_2)\in\mathbb R^2:d_1\leq0\}=T_C(x).\] In particular, every nonzero vertical direction lies in \(T_C(x)\setminus R_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the rightmost boundary point of the Euclidean unit disk, the radial cone contains only zero and directions pointing strictly left. Its closure also contains vertical tangent directions, so the radial cone is strictly smaller than the closed tangent cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in C\). The closed tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[T_C(x):=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}=\overline{R_C(x)}.\] Equivalently, \[T_C(x)=\left\{d\in X:\exists\,t_n\downarrow0,\ \exists\,x_n\in C,\ \frac{x_n-x}{t_n}\to d\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed tangent cone at x is the norm closure of the radial cone. Equivalently, its directions are limits of rescaled displacements from x to nearby points of C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Distance Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This metric formulation characterizes the closed tangent cone of a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). For every \(d\in X\),
\[
d\in T_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x+td,C)}{t}=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is tangent exactly when a step of length t in that direction misses the set by an amount negligible relative to t.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Closed-Cone Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the structural universal property of the closed tangent cone for a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real normed vector space, let \(C\subset X\) be convex, and let \(x\in C\). Then \(T_C(x)\) is a closed convex cone and is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(C-x\). Equivalently, for every closed convex cone \(K\subset X\),
\[
C-x\subseteq K\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_C(x)\subseteq K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed tangent cone is the smallest closed convex cone containing all displacements from the base point to the set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C(x)\text{ is the smallest closed convex cone containing }C-x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Interior Characterization by Tangent and Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite dimensionality permits the equivalence without separately assuming that the convex set has nonempty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that \(\mathcal H\) is finite-dimensional. Let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(x\in C\). Then
\[
x\in\operatorname{int}C\iff T_Cx=\mathcal H\iff N_Cx=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, a point of a nonempty convex set is an ambient interior point exactly when its tangent cone is the whole space, equivalently when its normal cone is trivial.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand contingent cone and associated normal cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded evidence. The extracted convex-set formula displays \(\overline{\mathbb R(\Omega-x)}\), which is inconsistent with the standard contingent-cone formula unless a nonnegative-scalar marker was lost; that clause is therefore not asserted here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne\Omega\subset\mathbb R^N\) and \(x\in\overline\Omega\). A vector \(h\in\mathbb R^N\) belongs to the Bouligand contingent cone \(T_x\Omega\) if there exist \(\varepsilon_n>0\) with \(\varepsilon_n\searrow0\) and \(x_n\in\Omega\) such that \((x_n-x)/\varepsilon_n\to h\). The associated normal cone is \((-T_x\Omega)^*\). The cone \(T_x\Omega\) is closed; if \(\Omega\) is convex, it is also convex. If \(x\in\operatorname{int}\Omega\), then \(T_x\Omega=\mathbb R^N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand contingent cone consists of limits of scaled feasible displacements. It is closed, is convex when the underlying set is convex, and equals the whole space at an interior point. The associated normal cone is the dual of its negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_x\Omega=\left\{h:\exists\varepsilon_n\searrow0,\ \exists x_n\in\Omega,\ \frac{x_n-x}{\varepsilon_n}\to h\right\},\quad N_\Omega(x)=(-T_x\Omega)^*;\quad T_x\Omega\text{ is closed};\quad \Omega\text{ convex}\Rightarrow T_x\Omega\text{ convex};\quad x\in\operatorname{int}\Omega\Rightarrow T_x\Omega=\mathbb R^N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Cone via Limiting Secant Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential tangent-cone definition by limits of normalized secants, with no convexity assumption on the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in X\). A vector \(y\) is tangent to \(X\) at \(x\) if \(y=0\), or if \(y\ne0\) and there exists a sequence \(x^k\in X\setminus\{x\}\) such that
\[
x^k\to x,
\qquad
\frac{x^k-x}{\|x^k-x\|}\to\frac{y}{\|y\|}.
\]
The set of all such vectors is the tangent cone \(T_X(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero is tangent to the set at the point. A nonzero vector is tangent when its direction is the limit of directions from the point to distinct points of the set converging to it. All such vectors form the tangent cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Duality and the Core Regime for Convex Tangent and Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The polar identities hold for every point of the convex set. Core membership implies the full tangent-space condition but is not asserted to be equivalent to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(x\in C\). Then
\[
(T_Cx)^\ominus=N_Cx,\qquad (N_Cx)^\ominus=T_Cx.
\]
Moreover,
\[
x\in\operatorname{core}C\implies T_Cx=\mathcal H,
\qquad
T_Cx=\mathcal H\iff N_Cx=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a nonempty convex set, the closed tangent cone and normal cone are negative polars of one another. Core membership implies that the tangent cone is the whole Hilbert space, and a full tangent cone is equivalent to a trivial normal cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand tangent cone of a closed convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and closed-conical-hull representations at a boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\bar x\in\partial Q\). Define
\[
\mathcal T_Q(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists x_k\in Q,\ x_k\to\bar x,\ \frac{x_k-\bar x}{t_k}\to v\right\}
\]
and \(\mathcal K(S):=\{\lambda s:\lambda\geq0,\ s\in S\}\). Then
\[
Q-\bar x\subseteq\mathcal T_Q(\bar x),\qquad
\mathcal T_Q(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\mathcal K(Q-\bar x)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set, every displacement from the point is tangent, and the Bouligand tangent cone equals the closure of the conical hull of all such displacements.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal T_Q(\bar x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists x_k\in Q,\ x_k\to\bar x,\ (x_k-\bar x)/t_k\to v\right\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q-\bar x\subseteq\mathcal T_Q(\bar x)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal T_Q(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\mathcal K(Q-\bar x)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-interior and boundary tangent regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(L:=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)\), and let \(x\in C\). Tangent cones are understood relative to the affine hull through the subspace \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the classification separates full-dimensional interior, relative interior, and relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tangent location regime of \(x\) is determined by its membership in \(\operatorname{int}C\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\), or \(\operatorname{rbd}C\). Precisely, \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff T_C(x)=L.\] Consequently, if \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(L=\mathbb R^n\) and \(T_C(x)=\mathbb R^n\). If \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}C\), then \(T_C(x)\subsetneq L\) is a proper closed convex cone and has a nonzero supporting normal relative to \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every relative-interior point, the tangent cone is the full subspace parallel to the affine hull. At an ordinary interior point this is the whole ambient space. At a relative-boundary point the tangent cone is a proper cone inside the affine-hull direction space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff N_C(x)=L^\perp.\]
For full-dimensional \(C\), \[x\in\operatorname{int}C\iff N_C(x)=\{0\}\iff T_C(x)=\mathbb R^n.\]
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedron, the relative-boundary regime is determined by its active inequalities.
For a singleton, \(L=\{0\}\), its unique point lies in the relative interior, and its tangent cone is \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only relative-boundary points yield a proper tangent approximation within \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
The normal cone enlarges as the point moves from relative interior to lower-dimensional facial locations.
boundary_notes: Ordinary interior is empty for lower-dimensional convex sets, so relative interior is the intrinsic notion.
A boundary point of a full-dimensional set may still have a tangent cone containing a nontrivial lineality space.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary point of a closed convex set with nonempty interior, there is a nonzero supporting normal. Every tangent direction lies in the corresponding closed halfspace, so the tangent cone is not the whole space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex normal-cone field
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. The Euclidean inner product identifies linear functionals with vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-analytic normal cones; this is not a nonconvex limiting-normal construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in C\), the normal cone is \[N_C(x):=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\langle s,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}.\] The normal-cone family is the set-valued mapping \(N_C:C\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), \(x\mapsto N_C(x)\). Equivalently, \(s\in N_C(x)\) when the linear functional \(y\mapsto\langle s,y\rangle\) attains its maximum over \(C\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal-cone family assigns to each point all vectors defining supporting half-spaces of the convex set at that point. A vector is normal precisely when its linear functional is maximized at the base point.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s\in N_C(x)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle.\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\iff x=P_C(x+s).\]
\[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
For \(C=\{y:\langle a,y\rangle\le b\}\) and \(\langle a,x\rangle=b\), \(N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+a\).
For a polyhedron, the normal cone is generated by the normals of active inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each \(N_C(x)\) is a closed convex cone containing \(0\).
boundary_notes: At points outside \(C\), this record does not define a normal cone.
For nonconvex sets, proximal, regular, and limiting normal cones are generally different.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone consequence of attaining a nonconstant convex function's maximum over a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and let \(C\) be convex. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting-inequality representation of the normal cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise inequality characterization of the normal cone to a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, and let $\mathbf{x}\in S$. Then
\[
N_S(\mathbf{x})=\left\{\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \mathbf{z}^{T}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})\leq 0\text{ for all }\mathbf{y}\in S\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point x of a nonempty convex set S, the normal cone consists exactly of the vectors z whose inner product with y minus x is nonpositive for every y in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Vectors and Feasible Chord Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-vector geometry for a convex set, together with its constrained first-order interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex and $x^*\in Q$. A vector $a\in\mathbb R^n$ supports $Q$ at $x^*$ if $\langle a,x-x^*angle\leq0$ for every $x\in Q$; if $a
eq0$, the equation $\langle a,x-x^*angle=0$ defines a supporting hyperplane. For each $x\in Q$, the vector $s=x-x^*$ is a feasible chord direction because $x^*+\alpha s\in Q$ for all $\alpha\in[0,1]$. If, additionally, $x^*$ is a local minimizer of a function differentiable at $x^*$, then $-
abla f(x^*)$ supports $Q$ and $f'(x^*;s)=\langle
abla f(x^*),sangle\geq0$ for every such direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting vector pairs nonpositively with every chord from the base point into the convex set. Every such chord remains feasible along its unit segment. At a differentiable constrained local minimizer, the negative gradient is supporting, so all these directional derivatives are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is differentiable at }x^*\text{ for the optimality conclusion}
x^*\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\text{ over }Q\text{ for the optimality conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall x\in Q,\ \langle a,x-x^*\rangle\leq0\right];\quad s=x-x^*\Rightarrow x^*+\alpha s\in Q\ \forall\alpha\in[0,1];\quad -\nabla f(x^*)\text{ supports }Q\text{ and }f'(x^*;s)\geq0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximizer and Orientation Tests for Supporting Normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive rescaling preserves the oriented supporting halfspace. Reversing the normal generally does not; both orientations support at the same point exactly when the whole set lies in the contact hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(v\neq0\). Then \(v\) is a supporting normal to \(C\) at \(x\) if and only if \[x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle v,y\rangle,\] equivalently \(\sigma_C(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\). If \(v\) is supporting, then every \(\lambda v\), \(\lambda>0\), is supporting at \(x\). Moreover, both \(v\) and \(-v\) are supporting at \(x\) if and only if \(C\subset H(v,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector supports the set at x exactly when x maximizes its linear functional. Positive multiples preserve support, while the opposite orientation also supports precisely when the entire set lies in the contact hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ supports }C\text{ at }x\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle v,y\rangle\iff\sigma_C(v)=\langle v,x\rangle, with positive-ray invariance and the stated criterion for reversal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Fréchet normals to a convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the global relaxed supporting inequality and recovers the convex-analysis normal cone when the error is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(\Omega\subset X\) be convex, and let \(\bar x\in\Omega\). For every \(\varepsilon\ge 0\),
\[
\widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;\Omega)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\le \varepsilon\|x-\bar x\|\ \text{for every }x\in\Omega\right\}.
\]
In particular, \(\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)\) is the normal cone of convex analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set, approximate Fréchet normals are exactly the functionals satisfying a global supporting inequality with error proportional to distance. At zero error this becomes the usual convex normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat N_\varepsilon(\bar x;\Omega)=\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\le \varepsilon\|x-\bar x\|\ \forall x\in\Omega\},\qquad \widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=N_{\mathrm{conv}}(\bar x;\Omega)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal cone as the cone of exposing directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For \(s\in\mathbb R^n\), define the exposed face \(F_C(s):=\{y\in C:\langle s,y\rangle=\sigma_C(s)\}\), where \(\sigma_C(s):=\sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial geometry; empty exposed faces are allowed when the support supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial normal-cone geometry at \(x\in C\) is the incidence correspondence \[N_C(x)=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:x\in F_C(s)\}=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle=\sigma_C(s)\}.\] Hence the normal cone consists exactly of directions exposing faces that contain \(x\). If \(F\) is a face of \(C\) and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), its facial normal cone is well defined by \[N_C(F):=N_C(x),\] because this value is constant on \(\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal geometry and facial geometry are linked by incidence: a vector is normal at a point exactly when that point belongs to the face exposed by the vector. The normal cone is constant over the relative interior of a fixed face, so it can be attached to the face itself.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[N_C(x)=\{s:x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle\}.\]
special_cases_latex: At a relative-interior point of \(C\), \(N_C(x)=\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp\).
For a polyhedron, points with the same active face have the same cone generated by active constraint normals.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F\subseteq G\) are faces and both relative interiors are nonempty, then \(N_C(G)\subseteq N_C(F)\).
A nonzero element of \(N_C(x)\) identifies a supporting hyperplane through \(x\).
boundary_notes: Different faces may share the same normal cone when the facial structure is not exposed sufficiently to distinguish them.
The whole set is the face exposed by \(s=0\).

normal cone at any relative-interior point of F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outside the polyhedral regime, a proper facial inclusion can preserve the normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(s)=(\max\{s,0\})^2,\qquad C=\operatorname{epi}f\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
and set
\[
F=\{(0,0)\},\qquad G=\{(s,0):s\leq0\}.
\]
Then \(F\subsetneq G\) are faces of \(C\), \((0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and \((s,0)\in\operatorname{ri}G\) for every \(s<0\), but
\[
N_C(0,0)=N_C(s,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\geq0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The endpoint of a flat boundary ray can be a proper subface while having the same downward normal ray as the relative interior of the larger face.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Normal-Cone Growth for Polyhedral Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral facial incidence strengthens the general inclusion to strict inclusion for proper face containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and let \(F\subsetneq G\) be nonempty faces of \(C\). If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(z\in\operatorname{ri}G\), then
\[
N_C(z)\subsetneq N_C(x).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\dim N_C(x)=n-\dim F,\qquad \dim N_C(z)=n-\dim G.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For polyhedra, descending properly to a smaller face strictly enlarges the normal cone; its dimension is the ambient dimension minus the face dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_C(z)\subsetneq N_C(x),\qquad \dim N_C(x)=n-\dim F,\quad \dim N_C(z)=n-\dim G.

notation.meaning: dimension of the affine hull of face F

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Normal-Cone Growth for Polyhedral Faces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A proper facial inclusion can preserve the normal cone in nonpolyhedral geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(s)=\max\{0,s^2\},\qquad C=\operatorname{epi}f\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
and define
\[
F=\{(0,0)\},\qquad G=\{(s,0):s\leq0\}.
\]
Then \(F\subsetneq G\) are faces of \(C\), \((0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and every \((s,0)\) with \(s<0\) lies in \(\operatorname{ri}G\), but
\[
N_C(0,0)=N_C(s,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\geq0\}.
\]
Thus the order-reversing normal-cone inclusion associated with \(F\subsetneq G\) need not be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The endpoint of a flat boundary ray can be a proper subface while having the same downward normal ray as the relative interior of the larger face. Proper face inclusion therefore need not cause strict normal-cone growth.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Inclusion Need Not Strictly Enlarge Normal Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-normal and multi-normal regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional closed convex set and let \(x\in C\). The normal cone \(N_C(x)\) contains all outward supporting directions at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional finite-dimensional convex sets; smoothness here is defined only through uniqueness of the supporting normal ray, not differentiability of a parametrized boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A boundary point \(x\in\partial C\) is in the single-normal regime when there exists a nonzero vector \(n_x\), unique up to positive scaling, such that \[N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+n_x.\] It is in the multi-normal regime when \(N_C(x)\) contains two non-collinear nonzero vectors, equivalently \(\dim N_C(x)\ge2\). Interior points form the zero-normal regime, characterized by \[N_C(x)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary point is single-normal when all supporting normals lie on one ray. It is multi-normal when at least two non-collinear supporting normals occur. Interior points have only the zero normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed, convex, and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\begin{cases}N_C(x)=\{0\},&x\in\operatorname{int}C,\\N_C(x)=\mathbb R_+n_x,&x\in\partial C\ \text{in the single-normal regime},\\\dim N_C(x)\ge2,&x\in\partial C\ \text{in the multi-normal regime}.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The single-normal condition is equivalent to uniqueness, up to positive scaling, of the nonzero linear functional maximized over \(C\) at \(x\).
The multi-normal condition is equivalent to the existence of distinct supporting hyperplanes through \(x\) with nonparallel normals.
special_cases_latex: A boundary point of a closed half-space is single-normal.
A vertex of a full-dimensional polyhedron is typically multi-normal; its normal cone is generated by the active facet normals.
immediate_consequences_latex: In the single-normal regime, \(T_C(x)=\{d:\langle n_x,d\rangle\le0\}\).
In the multi-normal regime, \(T_C(x)\) is the intersection of at least two nonredundant supporting homogeneous half-spaces.
boundary_notes: For lower-dimensional \(C\), every normal cone contains \(\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp\); an intrinsic smoothness convention should quotient out that subspace.
Uniqueness of a normal ray does not by itself assert second-order smoothness or curvature.

notation.meaning: representative nonzero outward normal at x
nonnegative ray generated by the normal

assumptions_latex: \(x_k\to x\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in N_C(x_k)\) for every \(k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), the normal-cone mapping has closed graph: if \(x_k\to x\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in N_C(x_k)\) for every \(k\), then \(v\in N_C(x)\). At a point with multiple unit normal directions, the set \(N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) contains more than one element. Thus every convergent selection of nearby normals has a limit that remains normal at the limiting point, without asserting that all normal directions are realized at distinct nearby smooth points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limits of normals at converging points remain normal at the limit point. Normal multiplicity means that the unit-normal section at the limiting point contains more than one direction; this does not imply that every such direction occurs at a distinct nearby smooth point.
