knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Inner Semicontinuity at a Multiplicity Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-graph outer stability does not make every limiting-point normal approximable along an arbitrary convergent sequence of nearby points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb{R}_+^2\), \(x=(0,0)\), and \(x_k=(1/k,0)\). Then \(x_k\to x\), while
\[
N_C(x)=\mathbb{R}_-^2,
\qquad
N_C(x_k)=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}_-.
\]
Consequently \((-1,-1)\in N_C(x)\), but no sequence \(v_k\in N_C(x_k)\) converges to \((-1,-1)\). Thus the normal-cone mapping can fail to be inner semicontinuous where normal multiplicity increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the quadrant's vertex the normal cone gains horizontal negative components that cannot be approximated while approaching along one edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Inner Semicontinuity at a Multiplicity Transition

children.title: Tangent-Normal Polarity
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence between feasible local directions and supporting normals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mutual polarity of tangent and normal cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\in C\), and use the negative polar \(K^\circ:=\{s:\langle s,d\rangle\le0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets with closed tangent cones and the negative-polar sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Tangent-normal polarity at \(x\) is the mutual-polar relation \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,\qquad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\] Equivalently, a vector \(s\) is normal at \(x\) precisely when it pairs nonpositively with every tangent direction, and a vector \(d\) is tangent precisely when it pairs nonpositively with every normal: \[s\in N_C(x)\iff \langle s,d\rangle\le0\ \forall d\in T_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent and normal cones at a point are exact polar duals. Normals are precisely the vectors nonpositive on every tangent direction, and tangent directions are precisely the vectors nonpositive on every normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in T_C(x)\iff \sup_{s\in N_C(x)}\langle s,d\rangle\le0.\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\iff \sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y-x\rangle\le0.\]
special_cases_latex: At an interior point, the polar pair is \((\mathbb R^n,\{0\})\).
At the vertex of a closed convex cone \(K\), the pair is \((K,K^\circ)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Inclusion reverses under polarity: enlargement of the tangent cone corresponds to contraction of the normal cone.
Each cone determines the other uniquely.
boundary_notes: Using the positive dual cone changes the sign in the pairing.
For nonconvex sets, regular and limiting tangent-normal constructions need not be mutual polars.

notation.meaning: negative polar of a cone K

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This sharpens the seed's assumptions when the tangent cone is defined as the closed conic hull of C-x; the set C itself need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(x\in C\), and define \[T_C(x)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)},\qquad N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}.\] With \(K^\circ=\{v:\langle v,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\), one has \[N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\quad\text{and}\quad T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local tangent-normal bilinear pairing
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, let \(x\in C\), and let \(T:=T_C(x)\) and \(N:=N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local primal-dual geometry at one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local polar pairing is the restriction of the Euclidean bilinear form to \(N\times T\): \[\pi_x:N\times T\to\mathbb R_-,\qquad \pi_x(s,d):=\langle s,d\rangle.\] Its defining order property is \(\pi_x(s,d)\le0\) for all \((s,d)\in N\times T\), together with the recovery formulas \[N=\{s:\pi_x(s,d)\le0\ \forall d\in T\},\qquad T=\{d:\pi_x(s,d)\le0\ \forall s\in N\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local polar pairing evaluates a normal against a tangent direction. It is always nonpositive, and either local cone can be recovered as the set of all vectors pairing nonpositively with the other cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\pi_x(s,d)=\langle s,d\rangle\le0\quad\forall(s,d)\in N_C(x)\times T_C(x),\] with each cone equal to the polar determined by this pairing.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For subsets \(D\subseteq T\) and \(S\subseteq N\), define \[D^{\triangle}:=\{s\in N:\langle s,d\rangle=0\ \forall d\in D\},\quad S^{\triangle}:=\{d\in T:\langle s,d\rangle=0\ \forall s\in S\}.\] These are the zero-pair sets induced by \(\pi_x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(N=\{0\}\), the pairing is identically zero and \(T=\mathbb R^n\).
For \(C=K\) and \(x=0\), the pairing is the usual polar pairing between \(K^\circ\) and \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The zero level \(\langle s,d\rangle=0\) selects complementary tangent and normal directions.
The pairing is invariant under positive rescaling of either cone element.
boundary_notes: Nonpositive pairing is the polar condition; equality is the stronger complementarity condition.
The codomain \(\mathbb R_-\) follows from the negative-polar convention.

children.title: Tangent-Normal Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Orthogonal relationships between active directions and normals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary tangent-normal pairs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, \(x\in C\), \(d\in T_C(x)\), and \(s\in N_C(x)\). Polarity always gives \(\langle s,d\rangle\le0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional first-order complementarity at a fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tangent-normal pair \((d,s)\) is complementary at \(x\) when \[d\in T_C(x),\qquad s\in N_C(x),\qquad \langle s,d\rangle=0.\] For fixed \(s\), the complementary tangent directions form the exposed cone face \[F_T(s):=T_C(x)\cap s^\perp.\] For fixed \(d\), the complementary normals form \[F_N(d):=N_C(x)\cap d^\perp.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent direction and a normal are complementary when their polar inequality is active, meaning that they are orthogonal. Fixing either member selects the orthogonal exposed face of the opposite cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in F_T(s)\iff s\in F_N(d).\]
\[F_T(s)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in T_C(x)}\langle s,v\rangle,\] where the maximum equals \(0\).
special_cases_latex: For cone projection, \(d=P_K(z)\) and \(s=P_{K^\circ}(z)\) form a complementary pair.
For a polyhedron, complementary tangent directions keep every constraint with a positive normal multiplier active to first order.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Faces of the Local Polar Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-reversing correspondence for exposed faces of the mutually polar tangent and normal cones, including its exact nonexposed-face boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=T_C(x)\) and \(K^\circ=N_C(x)\). For a nonempty face \(F\unlhd K\), define \(F^\triangle:=K^\circ\cap F^\perp\), and define conjugation symmetrically for faces of \(K^\circ\). Then \(F^\triangle\) is an exposed face of \(K^\circ\), and \(F^{\triangle\triangle}\) is the smallest exposed face of \(K\) containing \(F\). Consequently, \(F^{\triangle\triangle}=F\) exactly when \(F\) is exposed, and conjugation restricts to an inclusion-reversing bijection between the exposed faces of \(K\) and those of \(K^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal conjugation reverses inclusion and bijects the exposed faces of the tangent and normal cones. For a nonexposed face, double conjugation instead returns its smallest exposed hull.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x\in C\).
\(K=T_C(x)\) and \(K^\circ=N_C(x)\) use the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{\triangle\triangle}=F\ \Longleftrightarrow\ F\text{ is exposed},\quad\text{and }F\mapsto F^\triangle\text{ bijects the exposed faces of }T_C(x)\text{ and }N_C(x)\text{ in reverse order}.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, \(x\in C\), and \(s\in N_C(x)\). Define the exposed face \(F_C(s):=\{y\in C:\langle s,y\rangle=\langle s,x\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exposed facial geometry localized at a point belonging to the exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial interpretation of local polarity associates with \(s\in N_C(x)\) the directions on which the polar inequality is active. These directions are simultaneously the tangent cone to the exposed face and the orthogonal face of the tangent cone: \[T_{F_C(s)}(x)=T_C(x)\cap s^\perp=\{d\in T_C(x):\langle s,d\rangle=0\}.\] Thus strict negativity identifies directions entering below the supporting hyperplane, while equality identifies first-order motion within the face exposed by \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal exposes a face containing the base point. The tangent directions that remain in that exposed face are exactly the tangent directions orthogonal to the normal. Hence the zero set of the local polar pairing is the tangent geometry of the exposed face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in T_{F_C(s)}(x)\iff d\in T_C(x)\ \text{and}\ \langle s,d\rangle=0.\]
\[s\in N_C(x)\iff x\in F_C(s).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(s=0\), then \(F_C(0)=C\) and the identity is tautological.
For a polyhedron, choosing an active facet normal restricts the tangent cone by turning that active inequality into an equality.
immediate_consequences_latex: The complementary tangent directions form an exposed face of \(T_C(x)\).
Several active normals intersect their orthogonal tangent faces and thereby describe lower-dimensional local facial motion.
boundary_notes: Only exposed faces arise directly from a single normal vector.
The identity concerns first-order geometry at \(x\); it does not assert that nearby boundary points lie on a smooth manifold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calculus of tangent and normal cone fields
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let all sets below be nonempty, closed, and convex in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let every base point belong to the indicated set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact product and Minkowski-sum rules together with unconditional intersection inclusions; closure is retained where linear images or cone sums need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Local cone calculus is the collection of operation rules transporting tangent-normal pairs through convex-set constructions. In particular, \[T_{C_1\times C_2}(x_1,x_2)=T_{C_1}(x_1)\times T_{C_2}(x_2),\quad N_{C_1\times C_2}(x_1,x_2)=N_{C_1}(x_1)\times N_{C_2}(x_2),\] and \[T_{C_1+C_2}(x_1+x_2)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(T_{C_1}(x_1)+T_{C_2}(x_2)\bigr),\quad N_{C_1+C_2}(x_1+x_2)=N_{C_1}(x_1)\cap N_{C_2}(x_2).\] For intersections, the unconditional relations are \[T_{C_1\cap C_2}(x)\subseteq T_{C_1}(x)\cap T_{C_2}(x),\quad N_{C_1\cap C_2}(x)\supseteq N_{C_1}(x)+N_{C_2}(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local cone calculus transports tangent and normal cones through products, sums, intersections, and affine operations. Products and Minkowski sums have the displayed exact rules, while intersections give inclusions unless a qualification condition is added.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in C_i\), and \(x\in C_1\cap C_2\) for the intersection rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tangent-normal assignments obey the displayed product, Minkowski-sum, and intersection rules.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The normal formulas are polar counterparts of the tangent formulas under \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: Cartesian powers satisfy \(T_{C^m}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\prod_iT_C(x_i)\).
Translation does not change cone shape: \(T_{C+b}(x+b)=T_C(x)\) and \(N_{C+b}(x+b)=N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite products and sums follow by iteration.
Qualification conditions are needed specifically where an unconditional inclusion may be strict.
boundary_notes: Closure in a tangent image or sum cannot be discarded without an additional closedness condition.
The rules are stated for convex sets; nonconvex tangent-normal calculi require different qualifications.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine transport of local cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(A(z)=b+A_0z\) with linear part \(A_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(x\in C\), \(y=A(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct affine images; closures and adjoint preimages are retained to cover noninjective and non-surjective maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local tangent cone transported from \(C\) through \(A\) is \[T_{A(C)}(y)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(A_0T_C(x)\bigr).\] The normal cone transforms contravariantly: \[N_{A(C)}(y)=\{v\in\mathbb R^m:A_0^*v\in N_C(x)\},\] whenever \(x\) represents the local fiber at \(y\); in general the right-hand condition must hold for every \(z\in C\) with \(A(z)=y\). Thus tangent directions are pushed forward by \(A_0\), while normals are pulled back by its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an affine map, tangent directions are sent forward by the linear part and then closed. A vector normal to the image is characterized by its adjoint pullback being normal to the original set at every point in the relevant fiber.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
For the single-point normal formula, the fiber \(C\cap A^{-1}(A(x))\) has the same normal pullback condition as at \(x\), in particular when \(A_0\) is injective on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{A(C)}(A(x))=\operatorname{cl}(A_0T_C(x)),\qquad N_{A(C)}(A(x))=\{v:A_0^*v\in N_C(x)\}\] in the stated single-fiber regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For arbitrary fibers, \[N_{A(C)}(y)=\{v:A_0^*v\in\bigcap_{z\in C,\ A(z)=y}N_C(z)\}.\]
For a translation \(A_0=I\), \[T_{C+b}(x+b)=T_C(x),\qquad N_{C+b}(x+b)=N_C(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A_0\) is an orthogonal isomorphism, the closure is unnecessary and both cones are rotated by \(A_0\).
If \(C=C_1\times C_2\) and \(A_0(x_1,x_2)=x_1+x_2\), the tangent formula yields the Minkowski-sum rule.

Loss of directions under a rank-deficient map is reflected dually by the adjoint condition on normals.
boundary_notes: A linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed, which explains the closure in the tangent formula.
For a nontrivial fiber, using the normal cone at only one arbitrary preimage can overstate the image normal cone.

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification and Degeneracy of Linearized Local Cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), where each \(c_j\) is convex, and let \(\bar x\in C\). Write \(J(\bar x)=\{j:c_j(\bar x)=0\}\), let \(T_C(\bar x)\) and \(N_C(\bar x)\) be the tangent and normal cones, and define the constraint-linearized cones \(T'(\bar x)\) and \(N'(\bar x)\) below.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex constraint systems; the definition distinguishes exact local cone calculus from representation-dependent degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linearized tangent cone and generated normal cone at \(\bar x\) are
\[T'(\bar x):=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Ad=0,\ c_j'(\bar x;d)\leq0\ \forall j\in J(\bar x)\},\]
\[N'(\bar x):=\left\{A^\top\lambda+\sum_{j\in J(\bar x)}\mu_js_j:\lambda\in\mathbb R^m,\ \mu_j\geq0,\ s_j\in\partial c_j(\bar x)\right\}.\]
The representation is qualified for local cone calculus at \(\bar x\) when
\[T_C(\bar x)=T'(\bar x)\quad\text{and}\quad N_C(\bar x)=N'(\bar x).\]
Its qualification boundary consists of feasible points where at least one equality fails. A primal degeneracy is \(T_C(\bar x)\subsetneq T'(\bar x)\); a dual degeneracy is \(N'(\bar x)\subsetneq N_C(\bar x)\), including the case in which \(N'(\bar x)\) is nonclosed and only \(\operatorname{cl}N'(\bar x)\) agrees with \(N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set represented by affine equalities and convex inequalities, the constraint data define a linearized tangent cone from the active directional inequalities and a generated normal cone from equality normals and nonnegative combinations of active subgradients. Local cone calculus is qualified at a feasible point precisely when these data-derived cones equal the intrinsic tangent and normal cones. The qualification boundary is the set of feasible points where either equality fails. Thus degeneracy is representation-dependent: the same feasible set can have exact cone formulas under one constraint representation and strict inclusions under another.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) and every \(c_j\) is convex and directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
The tangent and normal cones use the Euclidean finite-dimensional convention, with \(N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\text{ is a qualification-boundary point}\iff T_C(\bar x)\neq T'(\bar x)\ \text{or}\ N_C(\bar x)\neq N'(\bar x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The basic constraint qualification at \(\bar x\) is the dual equality \(N'(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\); it entails closedness of \(N'(\bar x)\) and the corresponding tangent equality.
Failure can be detected by a direction in \(T'(\bar x)\setminus T_C(\bar x)\) or a normal in \(N_C(\bar x)\setminus N'(\bar x)\).
special_cases_latex: For affine equalities and affine inequalities, \(N_C(\bar x)=\operatorname{Im}A^\top+\operatorname{cone}\{s_j:j\in J(\bar x)\}\), so the basic qualification holds at every feasible point.
Representing \(C\) by \(\tfrac12d_C(x)^2\leq0\) gives a zero generated normal at boundary points and can therefore create degeneracy.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a qualified point, intrinsic first-order conditions may be written entirely using active constraint data.
At an unqualified point, replacing \(T_C\) by \(T'\) or \(N_C\) by \(N'\) can lose necessary local information.
boundary_notes: The definition concerns exact first-order cone calculus, not metric regularity or second-order constraint qualifications.
Equality with \(\operatorname{cl}N'(\bar x)\) alone does not remove the multiplier-attainment failure caused by a nonclosed \(N'(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Active inequality index set at the feasible point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separating and Supporting Affine Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\). For \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), set \(H(a,\beta)=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\beta\}\), with closed half-spaces \(H^-(a,\beta)\) and \(H^+(a,\beta)\) defined by \(\leq\beta\) and \(\geq\beta\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine-hyperplane geometry for arbitrary nonempty sets, with convexity imposed when separation and support existence results are invoked.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine hyperplane \(H(a,\beta)\) separates nonempty sets \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) when
\[A\subseteq H^-(a,\beta),\qquad B\subseteq H^+(a,\beta),\]
equivalently
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
It strictly separates them when both displayed half-space inclusions use open half-spaces, equivalently
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\beta<\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
The hyperplane supports a nonempty set \(C\) when \(C\) lies in one closed half-space and meets the hyperplane; in the chosen orientation,
\[C\subseteq H^-(a,\beta),\qquad C\cap H(a,\beta)\neq\varnothing.\]
The contact set \(C\cap H(a,\beta)\) is the exposed face selected by \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero normal and scalar define an affine hyperplane and its two half-spaces. The hyperplane separates two sets when they lie in opposite closed half-spaces and strictly separates them when they lie in opposite open half-spaces. It supports a set when the entire set lies on one closed side and at least one point of the set lies on the hyperplane. For a convex set, the contact set is an exposed face. Reversing the normal exchanges the two orientations without changing the underlying hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: \(a\neq0\) so that \(H(a,\beta)\) is an affine hyperplane.
All suprema and infima are interpreted in the extended-real sense unless finiteness is explicitly required.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Separation is equivalently \(\sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)\leq0\) after translating the separating level to zero.
Support at \(x\in C\) is equivalently \(a\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta=\langle a,x\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For a cone, a supporting hyperplane at the origin is homogeneous: \(\beta=0\).
For a singleton \(B=\{z\}\), strict separation reduces to \(\sigma_A(a)<\langle a,z\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every supporting hyperplane that meets a convex set determines an exposed face.
A closed convex set equals the intersection of all closed half-spaces containing it.
boundary_notes: A half-space containing \(C\) need not support \(C\) if its boundary does not meet \(C\).

A hyperplane containing all of a lower-dimensional set is a trivial ambient support; nontrivial relative support requires a normal with nonzero component in the direction space of \(\operatorname{aff}C\).

notation.meaning: The two closed half-spaces bounded by \(H(a,\beta)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting hyperplanes and weak, strict, and strong separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-specific terminology jointly defining support, point–set separation, and set–set separation. In particular, the source calls a hyperplane supporting when the set lies in one closed halfspace, without separately requiring contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. For \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\), define
\[
\mathcal H(g,\gamma):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle g,x\rangle=\gamma\}.
\]
The hyperplane \(\mathcal H(g,\gamma)\) is supporting to \(Q\) when
\[
\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\qquad\forall x\in Q.
\]
It separates a point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) from \(Q\) when
\[
\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,x_0\rangle
aqquad\forall x\in Q.
\]
Two sets \(Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are separable when there exist \(g\neq0\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,y\rangle
\qquad\forall x\in Q_1,\ \forall y\in Q_2.
\]
The point–set or set–set separation is strict when at least one of the two inequalities in its defining condition holds strictly. The sets are strongly separable when there exist \(g\neq0\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
\sup_{x\in Q_1}\langle g,x\rangle<\gamma<\inf_{y\in Q_2}\langle g,y\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the source's convention, a supporting hyperplane places the convex set in one closed halfspace and need not separately be required to meet it. Point–set and set–set separation put the objects in opposing closed halfspaces; strict separation makes at least one defining inequality strict, while strong separation places a hyperplane strictly between the two directional bounds.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is convex for the supporting-hyperplane definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal H(g,\gamma)\text{ supports }Q\iff\forall x\in Q,\ \langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma;\quad \mathcal H(g,\gamma)\text{ separates }x_0\text{ from }Q\iff\forall x\in Q,\ \langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,x_0\rangle;\quad Q_1,Q_2\text{ are strongly separable}\iff\exists g\neq0,\exists\gamma:\sup_{x\in Q_1}\langle g,x\rangle<\gamma<\inf_{y\in Q_2}\langle g,y\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting, Separating, Strictly Separating, and Strongly Separating Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded bundled terminology for support and several strengths of finite-dimensional hyperplane separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), and let \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\). Define \[\mathcal H(g,\gamma)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle g,x\rangle=\gamma\}.\] It is a supporting hyperplane to \(Q\) when \(\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\) for every \(x\in Q\). It separates \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) from \(Q\) when \(\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,x_0\rangle\) for every \(x\in Q\); the source calls the separation strict if at least one of the two inequalities is strict. Sets \(Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are separable when there exist \(g\neq0\) and \(\gamma\) such that \(\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,y\rangle\) for every \(x\in Q_1\) and \(y\in Q_2\), again with strict separation when at least one of the two inequalities is strict. Their separation is strong when there exist \(g\neq0\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\sup_{x\in Q_1}\langle g,x\rangle<\gamma<\inf_{y\in Q_2}\langle g,y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero normal and scalar level define a hyperplane. The source defines support by containment of a convex set in the corresponding closed halfspace. Point–set and set–set separation place the level between the relevant linear-functional values; strict separation makes at least one bounding inequality strict, while strong separation places the level strictly between the supremum over the first set and the infimum over the second.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is convex for the supporting-hyperplane definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal H(g,\gamma)=\{x:\langle g,x\rangle=\gamma\};\quad [\forall x\in Q,\ \langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma]\text{ defines support};\quad [\forall x\in Q,\ \langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,x_0\rangle]\text{ defines point--set separation};\quad [\forall x\in Q_1,\forall y\in Q_2,\ \langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\leq\langle g,y\rangle]\text{ defines set separation};\quad \sup_{x\in Q_1}\langle g,x\rangle<\gamma<\inf_{y\in Q_2}\langle g,y\rangle\text{ defines strong separation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting hyperplane at every boundary point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-support theorem for nonempty closed convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x_0\in\partial Q$. Then there exist $g\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
\langle g,x\rangle\leq\gamma\quad\text{for every }x\in Q,
\qquad
\langle g,x_0\rangle=\gamma.
\]
Thus the hyperplane $\mathcal H(g,\gamma)=\{x:\langle g,x\rangle=\gamma\}$ contains $x_0$ and supports $Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set lies on a supporting hyperplane with a nonzero normal.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Separation Configurations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). A separation problem asks for a nonzero linear functional whose values order two prescribed geometric objects.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A classification of finite-dimensional convex separation problems by the objects being separated and by whether the separating hyperplane is affine or homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separation problem geometry is one of the following configurations:
\[(\mathrm{PS})\quad z\notin C,\qquad \{z\}\ \text{versus a convex set }C;\]
\[(\mathrm{SS})\quad A\cap B=\varnothing,\qquad A\ \text{versus }B;\]
\[(\mathrm{H})\quad 0\notin D,\qquad \{0\}\ \text{versus a convex set }D,\]
where the homogeneous case requires a separator through the origin. In every case, a certificate is a pair \((a,\beta)\), \(a\neq0\), satisfying
\[\sup_{x\in A_0}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\inf_{y\in B_0}\langle a,y\rangle,\]
with \((A_0,B_0)=(C,\{z\})\), \((A,B)\), or an oriented version of \((D,\{0\})\). Strict separation replaces the weak ordering by a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical separation problems have three geometries. Point-set separation compares an exterior point with a convex set. Set-set separation compares two disjoint convex sets. Homogeneous separation compares the origin with a convex set or cone and seeks a hyperplane through the origin. In each geometry, a certificate is a nonzero linear functional and a level that place the two objects in opposite closed half-spaces; a strict certificate leaves a positive interval between their functional values.
assumptions_latex: The sets named in each configuration are nonempty and convex.
The disjointness or exterior-point condition is part of the problem data, not part of the certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{A valid separation certificate orders the two image intervals under }x\mapsto\langle a,x\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Set-set separation is point-set separation of \(0\) from the difference set \(A-B\).
Point-set separation is set-set separation with one set equal to a singleton.
A separator is homogeneous exactly when its level can be chosen as \(\beta=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed convex and \(z\notin C\), the point-set geometry admits a strict certificate.
If one of two disjoint closed convex sets is bounded, the set-set geometry admits a positive-gap certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Translation by the same vector preserves separation geometry and functional gaps.
Difference-set reformulation converts many set-set questions into origin-exclusion questions.
boundary_notes: Disjointness alone does not guarantee strict separation for two unbounded convex sets.
Weak separation can be geometrically trivial in the full ambient space when both sets lie in a proper affine subspace.

notation.meaning: Point-set, set-set, and homogeneous separation configurations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Point-Set Separability
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\setminus C\). For \(a\neq0\), compare \(\langle a,z\rangle\) with the support value \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separation of one exterior point from a convex target; closedness is not built into the definition but controls the existence of a strict certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(z\) and set \(C\) are weakly separated when there exist \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\forall x\in C.\]
They are strongly separated when
\[\sigma_C(a)<\langle a,z\rangle,\]
equivalently when some \(\beta\) satisfies
\[\langle a,x\rangle<\beta<\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\forall x\in C.\]
The normalized directional margin of the certificate is
\[m(a;z,C):=\frac{\langle a,z\rangle-\sigma_C(a)}{\|a\|}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exterior point and a set are weakly separated if a nonzero linear functional places the set at or below a level and the point at or above it. They are strongly separated if the point's functional value is strictly greater than the support value of the set. Dividing this positive gap by the norm of the functional gives a scale-invariant directional margin. Reversing the functional yields the equivalent opposite orientation.
assumptions_latex: For a finite strong margin, the chosen direction satisfies \(\sigma_C(a)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z\text{ is strongly separable from }C\text{ by }a\iff m(a;z,C)>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong separation is \(\langle a,z\rangle>\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
After translation, it is homogeneous strict separation of \(0\) from \(C-z\).
For closed convex \(C\), membership has the support-function characterization \(z\in C\iff\langle a,z\rangle\leq\sigma_C(a)\) for every \(a\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed convex, every \(z\notin C\) is strongly separable from \(C\).
If \(p=P_Cz\), then \(a=z-p\) is a separating direction and the normalized gap equals \(\|z-p\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strong certificate proves \(z\notin\operatorname{cl}C\).
Any positive rescaling of \(a\) preserves the normalized margin.
boundary_notes: If \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), no positive-gap separator exists, although weak separation may exist.
Point-set separation does not require the separating hyperplane to support \(C\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak, Proper, and Strict Set Separation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets. Orient a prospective separator so that functional values on \(A\) do not exceed those on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex set-set separation, explicitly distinguishing weak, proper, and positive-gap notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(A\) and \(B\) are weakly separated by \(a\neq0\) if
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\leq\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
They are properly separated by \(a\) if this inequality holds and the functional is not constant across both sets, namely
\[\inf_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\sup_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
They are strictly, or strongly, separated by \(a\) if
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
In the strict case, every level strictly between the two bounds defines an affine hyperplane placing \(A\) and \(B\) in opposite open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets are weakly separated when a nonzero linear functional orders all points of the first set below all points of the second. Separation is proper when this ordering is not merely caused by the functional being constant on their common affine environment. It is strict or strong when there is a positive gap between the largest value on the first set and the smallest value on the second. Any scalar inside that gap is the level of a strictly separating hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: The orientation is conventional and may be reversed by replacing \(a\) with \(-a\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Weak separation is \(\sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)\leq0\).
Strict separation is strict point-set separation of \(0\) from \(A-B\).
Proper separation excludes the case in which \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\) has one common value on \(A\cup B\).
special_cases_latex: When \(B=\{z\}\), strict set-set separation is strict point-set separation.
If \(A,B\) are closed and disjoint and one is bounded, they are strictly separable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict separation implies \(A\cap B=\varnothing\).
Proper separation is available when \(\operatorname{ri}A\cap\operatorname{ri}B=\varnothing\).
boundary_notes: Weak separation alone may be improper for lower-dimensional sets.
Disjoint closed unbounded convex sets need not possess a positive-gap separator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogeneous Separation and Polar Certificates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex cone. Its negative polar is \(K^\circ=\{a:\langle a,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\). A homogeneous hyperplane has the form \(H(a,0)\) with \(a\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone separation through the origin, the geometric form underlying polar certificates and linear alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(z\) and cone \(K\) are homogeneously separated in the orientation \(K\) below \(z\) when there exists \(a\neq0\) such that
\[\langle a,k\rangle\leq0\leq\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\forall k\in K.\]
Equivalently, \(a\in K^\circ\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\langle a,z\rangle\geq0\). The separation is strict on the point side when
\[a\in K^\circ\quad\text{and}\quad\langle a,z\rangle>0.\]
For two cones \(K_1,K_2\), homogeneous separation means
\[\sup_{x\in K_1}\langle a,x\rangle\leq0\leq\inf_{y\in K_2}\langle a,y\rangle,\]
which, because of positive homogeneity, is equivalent to \(a\in K_1^\circ\cap(-K_2^\circ)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogeneous separation uses a linear hyperplane through the origin. A point and a cone are homogeneously separated when a nonzero functional is nonpositive on the cone and nonnegative at the point; strictness means it is positive at the point. This is precisely a polar-cone certificate. For two cones, the functional must be nonpositive on the first and nonnegative on the second, so it belongs to the intersection of the appropriate polar cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K\), or \(K_1,K_2\), is a nonempty convex cone containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[H(a,0)\text{ homogeneously separates }K\text{ from }z\iff a\in K^\circ\setminus\{0\},\ \langle a,z\rangle\geq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict homogeneous point-cone separation is a certificate \(a\in K^\circ\) with \(\langle a,z\rangle>0\).
For a closed convex cone, \(z\in K\iff\langle a,z\rangle\leq0\) for every \(a\in K^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: Supporting hyperplanes of a convex cone at the origin are homogeneous.
For \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), membership in \(K^\circ\) is the finite system \(\langle a,v_i\rangle\leq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Homogeneous separation converts cone nonmembership into a dual linear inequality certificate.
Positive rescaling of \(a\) leaves the homogeneous separator unchanged.
boundary_notes: A homogeneous separator cannot place the origin in an open half-space because every cone contains the origin.
Strictness therefore refers to the excluded point or to nonzero cone directions, not to both entire cones when they share the origin.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strength and Ambient Classification of Separators
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and put \(L=\operatorname{aff}(A\cup B)\), with direction space \(V=L-L\). For \(a\neq0\), define \(u_A(a)=\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\) and \(\ell_B(a)=\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A definition of the theorem-family regimes, organized by inequality strength and by whether separation is taken in the full or effective affine ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separating-hyperplane regime is classified by the relation between \(u_A(a)\) and \(\ell_B(a)\):
\[\text{weak: }u_A(a)\leq\ell_B(a);\qquad\text{strict: }u_A(a)<\ell_B(a).\]
A weak separator is proper when it is not constant on \(A\cup B\), equivalently when its restriction to \(V\) is nonzero and
\[\inf_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle<\sup_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
It is an effective-ambient separator when only the component \(P_Va\) is retained and \(P_Va\neq0\). Thus the family distinguishes weak, proper, strict, closed-target, and relative-affine regimes by adding the corresponding topological and dimensional hypotheses to the same functional ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The separating-hyperplane family is organized by the strength of one functional inequality and by the ambient affine space. Weak separation permits contact at the separating level. Proper separation excludes a functional that is constant on both sets. Strict separation requires a positive functional gap. If the sets are lower-dimensional, the meaningful normal is the component in the direction space of their affine hull; a separator whose normal is purely orthogonal to that space is ambiently trivial.
assumptions_latex: When strict separation is asserted, both extremal functional bounds are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{strict separation}\Rightarrow\text{proper separation}\Rightarrow\text{weak separation},\] with effective-ambient nontriviality imposed by \(P_Va\neq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict separation is \(\sigma_A(a)+\sigma_B(-a)<0\).
Proper separation is weak separation together with nonconstancy of \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\) on \(A\cup B\).
Effective-ambient separation is ordinary separation after identifying \(L\) with \(\mathbb R^{\dim L}\).
special_cases_latex: For full-dimensional \(A\cup B\), every nonzero normal is effective-ambient.
For point-set separation with closed convex target, the closed-target regime supplies a strict separator.
immediate_consequences_latex: The same pair of convex sets may admit separators of several strengths.
Projection of a separating normal onto \(V\) removes the component that is constant along \(L\).
boundary_notes: The labels describe distinct hypotheses and conclusions; they are not interchangeable theorem statements.
Weak ambient separation can be vacuous for sets contained in a common proper affine subspace.

notation.meaning: Direction space parallel to the effective affine ambient set.
Orthogonal projection of the normal onto \(V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Functional Characterizations of Proper and Strong Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes proper and strong separation of arbitrary nonempty subsets of Euclidean space through extrema of a linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty. A hyperplane properly separates C_1 and C_2 if and only if there exists b\in\mathbb{R}^n such that \inf_{x\in C_1}\langle x,b\rangle\ge\sup_{x\in C_2}\langle x,b\rangle and \sup_{x\in C_1}\langle x,b\rangle>\inf_{x\in C_2}\langle x,b\rangle. A hyperplane strongly separates C_1 and C_2 if and only if there exists b\in\mathbb{R}^n such that \inf_{x\in C_1}\langle x,b\rangle>\sup_{x\in C_2}\langle x,b\rangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty sets are properly separated exactly when some linear functional weakly orders them while preventing both sets from lying in the separating hyperplane. They are strongly separated exactly when some linear functional has a strictly positive gap between its values on the two sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}\exists H\text{ properly separating }C_1,C_2&\iff\exists b:\ \inf_{C_1}\langle\cdot,b\rangle\ge\sup_{C_2}\langle\cdot,b\rangle\ \land\ \sup_{C_1}\langle\cdot,b\rangle>\inf_{C_2}\langle\cdot,b\rangle,\\\exists H\text{ strongly separating }C_1,C_2&\iff\exists b:\ \inf_{C_1}\langle\cdot,b\rangle>\sup_{C_2}\langle\cdot,b\rangle.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation, proper separation, strict separation, and strong separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for two nonempty subsets of Euclidean space; convexity and disjointness are not assumed. Proper separation permits one set to lie in the hyperplane, while strict separation alone need not provide a uniform positive margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S_1,S_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and let $H=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^Tx=b\}$, where $a\ne0$. The hyperplane $H$ separates $S_1$ and $S_2$ if $a^Tx\ge b$ for all $x\in S_1$ and $a^Tx\le b$ for all $x\in S_2$. The separation is proper if $S_1\cup S_2\nsubseteq H$; strict if $a^Tx>b$ for all $x\in S_1$ and $a^Tx<b$ for all $x\in S_2$; and strong if there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $a^Tx>b+\varepsilon$ for all $x\in S_1$ and $a^Tx<b-\varepsilon$ for all $x\in S_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane separates two nonempty sets when they lie in opposite closed halfspaces. Separation is proper when their union is not contained in the hyperplane, although one set may be contained in it. Strict separation uses pointwise strict inequalities but allows points to approach the hyperplane arbitrarily closely. Strong separation requires a uniform positive margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{separation: }a^Tx\ge b\ \forall x\in S_1,\quad a^Tx\le b\ \forall x\in S_2;\\&\text{proper: }S_1\cup S_2\nsubseteq H;\\&\text{strict: }a^Tx>b\ \forall x\in S_1,\quad a^Tx<b\ \forall x\in S_2;\\&\text{strong: }\exists\varepsilon>0:\ a^Tx>b+\varepsilon\ \forall x\in S_1,\quad a^Tx<b-\varepsilon\ \forall x\in S_2.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hyperplane Isolation and Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict and non-strict isolation of one set and separation of two sets by an affine hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an affine hyperplane with open halfspaces \(H_+,H_-\) and corresponding closed halfspaces \(\overline H_+,\overline H_-\). The hyperplane \(H\) isolates \(A\subseteq V\) if \(A\subseteq\overline H_+\) or \(A\subseteq\overline H_-\), and strictly isolates \(A\) if \(A\subseteq H_+\) or \(A\subseteq H_-\). It separates \(A,B\subseteq V\) if, after possibly interchanging signs, \(A\subseteq\overline H_+\) and \(B\subseteq\overline H_-\); it strictly separates them if, after possibly interchanging signs, \(A\subseteq H_+\) and \(B\subseteq H_-\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane isolates a set when the set lies in one closed halfspace, and strictly isolates it when the set lies in one open halfspace. It separates two sets when they lie in opposite closed halfspaces, and strictly separates them when they lie in opposite open halfspaces.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a real vector space}
H\subseteq V\text{ is an affine hyperplane}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\subseteq\overline H_{\pm}\text{ or }A\subseteq H_{\pm};\qquad A\subseteq\overline H_+,\ B\subseteq\overline H_-\text{ or }A\subseteq H_+,\ B\subseteq H_-\text{, up to sign exchange}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sets Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n are separable if there exist a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\} and \alpha\in\mathbb{R} such that \langle a,x\rangle\ge\alpha for every x\in Q_1 and \langle a,x\rangle\le\alpha for every x\in Q_2. They are strictly separable if there exist a\in\mathbb{R}^n and \alpha_1>\alpha_2 such that \langle a,x\rangle\ge\alpha_1 for every x\in Q_1 and \langle a,x\rangle\le\alpha_2 for every x\in Q_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets are separable if a nontrivial hyperplane places them in opposite closed half-spaces. They are strictly separable if two separating levels can be chosen with a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists a\ne0,\alpha:\ \langle a,x\rangle\ge\alpha\ \forall x\in Q_1,\ \langle a,x\rangle\le\alpha\ \forall x\in Q_2;\quad\text{strict separation means }\exists a,\alpha_1>\alpha_2:\ \langle a,x\rangle\ge\alpha_1\ \forall x\in Q_1,\ \langle a,x\rangle\le\alpha_2\ \forall x\in Q_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eidelheit Separation Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak separation when one convex set has nonempty interior and the other avoids that interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a normed linear space and let $K_1,K_2\subseteq X$ be convex. Suppose $\operatorname{int}K_1\ne\varnothing$ and $K_2\cap\operatorname{int}K_1=\varnothing$. Then there exists a nonzero $x^*\in X^*$ such that
\[
\sup_{x\in K_1}\langle x,x^*\rangle\le \inf_{x\in K_2}\langle x,x^*\rangle.
\]
Consequently, a closed hyperplane separates $K_1$ and $K_2$ into opposite closed half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the first of two convex sets has nonempty interior and the second contains none of its interior points, a nonzero continuous linear functional weakly separates the sets into opposite closed half-spaces.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a normed linear space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in X^*\setminus\{0\}:\ \sup_{x\in K_1}\langle x,x^*\rangle\le\inf_{x\in K_2}\langle x,x^*\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hyperplane Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ordinary, proper, strong, and strict separation for two nonempty subsets of Euclidean space; convexity and disjointness are not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, let H=\{x:\langle b,x\rangle=\alpha\} with b\ne0, and let B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}. Up to reversing b, H separates C_1 and C_2 if C_1\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle\ge\alpha\} and C_2\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle\le\alpha\}. The separation is proper if C_1 and C_2 are not both contained in H. It is strong if there exists \varepsilon>0 such that C_1+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle>\alpha\} and C_2+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{x:\langle b,x\rangle<\alpha\}. It is strict if C_1 and C_2 themselves are contained in the opposing open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane separates two nonempty sets when they lie in opposing closed half-spaces. Separation is proper when the sets are not both contained in the hyperplane, strong when uniform Euclidean neighborhoods of both sets lie in opposing open half-spaces, and strict when the sets themselves lie in opposing open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}H\text{ separates }C_1,C_2&\iff C_1\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle\ge\alpha\},\ C_2\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle\le\alpha\}\quad\text{(up to orientation)},\\H\text{ separates properly}&\iff H\text{ separates and }\neg(C_1\subseteq H\land C_2\subseteq H),\\H\text{ separates strongly}&\iff \exists\varepsilon>0:\ C_1+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle>\alpha\},\ C_2+\varepsilon B\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle<\alpha\},\\H\text{ separates strictly}&\iff C_1\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle>\alpha\},\ C_2\subseteq\{\langle b,\cdot\rangle<\alpha\}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Characterization of Weak Separators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural characterization for arbitrary nonempty convex pairs, including pairs that intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and define \(S^\circ:=\{a:\langle a,s\rangle\le0\text{ for every }s\in S\}\). The normals oriented from \(C\) toward \(D\) that satisfy the weak-separation inequalities are exactly \((C-D)^\circ\). Hence a nonzero such normal exists if and only if \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-D)\ne\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-separation normals form the polar of the difference set; a nonzero normal exists exactly when the closed conic hull of that difference does not fill the space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{a:\sup_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\le\inf_{d\in D}\langle a,d\rangle\}=(C-D)^\circ\), and this cone contains a nonzero vector iff \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-D)\ne\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak separation of disjoint convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No closedness, compactness, full-dimensionality, or positive separation margin is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty, convex, and disjoint, then there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(a^{\top}x_1\le a^{\top}x_2\) for all \(x_1\in C_1\) and \(x_2\in C_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two nonempty disjoint convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space admit weak separation by a nonzero linear functional, without a guaranteed strict or positive gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\ \forall x_1\in C_1\ \forall x_2\in C_2:\ a^{\top}x_1\le a^{\top}x_2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper hyperplane separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and scalar characterization of proper separation, together with the stated relative-interior boundary criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hyperplane \(H\) properly separates \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) if it separates them and does not contain both sets. Equivalently, such a hyperplane exists if and only if there is a nonzero \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[\sup_{x_1\in C_1}a^\top x_1\leq\inf_{x_2\in C_2}a^\top x_2,\qquad \inf_{x_1\in C_1}a^\top x_1<\sup_{x_2\in C_2}a^\top x_2.\] Proper separation of \(C\) and \(\bar x\) means proper separation of \(C\) and \(\{\bar x\}\). If a nonempty convex set \(C\) lies in a closed halfspace bounded by \(H\), then \[C\subseteq H\iff\operatorname{ri}(C)\cap H\neq\varnothing.\] Consequently, disjoint convex sets are properly separable when \(\dim\operatorname{aff}(C_1\cup C_2)=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper separation means separation by a hyperplane that does not contain both sets. It has the stated scalar-functional characterization. A nonempty convex set lying on one side of a hyperplane is contained in that hyperplane exactly when its relative interior meets it. In particular, disjoint convex sets whose union has full-dimensional affine hull can be properly separated.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}
C\text{ lies in a closed halfspace bounded by }H
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a proper separating hyperplane}\iff\exists a\neq0:\ \sup_{C_1}a^\top x\leq\inf_{C_2}a^\top x\ \text{ and }\ \inf_{C_1}a^\top x<\sup_{C_2}a^\top x;\quad C\subseteq H\iff\operatorname{ri}(C)\cap H\neq\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Target Membership-Exclusion Certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Its support function is \(\sigma_C(a)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separation used as an exact membership-exclusion test for a nonempty closed convex target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed-target separation certificate for exclusion of \(z\) from \(C\) is a vector \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying
\[\sigma_C(a)<\langle a,z\rangle.\]
The closed-target separation regime is the pair \((C,z)\) with \(C\) nonempty closed convex and \(z\notin C\). In this regime such a certificate exists. Equivalently,
\[z\in C\iff \langle a,z\rangle\leq\sigma_C(a)\quad\forall a\in\mathbb R^n,\]
whereas one strict violation certifies \(z\notin C\). Any \(\beta\) between \(\sigma_C(a)\) and \(\langle a,z\rangle\) defines a hyperplane that places \(C\) and \(z\) in opposite open half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex target, an exterior point has a nonzero linear functional whose value at the point is strictly larger than its support value on the target. Such a functional is a membership-exclusion certificate. Consequently, a point belongs to the closed convex target exactly when it satisfies every support inequality of the target; a single strict violation proves nonmembership.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The certificate is strict separation of \(\{z\}\) and \(C\).
It is strict homogeneous separation of \(0\) from \(C-z\).
It is a violated half-space inequality in the outer representation of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: The projection direction \(a=z-P_Cz\) supplies a certificate.
For a closed convex cone \(K\), exclusion is certified by a polar vector \(a\in K^\circ\) with \(\langle a,z\rangle>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed convex sets are intersections of their supporting closed half-spaces.
Support inequalities form a complete, possibly infinite, certificate system for membership.
boundary_notes: Closedness is essential: a point in \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) cannot be strictly separated from \(C\).
The certificate need not correspond to a support value attained by an unbounded target unless an appropriate maximizing point exists.

notation.meaning: Support function of the closed convex target.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), define \(H^-_{u,\beta}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,z\rangle\leq\beta\}\). For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\). Every nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies
\[
C=\bigcap_{\substack{u\neq0,\,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\\ C\subset H^-_{u,\beta}}}H^-_{u,\beta}
=\bigcap_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,z\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\},
\]
where an inequality with \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\) imposes no restriction. Equivalently, every point in \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C\) violates at least one valid affine inequality for \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set equals the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing it; every exterior point violates some valid affine inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets with \(\delta=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\). Then there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\|u\|=1\) such that
\[
\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle+\delta\leq\inf_{d\in D}\langle u,d\rangle.
\]
Consequently, any \(\alpha\) strictly between the two displayed bounds defines a hyperplane that strongly separates \(C\) and \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets at positive Euclidean distance admit a unit-normal separating hyperplane whose directional gap is at least their distance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp characterization of strict separation from a possibly nonclosed convex target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\langle u,c\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }c\in C\] if and only if \(x\notin\overline C\). In particular, every \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\) is a nonmember for which strict separation fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is strictly separable from a convex target exactly when it lies outside the target's closure; omitted boundary points are the precise obstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict affine separation of \(x\) from \(C\) holds if and only if \(x\notin\overline C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation Relative to the Effective Affine Ambient Space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets, \(L=\operatorname{aff}(A\cup B)\), and \(V=L-L\). Every affine functional on \(L\) has a normal represented by a vector in \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative separation for lower-dimensional convex sets; nontriviality is measured inside their joint affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An effective-ambient separator of \(A\) and \(B\) is an affine hyperplane of \(L\),
\[H_L(v,\beta):=\{x\in L:\langle v,x\rangle=\beta\},\qquad v\in V\setminus\{0\},\]
such that
\[\sup_{x\in A}\langle v,x\rangle\leq\beta\leq\inf_{y\in B}\langle v,y\rangle.\]
It is strict when both inequalities are strict. An ambient normal \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) induces this separator exactly through \(v=P_Va\). The separator is trivial relative to \(L\) when \(P_Va=0\), because then \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\) is constant on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective ambient space for two convex sets is their joint affine hull. Separation in this space uses a nonzero normal lying in its parallel direction space. An ambient normal matters only through its projection onto that direction space. If the projection vanishes, the functional is constant on the entire affine hull and any apparent separation is geometrically trivial. Strict and weak relative separation use the usual functional inequalities restricted to the effective ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[a\text{ defines a nontrivial separator relative to }L\iff P_Va\neq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Choose an affine isometry \(L\cong\mathbb R^{\dim L}\); effective-ambient separation becomes ordinary full-dimensional separation there.
Two ambient normals differing by an element of \(V^\perp\) induce the same ordering on \(L\), up to an additive constant.
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\mathbb R^n\), effective-ambient and ordinary separation coincide.
For support at \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}C\), taking \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\) excludes hyperplanes containing all of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative-boundary points can have nontrivial supporting hyperplanes even when ordinary interior is empty.
Orthogonal projection of an ambient separator onto \(V\) preserves all functional differences between points of \(L\).
boundary_notes: A hyperplane containing \(L\) is not a nontrivial effective-ambient separator.
Relative separation must use the affine hull of all participating sets, not necessarily the affine hull of either set alone.

notation.meaning: Joint affine hull and its parallel direction space.

Let \(A=a+L\) be an affine subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(C\subset A\) be nonempty, convex, and relatively closed in \(A\), and let \(x\in A\setminus C\). Then there exist \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that

Then there exists \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle.\] More generally, an ambient normal \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) can distinguish points of \(A\) only if \(P_Lw\neq0\); every \(w\in L^\perp\) is constant on \(A\) and cannot strictly separate \(x\) from \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(A=a+L\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(C\subset A\) is nonempty, convex, and relatively closed, and \(x\in A\setminus C\). Relative-ambient separation yields \(u\in L\setminus\{0\}\) with

\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle.

By contrast, every \(v\in L^\perp\) is constant on \(A\), since \(\langle v,z\rangle=\langle v,a\rangle\) for all \(z\in A\). Hence normals orthogonal to \(L\) cannot distinguish points within the lower-dimensional ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-dimensional target, useful separation uses a normal parallel to its affine direction space; orthogonal normals are constant and therefore degenerate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=a+L\) and define \(T:A\to L\) by \(T(z)=z-a\). The map \(T\) is an affine isometry. Consequently, \(C\subset A\) is convex or relatively closed in \(A\) exactly when \(T(C)\) is convex or closed in \(L\), respectively, and
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(T(C),T(D)).
\]
Moreover, an inequality \(\langle u,z\rangle\leq\alpha\) on \(A\), with \(u\in L\), corresponds to \(\langle u,T(z)\rangle\leq\alpha-\langle u,a\rangle\) on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation by a base point identifies an affine hull with its direction space while preserving convexity, relative closedness, distances, and separation inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Gap Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets. For \(a\neq0\), define the oriented gap \(g(a;A,B)=\inf_{y\in B}\langle a,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle a,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict or strong separation, with explicit distinction between the positive-gap property and hypotheses ensuring its existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(A\) and \(B\) are strictly separated when there exists \(a\neq0\) with
\[g(a;A,B)>0.\]
A normalized strict-separation certificate is \(u=a/\|a\|\) with margin
\[\gamma(u;A,B):=\inf_{y\in B}\langle u,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle u,x\rangle>0.\]
The strict-separation family comprises configurations for which this certificate is ensured, notably: a point outside a nonempty closed convex set, and two disjoint nonempty closed convex sets when one is bounded. Any \(\beta\) in the open gap gives
\[\langle u,x\rangle<\beta<\langle u,y\rangle\quad\forall(x,y)\in A\times B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict separation is the existence of a nonzero linear functional with a positive gap between its supremum on one convex set and its infimum on the other. Normalizing the functional makes the gap a geometric margin. The standard existence regimes include an exterior point versus a closed convex set and two disjoint closed convex sets when one is bounded. Every level inside the positive gap defines a hyperplane leaving both sets in opposite open half-spaces.
assumptions_latex: The relevant support bounds are finite in a strict-separating direction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict separation is \(\sigma_A(u)+\sigma_B(-u)<0\).
It is strict separation of \(0\) from \(A-B\).
It is the existence of disjoint parallel closed supporting levels with positive spacing.
special_cases_latex: For \(B=\{z\}\), the margin is \(\langle u,z\rangle-\sigma_A(u)\).
If \(A\) is compact, \(B\) is closed, and \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), a strict certificate exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict separation implies positive Euclidean distance between the two sets.
The normalized margin is invariant under positive rescaling of the original normal.
boundary_notes: Closedness without boundedness does not ensure strict separation of two disjoint sets.
Weak or proper separation may remain possible when every normalized strict margin is nonpositive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Conditions for Strict Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Five alternative closedness, compactness, polyhedrality, or recession-lineality hypotheses ensuring strict separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, convex, and disjoint. Suppose at least one of the following holds: (i) \(C_2-C_1\) is closed; (ii) \(C_1\) is closed and \(C_2\) is compact; (iii) \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are polyhedral; (iv) both sets are closed and \(R_{C_1}\cap R_{C_2}=L_{C_1}\cap L_{C_2}\); or (v) \(C_1\) is closed, \(C_2\) is polyhedral, and \(R_{C_1}\cap R_{C_2}\subseteq L_{C_1}\). Then there exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[a^\top x_1<b<a^\top x_2\qquad\forall x_1\in C_1,\ \forall x_2\in C_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty disjoint convex sets are strictly separated if their difference is closed; the first is closed and the second compact; both are polyhedral; both are closed with common recession directions equal to common lineality directions; or the first is closed, the second polyhedral, and every common recession direction lies in the first set's lineality space.
assumptions_latex: C_2-C_1\text{ is closed}\ \lor\ (C_1\text{ is closed and }C_2\text{ is compact})\ \lor\ (C_1,C_2\text{ are polyhedral})\ \lor\ (C_1,C_2\text{ are closed and }R_{C_1}\cap R_{C_2}=L_{C_1}\cap L_{C_2})\ \lor\ (C_1\text{ is closed},\ C_2\text{ is polyhedral},\ R_{C_1}\cap R_{C_2}\subseteq L_{C_1})
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\},\exists b\in\mathbb{R}:a^\top x_1<b<a^\top x_2\quad\forall x_1\in C_1,\forall x_2\in C_2

children.top_down_role: Strong separation when compactness and closedness prevent asymptotic contact.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact, \(C\) is closed, and \(K\cap C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(u\neq0\) and \(\alpha<\beta\) with \(\langle u,k\rangle\leq\alpha<\beta\leq\langle u,c\rangle\) for all \(k\in K,c\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K,C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets such that \(K\) is compact, \(C\) is closed, and \(K\cap C=\varnothing\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(K,C)>0\), and there exist \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) with \(\alpha<\beta\) such that
\[
\langle u,k\rangle\leq\alpha<\beta\leq\langle u,c\rangle
\qquad\text{for all }k\in K\text{ and }c\in C.
\]
Thus compactness and closedness rule out asymptotic contact and produce a positive separating gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint nonempty convex sets are strongly separated when one is compact and the other closed, because their Euclidean distance is positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Closed Positive-Margin Configuration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K,C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets with \(K\) compact, \(C\) closed, and \(K\cap C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict separation where compactness of one target and closedness of the other exclude asymptotic contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A compact-closed strict-separation regime is an ordered pair \((C,K)\) satisfying
\[C\neq\varnothing,\quad K\neq\varnothing,\quad C\text{ closed convex},\quad K\text{ compact convex},\quad C\cap K=\varnothing.\]
A certificate for this regime is a nonzero \(a\) such that
\[\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle<\min_{y\in K}\langle a,y\rangle.\]
Every compact-closed regime admits such a certificate. Its normalized gap is
\[\gamma=\frac{\min_{y\in K}\langle a,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle}{\|a\|}>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The compact-closed regime consists of two disjoint nonempty convex sets, one compact and the other closed. Compactness turns the relevant extremal functional value into a minimum and, together with closedness and disjointness, prevents asymptotic contact. The regime therefore admits a nonzero functional whose largest value on the closed set is strictly below its smallest value on the compact set. After normalization, the difference is a positive geometric margin.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(0\notin C-K\), and \(C-K\) is closed convex because \(K\) is compact.
There exist \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq\beta-\varepsilon\) on \(C\) and \(\langle u,y\rangle\geq\beta+\varepsilon\) on \(K\).
special_cases_latex: A singleton \(K=\{z\}\) yields strong point-set separation.
If both sets are compact, either set may be assigned the compact role.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Euclidean distance between \(C\) and \(K\) is positive and attained.
A separating level can be chosen anywhere inside the open functional gap.
boundary_notes: If compactness is removed, two disjoint closed convex sets can have zero distance and fail strict separation.
Convexity is required for the stated affine separation guarantee.

notation.meaning: Normalized positive separation gap for the certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C\), and let \(p=P_Cx\). For \(u=x-p\neq0\),
\[
\langle u,c-p\rangle\leq0\qquad\text{for every }c\in C,
\]
and
\[
\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\leq\langle u,p\rangle<\langle u,x\rangle.
\]
The corresponding unnormalized gap is \(\|x-p\|^2\); for the unit normal \(u/\|u\|\), the gap is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=\|x-p\|\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality and uniqueness of the normalized projection residual among unit-bounded directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x\notin C\), and put \(p=P_Cx\), \(\delta=\|x-p\|\), and \(u_*=(x-p)/\delta\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Separation of an Exterior Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\notin C\). Write \(p=P_Cz\) for the Euclidean projection and \(d_C(z)=\|z-p\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional positive-margin separation of a point from a closed convex set, including its canonical projection normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A strong point-set separator is a triple \((u,\beta,\varepsilon)\) with \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[\langle u,x\rangle\leq\beta-\varepsilon\quad\forall x\in C,\qquad \langle u,z\rangle\geq\beta+\varepsilon.\]
Equivalently, \(u\) is a unit vector satisfying
\[\langle u,z\rangle-\sigma_C(u)>0.\]
For the closed convex target, the canonical choice
\[u=\frac{z-P_Cz}{\|z-P_Cz\|}\]
has directional gap \(d_C(z)>0\). A midpoint level yields a symmetric half-gap \(\varepsilon=d_C(z)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong point-set separation places a closed convex set and an exterior point in opposite open half-spaces with a positive margin. Equivalently, a unit functional has a strictly larger value at the point than its support value on the set. The normalized displacement from the projection of the point onto the set is a canonical separating normal, and its functional gap equals the point-to-set distance.
assumptions_latex: \(z\notin C\), so \(d_C(z)>0\) and the normalized projection displacement is defined.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(a\neq0\) with \(\langle a,z\rangle>\sigma_C(a)\).
The singleton \(\{z\}\) and \(C\) have a positive normalized separation margin.
The projection residual belongs to \(N_C(P_Cz)\) and points toward \(z\).
special_cases_latex: For an affine subspace, \(u\) is the normalized orthogonal residual.
For a closed convex cone, the projection residual gives a polar-cone exclusion certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: The separating inequality certifies both \(z\notin C\) and \(z\notin\operatorname{cl}C\).
The best unit-direction point-set margin equals \(d_C(z)\).
boundary_notes: If the target is not closed and \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), the distance and every strong margin are zero.
The symmetric parameter \(\varepsilon\) is half the full functional gap when the midpoint level is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Normalized Separation Margin
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty sets. For each unit vector \(u\), define its oriented directional gap by \(g_u(A,B)=\inf_{y\in B}\langle u,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle u,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean finite-dimensional metric interpretation of strong separation; extended-real values are allowed directionwise, while positive finite values are separation margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum normalized separation margin from \(A\) toward \(B\) is
\[\Gamma(A,B):=\sup_{\|u\|=1}\left(\inf_{y\in B}\langle u,y\rangle-\sup_{x\in A}\langle u,x\rangle\right).\]
A direction \(u\) is a positive-margin separator when \(g_u(A,B)>0\). The corresponding parallel supporting levels are separated by Euclidean distance \(g_u(A,B)\), because \(u\) has unit norm. Thus
\[A,B\text{ are strongly separated}\iff\Gamma(A,B)>0.\]
Whenever a closest pair \((x_*,y_*)\in A\times B\) exists for closed convex \(A,B\), the unit displacement \(u=(y_*-x_*)/\|y_*-x_*\|\) realizes the margin and
\[\Gamma(A,B)=\operatorname{dist}(A,B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a unit direction, the separation margin is the smallest functional value on the second set minus the largest functional value on the first. Its supremum over unit directions is the maximum normalized margin. A positive value is exactly strong separation. Geometrically, the value is the distance between two parallel supporting levels orthogonal to the unit normal. When closed convex sets possess a closest pair, the normalized displacement between that pair is an optimal direction and the maximum margin equals their Euclidean distance.
assumptions_latex: Convexity is required for the stated closest-pair support interpretation.
The equality with distance assumes that a closest pair exists.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(g_u(A,B)=-\sigma_A(u)-\sigma_B(-u)\).
The symmetric half-margin about a midpoint separating level is \(g_u(A,B)/2\).
special_cases_latex: For \(B=\{z\}\) and closed convex \(A\), \(\Gamma(A,\{z\})=d_A(z)\).
For a compact set and a disjoint closed convex set, a closest pair exists and the margin is positive.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive margin implies positive set distance.
The margin is invariant under common translation and scales linearly under common positive dilation.
boundary_notes: Zero maximum margin does not imply intersection; disjoint sets may approach each other asymptotically.
Without closest-pair attainment, equality between the supremal directional margin and distance requires separate closure analysis.

notation.meaning: Oriented gap in the unit direction \(u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\inf_{c\in C,\,d\in D}\|c-d\|.
\]
With \(D-C=\{d-c:d\in D,\ c\in C\}\), one has
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(0,D-C)
=\operatorname{dist}(0,\overline{D-C}).
\]
Therefore \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=0\) exactly when \(0\in\overline{D-C}\). This condition need not mean that \(C\) and \(D\) intersect, even when both sets are closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance between two sets is the distance from zero to their displacement set; zero distance means zero is a limit displacement, not necessarily an intersection.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,C)=\operatorname{dist}(\overline C,\overline D).\] For every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) and scalar \(\lambda\), \[\operatorname{dist}(C+z,D+z)=\operatorname{dist}(C,D),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\lambda C,\lambda D)=|\lambda|\operatorname{dist}(C,D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set distance is symmetric, closure invariant, invariant under common translation, and homogeneous under common scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set distance is symmetric, closure invariant, translation invariant, and homogeneous under common scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure, Symmetry, and Scaling of Set Distance
