children.top_down_role: Geometric interpretation of positive separation width.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance between C and D

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean set distance as the optimal normalized affine separation gap.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
g(u)=\inf_{d\in D}\langle u,d\rangle-
\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle.
\]
Then the maximal normalized separating gap satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(C,D)=\sup_{\|u\|\leq1}g(u).
\]
In particular, a positive-margin separator exists exactly when \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\). When the supremum is attained by a unit vector \(u\), its directional gap equals the Euclidean distance between the sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty convex sets, Euclidean distance equals the largest directional gap over normals of norm at most one; positive distance is equivalent to positive-margin separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Separating-Margin Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-Pair Representation of an Optimal Margin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal normalized separator induced by an attained positive set distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) have a nearest pair \((c_*,d_*)\) with \(\delta=\|d_*-c_*\|>0\). Then \(u_*=(d_*-c_*)/\delta\) satisfies \[\sup_{c\in C}\langle u_*,c\rangle=\langle u_*,c_*\rangle,\qquad \inf_{d\in D}\langle u_*,d\rangle=\langle u_*,d_*\rangle,\] and the difference of these support levels is \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive nearest displacement, when it exists, supplies an optimal unit separator supported at the nearest points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u_*=(d_*-c_*)/\delta\), the directional gap equals \(\delta\) and is attained at \(c_*\) and \(d_*\).

notation.meaning: unit direction of the nearest displacement

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Pair Representation of an Optimal Margin

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of an Optimal Margin Normal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and normalization of the directional-gap maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and define \(g(u)=\inf_{d\in D}\langle u,d\rangle-\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\). The extended-real upper-semicontinuous function \(g\) attains its maximum on \(\{u:\|u\|\le1\}\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\), every maximizer has norm one and its gap equals \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized directional-gap problem has an optimal normal; at positive distance every optimizer is a unit vector realizing the distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{\|u\|\le1}g(u)\) is attained; if \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)>0\), every maximizer \(u_*\) satisfies \(\|u_*\|=1\) and \(g(u_*)=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Existence of an Optimal Margin Normal

children.title: Distance-Attainment Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings governing nearest-point realization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(k_*\in K\) and \(c_*\in C\) with \(\|k_*-c_*\|=\operatorname{dist}(K,C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional distance attainment when one set is compact and the other closed.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Some Results on the Euclidean Distance to a Closed Set p. 73
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K,C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, with \(K\) compact and \(C\) closed. Then there exist \(k_*\in K\) and \(c_*\in C\) such that
\[
\|k_*-c_*\|=\operatorname{dist}(K,C).
\]
If additionally \(K\cap C=\varnothing\), then this attained distance is positive. Closedness of both sets alone does not generally guarantee attainment when neither set is compact, because minimizing pairs may escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance between a nonempty compact set and a nonempty closed set is attained; if they are disjoint, the attained distance is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Attainment Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Some Results on the Euclidean Distance to a Closed Set p. 73

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-Pair Normal-Cone Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality certificate for a candidate nearest pair of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets and \((c_*,d_*)\in C\times D\). Then \((c_*,d_*)\) attains \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\) if and only if \[\langle d_*-c_*,c-c_*\rangle\le0\quad(c\in C),\qquad \langle d_*-c_*,d-d_*\rangle\ge0\quad(d\in D).\] Equivalently, \(d_*-c_*\in N_C(c_*)\) and \(c_*-d_*\in N_D(d_*)\), where \(N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair is nearest exactly when its connecting displacement is an outward normal to the two sets with opposite orientations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((c_*,d_*)\) is a nearest pair if and only if \(d_*-c_*\in N_C(c_*)\) and \(c_*-d_*\in N_D(d_*)\).

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to C at the candidate nearest point

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Pair Normal-Cone Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Displacement-Set Criterion for Distance Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nearest-pair existence criterion and a closed-displacement sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^n\), the distance \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\) is attained if and only if \(D-C\) contains an element of minimum norm. In particular, if \(D-C\) is closed, then some \(c_*\in C\) and \(d_*\in D\) satisfy \(\|d_*-c_*\|=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearest pair exists exactly when the displacement set has a minimum-norm element; closedness of that set guarantees attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\) is attained iff \(D-C\) has a minimum-norm element; closedness of \(D-C\) implies attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Displacement-Set Criterion for Distance Attainment

children.title: Zero-Margin Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometric transition from strong separation to vanishing margin.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\|u\|=1}\gamma(u)\le 0\), so no positive-margin affine separation exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional zero-distance obstruction to positive-margin separation.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Separation Between Convex Sets p. 121
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\|u\|=1\), let \(\gamma(u)=\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle-\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), then \(\gamma(u)\le 0\) for every such \(u\). Consequently, there do not exist \(u\), \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) satisfying \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sets at zero distance cannot have a positive uniform gap between two parallel separating hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Margin Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge e^x\}\) and \(B=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). These are nonempty, closed, convex, and disjoint sets satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\). There are no \(u\in\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential epigraph and the horizontal axis are disjoint closed convex sets at zero distance and admit no positive-margin affine separation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Touching-Closure Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-set failure of positive-margin separation caused by finite touching of the closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\) and \(B=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\le0\}\). Then \(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty, convex, and disjoint, but \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\). They are weakly separated by \(y=0\), yet no affine separator has a positive uniform margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open upper halfspace and the complementary closed lower halfspace are disjoint and weakly separable, but their touching closures prevent positive-margin separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), so no positive-margin affine separator exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Touching-Closure Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Distance and Asymptotic-Contact Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets with \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). Define \(D=A-B\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=\inf\{\|a-b\|:a\in A,b\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure boundary for positive-margin separation of disjoint convex sets, including nonclosed and asymptotically contacting configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pair \((A,B)\) lies on the strict-separation failure boundary when
\[0\in\operatorname{cl}(A-B).\]
Equivalently,
\[\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0,\]
or there exist sequences \(a_k\in A\), \(b_k\in B\) with \(\|a_k-b_k\|\to0\). At such a pair every unit directional gap satisfies
\[\inf_{b\in B}\langle u,b\rangle-\sup_{a\in A}\langle u,a\rangle\leq0,\]
so no positive-margin separator exists. The boundary includes nonclosed point-set configurations \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) and disjoint unbounded closed convex sets having asymptotic contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two disjoint convex sets are on the failure boundary for strict separation when zero belongs to the closure of their difference set. This is equivalent to zero set distance and to the existence of point sequences, one from each set, whose mutual distance tends to zero. Every normalized functional gap is then nonpositive, so no hyperplane can leave a positive margin. Typical boundary configurations arise from a missing limit point of a nonclosed set or from unbounded sets approaching one another only at infinity.
assumptions_latex: Closure and distance are taken in the Euclidean ambient space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There are \(a_k\in A\), \(b_k\in B\) such that \(a_k-b_k\to0\).
The maximum normalized separation margin is nonpositive.
For point-set separation, the boundary condition is \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is nonclosed and \(z\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), \(C\) and \(\{z\}\) are disjoint but not strongly separable.
Two unbounded closed convex sets may be disjoint while their difference is not closed and contains sequences converging to zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak or proper separation must replace strict separation at this boundary.
Compactness of either closed set rules out this failure configuration for disjoint sets.
boundary_notes: Zero distance is the failure boundary for positive margin, not necessarily for weak separation.
If the sets intersect, zero belongs to \(A-B\) itself; the definition here isolates the disjoint boundary case.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support, Contact, and Exposed-Face Geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set. For \(a\neq0\) and finite \(\sigma_C(a)\), put \(H_a=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support geometry, including ambient support, relative nontrivial support, and exposed contact faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A supporting hyperplane of \(C\) in direction \(a\neq0\) is
\[H_a=\{x:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\]
provided the support value is finite and attained:
\[F_C(a):=\{x\in C:\langle a,x\rangle=\sigma_C(a)\}\neq\varnothing.\]
The set \(F_C(a)=C\cap H_a\) is the exposed face associated with \(a\). The support is at \(x\in C\) when \(x\in F_C(a)\), equivalently
\[\langle a,y-x\rangle\leq0\quad\forall y\in C.\]
If \(V=\operatorname{aff}C-ar x\), the support is nontrivial relative to \(C\) when \(P_Va\neq0\); otherwise the hyperplane contains the whole affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting hyperplane is a level set of a nonzero linear functional at an attained finite support value. Its contact set with a convex set is an exposed face. A support is said to occur at a point when the point maximizes the functional over the set, equivalently when the normal belongs to the point's normal cone. For a lower-dimensional set, support is nontrivial only when the normal has a nonzero component parallel to the set's affine hull.
assumptions_latex: The direction \(a\neq0\), and \(\sigma_C(a)\) is finite and attained for a contacting support.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A hyperplane supports \(C\) at \(x\) when \(C\subseteq\{y:\langle a,y\rangle\leq\langle a,x\rangle\}\).
The contact set is \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle a,y\rangle\).
Relative nontriviality is \(a\notin V^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: A singleton exposed face is an exposed point.
For a convex cone, support at the origin uses a linear hyperplane and a polar normal.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is convex.
Every boundary point of a nonempty convex set has an ambient supporting hyperplane; every relative-boundary point has a nontrivial relative support.
boundary_notes: A finite support value need not be attained on a nonclosed or unbounded set.
Not every face is exposed, so supporting hyperplanes do not enumerate all faces in general.

notation.meaning: Exposed contact face selected by direction \(a\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Half-Spaces, Supporting Hyperplanes, and Nontriviality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of geometric support for convex subsets of Euclidean space, including the normal-direction correspondence and the trivial-support boundary for lower-dimensional sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex, let b\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}, and define H^-_{b, eta}=\{x:\langle x,bangle\leq eta\} and H_{b, eta}=\{x:\langle x,bangle= eta\}. The half-space H^-_{b, eta} supports C if and only if C\subseteq H^-_{b, eta} and C\cap H_{b, eta}
eq\varnothing; its boundary H_{b, eta} is then a supporting hyperplane. If a\in C\cap H_{b, eta}, the chosen supporting orientation satisfies b\in N_C(a). The supporting hyperplane is nontrivial if and only if C
subseteq H_{b, eta}. When \operatorname{aff}C
eq\mathbb{R}^n, supporting hyperplanes containing all of C are trivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting half-space contains the convex set and has boundary contact with it, and its boundary is a supporting hyperplane. With the containing side oriented by its outward normal, a contact normal belongs to the normal cone. A support is nontrivial exactly when its hyperplane does not contain the whole set; lower-dimensional sets also admit trivial supports containing the entire set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H^-_{b,\beta}\text{ supports }C\iff C\subseteq H^-_{b,\beta}\text{ and }C\cap H_{b,\beta}\neq\varnothing;\qquad H_{b,\beta}\text{ is nontrivial}\iff C\nsubseteq H_{b,\beta}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Hyperplanes and Support at a Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane geometry in finite-dimensional Euclidean space; a supporting hyperplane need not meet the set unless support at a point is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_{s,r}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle s,y\rangle=r\}\), with \(s\neq0\). The hyperplane \(H_{s,r}\) supports \(C\) if \(C\) lies in either closed half-space that it bounds; equivalently, after orienting \((s,r)\), \(\langle s,y\rangle\le r\) for every \(y\in C\). It supports \(C\) at \(x\in C\) if additionally \(\langle s,x\rangle=r\). If \(H_{s,r}\) supports \(C\) at \(x\), then \(x\in\operatorname{bd}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane supports a set when the set lies in one of its closed half-spaces. It supports at a point when that point also lies on the hyperplane. Reversing the normal reverses the orientation, and every supported point is a boundary point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Hyperplane Theorem and Partial Converse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of boundary support for nonempty convex sets and a converse convexity criterion requiring closedness, nonempty interior, and support at every boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, then for every \(x_0\in\operatorname{bd}C\) there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(a^Tx\le a^Tx_0\) for all \(x\in C\); hence \(\{x:a^Tx=a^Tx_0\}\) supports \(C\) at \(x_0\). Conversely, if \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, has nonempty interior, and has a supporting hyperplane at every point of \(\operatorname{bd}S\), then \(S\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every boundary point of a nonempty convex set admits a supporting hyperplane. Conversely, a closed set with nonempty interior is convex if every boundary point admits a supporting hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: \forall x_0\in\operatorname{bd}S,\ S\text{ has a supporting hyperplane at }x_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [\forall x_0\in\operatorname{bd}C,\ \exists a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}:\ \forall x\in C,\ a^Tx\le a^Tx_0]\quad\text{and}\quad[(S\text{ closed})\land(\operatorname{int}S\neq\varnothing)\land(\forall x_0\in\operatorname{bd}S,\operatorname{Supp}(S,x_0))\Rightarrow S\text{ is convex}].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Hyperplane Theorem at a Noninterior Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak support through a noninterior point, which need not belong to the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{int}C\). Then there exists \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[a^\top\bar x\le a^\top x\qquad\forall x\in C.\] Hence the hyperplane \(\{x:a^\top x=a^\top\bar x\}\) passes through \(\bar x\) and places \(C\) in one of its closed halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If C is a nonempty convex subset of R^n and x-bar is not an interior point of C, then a nonzero normal exists whose hyperplane passes through x-bar and places C in one closed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}:a^\top\bar x\le a^\top x\quad\forall x\in C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-boundary support and exposure of polyhedral faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines supporting-hyperplane existence at relative-boundary points with the polyhedral conclusion that each stated face is cut out by a supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and convex. If $p\in\operatorname{rb}C$, then there exists a supporting hyperplane to $C$ at $p$. Furthermore, if $C$ is a nonempty polyhedral set and $F$ is a $k$-face of $C$, then there exists a supporting hyperplane $H$ such that $F=H\cap C$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relative-boundary point of a nonempty convex set admits a supporting hyperplane. For a nonempty polyhedral set, every stated k-face is the intersection of the set with a supporting hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the second conclusion, }C\text{ is polyhedral and }F\text{ is a }k\text{-face of }C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists H_p\text{ supporting }C\text{ at }p;\qquad C\text{ polyhedral and }F\text{ a }k\text{-face}\implies\exists H\text{ supporting }C:\ F=H\cap C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Hyperplane at a Boundary Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary support for a convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq E^n\) be convex and let \(y\in\partial C\). Then there exist \(a\in E^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(a^Ty=c\) and either \(a^Tx\le c\) for every \(x\in C\), or \(a^Tx\ge c\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every boundary point of a convex set, there is a hyperplane through that point with the entire set contained in one associated closed half-space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Hyperplane at a Boundary Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(x\in C\). The normal cone is \(N_C(x)=\{a:\langle a,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ambient boundary support; a separate relative formulation is needed to exclude trivial supports for lower-dimensional sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hyperplane supports \(C\) at \(x\) when there exists \(a\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[H=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle a,y\rangle=\langle a,x\rangle\}\]
and
\[\langle a,y\rangle\leq\langle a,x\rangle\qquad\forall y\in C.\]
Thus boundary-point support is equivalent to the existence of a nonzero normal at the point. For every \(x\in\operatorname{bd}C\), such a supporting hyperplane exists. Its contact set is
\[F=C\cap H=\{y\in C:\langle a,y\rangle=\langle a,x\rangle\},\]
an exposed face containing \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting hyperplane at a point of a convex set has a nonzero normal whose linear functional is maximized over the set at that point. Equivalently, the normal belongs to the point's normal cone. Every ordinary boundary point of a nonempty convex set possesses such a support. The points sharing equality with the supporting level form an exposed face containing the supported point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Support at \(x\) is \(a\in N_C(x)\setminus\{0\}\).
It is attainment of the support function: \(\sigma_C(a)=\langle a,x\rangle\).
It is the half-space containment \(C\subseteq\{y:\langle a,y-x\rangle\leq0\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is full-dimensional, a point admitting a nonzero normal cannot lie in \(\operatorname{int}C\).
For lower-dimensional \(C\), every point has normals orthogonal to \(\operatorname{aff}C\); nontrivial relative support requires a normal component parallel to that affine hull.
immediate_consequences_latex: The contact set of a boundary support is an exposed face.
A uniquely exposed contact point is an exposed point of \(C\).
boundary_notes: An ambient supporting hyperplane may contain all of a lower-dimensional convex set and therefore be trivial relative to it.
Relative-interior points have no nontrivial support within \(\operatorname{aff}C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper support points, supporting functionals, and supporting hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a convex subset of a Banach space, including the closed-unit-ball specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq X\) be convex and let \(\bar x\in C\). The point \(\bar x\) is a proper support point of \(C\) if there exists a continuous linear functional \(\phi\in X^*\) such that
\[
\phi(\bar x)=\sigma=\sup_{y\in C}\phi(y)>\inf_{y\in C}\phi(y).
\]
Then \(\phi\) is a nontrivial supporting functional and \(H=\phi^{-1}(\sigma)\) is a supporting hyperplane. When \(C=B(X)\), the functional \(\phi\) is norm-attaining.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper support point is a point where a continuous linear functional attains its supremum over the convex set and is not constant on that set. The functional is a nontrivial supporting functional, its maximal level set is a supporting hyperplane, and in the unit-ball case the functional attains its norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is a proper support point}\iff \exists\phi\in X^*:\ \phi(\bar x)=\sup_{y\in C}\phi(y)>\inf_{y\in C}\phi(y);\quad H=\phi^{-1}(\sup_C\phi),\quad C=B(X)\Rightarrow\phi\text{ is norm-attaining}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Convex Subgradient Supports the Corresponding Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The supporting inequality holds for every subgradient, including the zero vector; the usual supporting-hyperplane interpretation requires a nonzero subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be convex, let $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and let $g\in\partial f(x_0)$. For $\mathcal L_f(f(x_0)):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\le f(x_0)\}$, one has $\langle g,x-x_0\rangle\le0$ for every $x\in\mathcal L_f(f(x_0))$. If $g\ne0$, the affine hyperplane $\{x:\langle g,x-x_0\rangle=0\}$ supports this sublevel set at $x_0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex subgradient at a point satisfies the outward-normal inequality for the sublevel set through that point. A nonzero subgradient therefore defines a supporting hyperplane there; a zero subgradient still satisfies the inequality but does not define a genuine hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle g,x-x_0\rangle\le0\quad\forall x\in\mathcal L_f(f(x_0));\qquad g\ne0\Longrightarrow\{x:\langle g,x-x_0\rangle=0\}\text{ supports }\mathcal L_f(f(x_0))\text{ at }x_0.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nontrivial support at a relative-boundary point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set. Its effective affine ambient space is \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\), its relative interior is \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and its relative boundary is \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex geometry; support is required to be nonconstant on the set, thereby excluding hyperplanes that merely contain the entire affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\in C\) has relative-boundary support if there exist \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \(\langle u,y\rangle\leq\alpha\) for every \(y\in C\), \(\langle u,x\rangle=\alpha\), and the functional \(y\mapsto\langle u,y\rangle\) is not constant on \(C\). Equivalently, \(H=\{y:\langle u,y\rangle=\alpha\}\) is a nontrivial supporting hyperplane of \(C\) through \(x\). For convex \(C\), the points admitting such support are precisely \(C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point of a convex set has relative-boundary support when a linear functional, nonconstant on the set, attains its maximum there at that point. Thus the associated hyperplane supports the set without containing all of it. Exactly the points of the set lying on its relative boundary have this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists u,\alpha:\ \langle u,y\rangle\leq\alpha\ \forall y\in C,\ \langle u,x\rangle=\alpha,\ \langle u,\cdot\rangle\text{ is nonconstant on }C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exposed maximizer set \(F_u=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle\) is nonempty, contains \(x\), and is a proper subset of \(C\).
Relative to \(L=\operatorname{aff}C\), the restriction of \(u\) has a nonzero component in the direction space \(L-L\), and \(C\subseteq\{y\in L:\langle u,y\rangle\leq\langle u,x\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is full-dimensional, then \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\partial C\), so this is ordinary boundary-point support.
If \(C\) is a singleton, its relative boundary is empty and no nontrivial supporting functional exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every relative-boundary point of a non-singleton convex set lies in at least one proper exposed face.
No point of \(\operatorname{ri}C\) can maximize a linear functional that is nonconstant on \(C\).
boundary_notes: The condition differs from allowing any ambient supporting hyperplane: when \(C\) is lower-dimensional, a hyperplane containing \(\operatorname{aff}C\) is trivial and does not certify relative-boundary membership.
Closure of \(C\) is used in the definition of relative boundary; the supported point itself is required to belong to \(C\).

maximizer set exposed by the functional with normal u

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed faces selected by support functionals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(u\in\mathbb R^n\). Write \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\), allowing the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional facial geometry. The definition covers empty and improper exposed faces by convention while distinguishing the proper faces cut out by nontrivial supporting hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The face exposed by \(u\) is \(F_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) when \(\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\), and \(F_C(u)=\varnothing\) otherwise. A subset \(F\subseteq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if \(F=F_C(u)\) for some \(u\). It is proper and nonempty precisely when the level hyperplane \(H(u,\sigma_C(u))\) is a nontrivial supporting hyperplane and \(F=C\cap H(u,\sigma_C(u))\). An exposed point is an exposed face consisting of one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed face is the set on which a linear functional attains its supremum over a convex set. A nonempty proper exposed face is exactly the intersection of the set with a nontrivial supporting hyperplane. A singleton exposed face is an exposed point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty proper \(F\), exposedness is equivalent to the existence of \(u\) and \(\alpha\) with \(C\subseteq\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\}\) and \(F=C\cap\{x:\langle u,x\rangle=\alpha\}\).
The set \(F_C(u)\) is the contact set between \(C\) and the supporting hyperplane normal to \(u\).
special_cases_latex: For \(u=0\) and nonempty \(C\), one has \(F_C(0)=C\).
If \(F_C(u)=\{x\}\), then \(x\) is exposed and therefore extreme.
For a convex cone, a one-dimensional exposed face is an exposed ray.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exposed face is a face: if a relative-interior point of a segment in \(C\) lies in \(F_C(u)\), both endpoints lie in \(F_C(u)\).
Different normals may expose the same face.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting-Face Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling and finite-intersection rules for attained support faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. For \(\alpha>0\), \(F_C(\alpha u)=F_C(u)\). If \(\sigma_C(u)\) and \(\sigma_C(v)\) are finite and attained and \(F_C(u)\cap F_C(v)\ne\varnothing\), then \[\sigma_C(u+v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_C(v),\qquad F_C(u+v)=F_C(u)\cap F_C(v).\] Iteration gives the analogous rule for any finite family with nonempty common intersection. If that intersection is proper, the summed functional is nonconstant on \(\operatorname{aff}C\), so the intersection is a proper exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling preserves a support face, and a nonempty finite intersection of support faces is selected by the sum of their directions; a proper intersection is a proper exposed face.
assumptions_latex: The relevant support values are finite and attained.
The support faces in the addition rule have nonempty common intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(\alpha u)=F_C(u)\) for \(\alpha>0\), and \(F_C(u+v)=F_C(u)\cap F_C(v)\) under the stated common-contact condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separator closure and separation recognition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A closed halfspace is a set \(H^-_{u,\alpha}=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\}\) with \(u\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean separation geometry; the object packages the outer representation and point-exclusion consequences of separation without assuming that the original set is convex or closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The separator closure of \(S\) is \(\operatorname{sepcl}(S)=\bigcap\{H^-_{u,\alpha}:S\subseteq H^-_{u,\alpha}\}\), with the intersection taken over all closed halfspaces containing \(S\). A point \(z\) is separation-recognized as outside \(S\) when some such halfspace contains \(S\) but excludes \(z\). In finite dimensions, \(\operatorname{sepcl}(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\); hence separator closure is exactly closed-convex closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The separator closure of a set is the intersection of every closed halfspace containing it. A point is recognized as exterior when one of those halfspaces excludes it. In finite-dimensional space this closure is the closed convex hull, so valid linear inequalities recognize precisely membership in that hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(z\in\operatorname{sepcl}(S)\) if and only if every valid inequality \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\) for \(S\) is also satisfied by \(z\).
\(z\notin\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) if and only if there exist \(u\neq0\) and \(\alpha\) such that \(\langle u,s\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,z\rangle\) for all \(s\in S\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S=C\) is closed and convex, then \(\operatorname{sepcl}(C)=C\).
If \(S=\varnothing\), the intersection of all closed halfspaces is empty, consistently with \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The operator \(\operatorname{sepcl}\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent.
Closed convex sets are exactly the fixed points of separator closure.
boundary_notes: Open or nonconvex sets are not generally recovered unchanged; separator closure first convexifies and closes them.
Strict inequalities are unnecessary for the outer representation, although strict exclusion occurs for a point outside a closed convex set.

notation.meaning: closed halfspace with outward normal u and level alpha
intersection of all closed halfspaces containing S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact outer representation by valid halfspaces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Define the set of valid affine inequalities by \(\mathcal V(C)=\{(u,\alpha)\in(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact representation. Arbitrary, possibly infinite families of valid halfspaces are allowed; finite representations constitute the narrower polyhedral case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outer halfspace representation generated by \(\mathcal V(C)\) is \(\mathcal H(C)=\bigcap_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal V(C)}\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\}\). The set \(C\) is outer-halfspace representable when \(C=\mathcal H(C)\). Every closed convex set has this property, and conversely every intersection of closed halfspaces is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical outer description of a set is the intersection of all closed halfspaces corresponding to its valid affine inequalities. A set is outer-halfspace representable when this intersection equals the set. In finite dimensions, this happens exactly for closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C=\bigcap_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal V(C)}\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\text{ is closed and convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the support function, the same representation is \(C=\bigcap_{u:\sigma_C(u)<+\infty}\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\) for nonempty closed convex \(C\).
Membership is equivalent to satisfaction of every valid inequality: \(x\in C\iff\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha\) for all \((u,\alpha)\in\mathcal V(C)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(\mathcal V(C)=\varnothing\) and the empty intersection is \(\mathbb R^n\).
A polyhedral convex set is one admitting an exact representation using finitely many members of \(\mathcal V(C)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point outside a closed convex set violates at least one valid affine inequality.
Intersecting any collection of outer-halfspace representable sets again yields an outer-halfspace representable set.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed or nonconvex set, \(\mathcal H(C)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}C)\), not generally \(C\).
The representation need not possess a finite or irredundant subfamily.

intersection of all valid closed halfspaces for C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separating certificate of nonmembership
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact separation of one point from a nonempty closed convex set. Closedness is essential for certifying every point outside the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separator certificate excluding \(z\) from \(C\) is a pair \((u,\alpha)\in(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,z\rangle\). Equivalently, the closed halfspace \(H^-_{u,\alpha}\) contains \(C\) and excludes \(z\). For nonempty closed convex \(C\), such a certificate exists exactly when \(z\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separator certificate for nonmembership is a valid affine inequality for the closed convex set that is strictly violated by the queried point. Such a certificate exists if and only if the point is outside the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z\notin C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists u\neq0,\alpha:\ \langle u,x\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,z\rangle\quad\forall x\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(u\neq0\) such that \(\sigma_C(u)<\langle u,z\rangle\); one may then take \(\alpha=\sigma_C(u)\).
There is a closed halfspace containing \(C\) whose complement contains \(z\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a closed affine subspace, an excluding certificate may be chosen from an orthogonal direction.
For \(C=\mathbb R^n\), no point is exterior and no excluding certificate exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Membership in a closed convex set is equivalent to satisfying all of its valid affine inequalities.
Any proposed pair satisfying the certificate inequalities is directly checkable as a nonmembership witness.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed, a point in \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) cannot be strictly separated from \(C\).
The definition certifies exclusion from \(C\), not a positive Euclidean distance unless additional normalization of \(u\) is imposed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Conic Bipolar Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This formula gives the exact closure-and-convexification effect of bidualization and characterizes exact bipolar recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[S^*:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in S\}\] and let \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) denote its convex conic hull. Then \[S^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(S)}.\] Consequently, \(S^{**}=S\) holds exactly when \(S\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the nonnegative dual twice produces the closed convex conic hull of a nonempty set; exact recovery occurs precisely for closed convex cones.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar and bipolar cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean pairing. Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional negative-polar convention. The bipolar recovers the closed convex conical hull for arbitrary nonempty input and recovers the original set exactly for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar cone of \(S\) is \(S^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in S\}\), and its bipolar is \(S^{\circ\circ}=(S^\circ)^\circ\). The bipolar is the intersection of all homogeneous closed halfspaces containing \(S\), and \(S^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}(S))\), where \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) denotes the convex conical hull. Thus a nonempty set equals its bipolar exactly when it is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar consists of all vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every vector in the original set. Polarizing again produces the intersection of every homogeneous closed halfspace containing the set, which is its closed convex conical hull. Consequently, closed convex cones are precisely the bipolar fixed points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}(S)),\qquad K^{\circ\circ}=K\ \text{for every nonempty closed convex cone }K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), \(x\in K\) if and only if \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K^\circ\).
The polar reverses inclusion: \(S_1\subseteq S_2\Rightarrow S_2^\circ\subseteq S_1^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(L\) is a linear subspace, then \(L^\circ=L^\perp\) and \(L^{\circ\circ}=L\).
For \(S=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), the polar is \(\bigcap_i\{y:\langle y,a_i\rangle\leq0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar of any nonempty set is always a closed convex cone.
A vector outside a closed convex cone is excluded by a homogeneous inequality supplied by an element of the polar cone.
boundary_notes: Some literature uses the opposite sign and calls \(\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\}\) the dual cone; the convention here is the nonpositive polar.
Without closedness and convexity, the bipolar generally enlarges the original set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension-controlled convex witness bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix a finite-dimensional affine space \(L\) of dimension \(d\). A convex-geometric assertion may concern generation of a point, partition of a point configuration, or feasibility of an intersection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An organizing definition for finite-dimensional witness phenomena. It records the common bounded-witness structure without identifying the distinct Carathéodory, Radon, and Helly constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex-geometric property on \(L\) has a dimension-controlled witness bound if there is an integer \(w(d)\), depending only on \(d\), such that every valid instance has a certificate involving at most \(w(d)\) input objects. In the generation mode, membership \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) has a subset witness \(T\subseteq S\) with \(|T|\leq w(d)\). In the infeasibility mode, \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\varnothing\) has a subfamily witness \(J\subseteq I\) with \(|J|\leq w(d)\) in the applicable finite-family regime. In the partition mode, a sufficiently large point set has bounded subconfigurations whose disjoint parts have intersecting convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-controlled witness principle is one in which a global convex-geometric fact can always be certified by a number of input objects bounded solely by affine dimension. The relevant certificates may be sparse convex generators, small infeasible subfamilies, or small point configurations admitting intersecting convex-hull partitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{certificate size}\leq w(d),\qquad d=\dim L,\] with \(w\) independent of the total size of the instance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In contrapositive intersection form, if every subfamily of size at most \(w(d)\) is feasible, then the whole finite family is feasible.
A witness bound is dimension-controlled when it is uniform over all instances embedded in affine spaces of dimension at most \(d\).
special_cases_latex: Carathéodory generation uses \(w(d)=d+1\).
Radon partitioning begins at \(d+2\) points.
Finite-family Helly infeasibility uses witnesses of at most \(d+1\) sets.
immediate_consequences_latex: Data lying in a proper affine subspace may use its affine dimension rather than the larger ambient dimension.
The definition separates witness size from the computational method used to find a witness.
boundary_notes: No single numerical constant applies to all three modes; the certificate type is part of the principle.
Infinite-family intersection statements require an additional compactness or recession hypothesis and are not included automatically.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radon property and Radon number
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(L\) be a real affine space and let \(r\geq2\) be an integer. Finite point configurations may be treated as indexed families, so repeated locations remain distinguishable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine convexity. This definition packages the classical two-part Radon phenomenon and its least universal threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine space \(L\) has the Radon property at \(r\) if every indexed family \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\subseteq L\) admits a partition of its index set into two nonempty disjoint parts \(I_+\dot\cup I_-=[r]\) such that \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_+\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_-\}\neq\varnothing\). The Radon number \(r(L)\) is the least such \(r\), when it exists. For \(L\cong\mathbb R^d\), the classical value is \(r(L)=d+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Radon property at a given size says that every point configuration of that size can be divided into two nonempty parts whose convex hulls meet. The Radon number is the smallest size for which this is always possible. A real affine space of dimension d has Radon number d plus two.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A Radon partition exists if and only if there are coefficients \(\gamma_i\), not all zero, with \(\sum_i\gamma_i x_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), whose positive and negative index sets are both nonempty.
The convex hull intersection contains a Radon point admitting convex-combination representations over both parts.
special_cases_latex: In dimension \(0\), two indexed points have the same location and give \(r=2\).
In \(\mathbb R\), every three points have a Radon partition and two distinct points need not.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every configuration with at least \(d+2\) points contains a \((d+2)\)-subconfiguration with a Radon partition.
The threshold is invariant under affine isomorphisms.
boundary_notes: The two parts must be nonempty and disjoint as indexed subfamilies.
Tverberg partitions into more than two parts are a distinct generalization and are not included.

notation.meaning: Radon number of the affine space L
two index classes of a Radon partition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radon Partition of an Affine Circuit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the uniqueness form for a minimally affinely dependent finite point configuration; uniqueness is up to interchanging the two parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be minimally affinely dependent. Then the nonzero solution of \[\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=0\] is unique up to nonzero scaling and has \(\alpha_i\neq0\) for every \(i\). Consequently \[I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\},\qquad I_-=\{i:\alpha_i<0\}\] is, up to swapping its parts, the unique partition of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) whose two convex hulls intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimally affinely dependent point configuration has a unique Radon partition, obtained from the positive and negative coefficients of its affine dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign classes of the unique affine dependence give the unique Radon partition, up to interchanging the two classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radon partition and Radon point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=(x_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite indexed family in a real affine space. For \(J\subseteq I\), write \(X_J=\{x_j:j\in J\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of a particular finite configuration; unlike the Radon-number definition, no universal dimension threshold is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Radon partition of \(X\) is an ordered or unordered pair \((I_+,I_-)\) of nonempty disjoint index sets with \(I_+\cup I_-=I\) and \(\operatorname{conv}X_{I_+}\cap\operatorname{conv}X_{I_-}\neq\varnothing\). Any point \(p\) in this intersection is a Radon point. Equivalently, there are coefficients \(\lambda_i\geq0\) for \(i\in I_+\) and \(\mu_j\geq0\) for \(j\in I_-\), each family summing to one, such that \(p=\sum_{i\in I_+}\lambda_i x_i=\sum_{j\in I_-}\mu_j x_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Radon partition divides an indexed point configuration into two nonempty parts whose convex hulls intersect. A point in that intersection is a Radon point and has one convex-combination representation using each side of the partition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: After subtracting the two convex representations, coefficients \(\gamma_k\) satisfy \(\sum_k\gamma_kx_k=0\), \(\sum_k\gamma_k=0\), with positive support in \(I_+\) and negative support in \(I_-\).
The lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\) admit a nonzero linear dependence having both positive and negative coefficients.
special_cases_latex: If one point lies in the convex hull of all the others, the singleton containing that point and its complement form a Radon partition.
Four vertices of a convex quadrilateral in the plane admit a partition into opposite pairs whose segments meet.
immediate_consequences_latex: Discarding indices with zero coefficients yields a smaller subconfiguration with the same Radon point.
Applying an affine map sends a Radon partition to a Radon partition, though distinct image points may coincide.
boundary_notes: A configuration may have several Radon partitions and several Radon points.
The parts partition indices, not necessarily distinct spatial locations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-dimensional Radon threshold
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite point configuration and put \(k=\dim(\operatorname{aff}X)\). Define the Radon threshold of an affine space as the least cardinality forcing a two-part intersecting-hull partition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real affine spaces. The effective affine dimension, rather than the dimension of an arbitrary containing space, controls the sharp threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-dimensional Radon bound assigns threshold \(k+2\) to configurations contained in a \(k\)-dimensional affine space: every configuration of at least \(k+2\) indexed points contains a subconfiguration admitting a Radon partition. The bound is sharp in the universal sense because \(k+1\) affinely independent points form a simplex and admit no partition into two nonempty parts with intersecting convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radon behavior is controlled by effective affine dimension. At least k plus two points in a k-dimensional affine space force an intersecting convex-hull partition, while the k plus one vertices of a simplex show that no smaller universal threshold is possible.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A family of \(m\geq k+2\) lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}\) is linearly dependent, producing a Radon partition after separating coefficient signs.
The absence of a Radon partition for \(k+1\) points is possible exactly at the sharp threshold, as witnessed by affine independence.
special_cases_latex: For points lying on an affine line, the controlling threshold is \(3\), even if the line is embedded in high-dimensional space.
In the plane, \(4\) points always admit a Radon partition, whereas the vertices of a triangle do not.
immediate_consequences_latex: Replacing ambient dimension \(d\) by \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}X)\) can strictly improve the bound.
Any larger configuration contains a Radon witness supported on at most \(k+2\) indices.
boundary_notes: Sharpness concerns a universal guarantee; particular configurations with fewer points may still have intersecting-hull partitions because of repetitions or affine dependence.
The result is specific to real affine convexity and two-part partitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{aff}A\) have dimension \(r\), and choose an affine isomorphism \(T:L\to\mathbb{R}^r\). For every \(B\subseteq A\), \(T(\operatorname{conv}B)=\operatorname{conv}T(B)\). Hence, for all \(B,C\subseteq A\), \[\operatorname{conv}B\cap\operatorname{conv}C\ne\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{conv}T(B)\cap\operatorname{conv}T(C)\ne\varnothing.\] Applying the ambient Radon theorem to \(T(A)\) therefore yields the effective-dimension form on \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i\), where \(\lambda_i>0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and the active points are affinely dependent. Choose \(\alpha\neq0\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i a_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=0,\] changing its sign if necessary so that some \(\alpha_i>0\). Define \[t=\min_{\alpha_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\alpha_i},\qquad \lambda_i'=\lambda_i-t\alpha_i.\] Delete points whose updated coefficient is zero and repeat while the active points remain affinely dependent. Each update preserves the convex representation and removes at least one active point, so the procedure terminates with affinely independent positive support after at most \(m-1\) updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine dependence permits a maximal coefficient shift that preserves the represented point and total weight while deleting a support point; iteration yields an affinely independent convex representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-dependence elimination route to sparse hull witnesses
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\), where \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional algebraic dependency connecting Radon-type signed affine dependence with Carathéodory-type sparse convex representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Radon–Carathéodory dependency step is an affine-dependence elimination applied when \(m>d+1\): choose \(\gamma\neq0\) with \(\sum_i\gamma_i s_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), and choose \(t\) so that \(\lambda_i-t\gamma_i\geq0\) for all \(i\) with equality for at least one index. Then \(x=\sum_i(\lambda_i-t\gamma_i)s_i\), the new coefficients remain convex weights, and the positive support strictly decreases. Iteration yields a representation of \(x\) using at most \(d+1\) points. The positive and negative supports of \(\gamma\) simultaneously define a Radon partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dependency route starts from an overlong convex representation and uses a signed affine dependence to adjust its weights without changing the represented point or the total weight. The adjustment makes at least one coefficient vanish. Repeating this operation gives a Carathéodory representation with at most d plus one generators, while the two signs of the affine dependence encode a Radon partition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Affine dependence of \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) is linear dependence of the lifted vectors \((s_i,1)\).
A signed affine dependence can be normalized on its positive and negative supports to give equal convex combinations and hence an intersecting-hull partition.
special_cases_latex: If the active points are already affinely independent, no elimination step is available or needed.
If \(S\) lies in a \(k\)-dimensional affine subspace, the terminal support bound improves to \(k+1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex-hull membership assertion in \(\mathbb R^d\) has a witness involving at most \(d+1\) generators.
Radon dependence and Carathéodory sparsification use the same lifted linear-algebraic certificate.
boundary_notes: The step concerns existence of sparse representations, not uniqueness.
For conical rather than convex combinations, the normalization equation and numerical bound change.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Helly property and Helly number
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of subsets of a common space and let \(h\geq1\). Families are finite unless a separate compactness condition is stated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-family Helly property specialized to convex subsets of finite-dimensional real affine spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(\mathcal C\) has the Helly property of order \(h\) if every finite family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal C\) satisfying \(\bigcap\mathcal G\neq\varnothing\) for every subfamily \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) with \(|\mathcal G|\leq h\) also satisfies \(\bigcap\mathcal F\neq\varnothing\). The Helly number \(h(\mathcal C)\) is the least such \(h\). For all convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\), the Helly number is \(d+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class has Helly order h when feasibility of every subfamily of at most h members guarantees feasibility of the whole finite family. The least valid order is its Helly number. The class of convex subsets of d-dimensional Euclidean space has Helly number d plus one.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Contrapositively, every finite family of convex sets in \(\mathbb R^d\) with empty total intersection has an empty-intersection subfamily of at most \(d+1\) members.
When the family has at least \(d+1\) members, it suffices to test subfamilies of exactly \(d+1\), since smaller subfamilies can be extended.
special_cases_latex: For intervals on a line, pairwise intersection implies common intersection, so the Helly number is \(2\).
For convex sets in the plane, triplewise intersection implies total intersection for finite families.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite convex feasibility has an infeasibility witness whose size is controlled only by dimension.
Affine isomorphisms preserve the Helly number.
boundary_notes: Convexity is essential; arbitrary nonconvex families need not have this dimension-controlled property.
For infinite families, the finite Helly condition alone is insufficient without compactness or another global hypothesis.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{C_i\mid i\in I\}\) be an arbitrary collection of nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Assume that the sets have no common direction of recession. If \(\bigcap_{i\in J}C_i\neq\varnothing\) for every \(J\subseteq I\) with \(|J|\leq n+1\), then \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an arbitrary family of nonempty closed convex sets in n-dimensional space with no common recession direction, nonempty intersection of every subfamily of at most n+1 sets implies nonempty intersection of the entire family.
assumptions_latex: C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex for every }i\in I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-family Helly feasibility condition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex sets; they need not be closed or bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-family regime. No compactness, closedness, boundedness, or recession condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((C_i)_{i=1}^m\) satisfies the \((d+1)\)-wise Helly condition if \(\bigcap_{i\in J}C_i\neq\varnothing\) for every \(J\subseteq\{1,ldots,m\}\) with \(|J|\leq d+1\). It is Helly-feasible when this local condition certifies \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i\neq\varnothing\). Every finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\) is Helly-feasible in this sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex family satisfies the local Helly condition when every subfamily of at most d plus one sets intersects. In the finite-family regime that local condition guarantees a common point of all sets, without requiring the sets to be closed or bounded.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(m\geq d+1\), testing all subfamilies of exactly \(d+1\) members is sufficient.
If the total intersection is empty, some subfamily of at most \(d+1\) sets already has empty intersection.
special_cases_latex: When \(m\leq d+1\), the condition includes the whole family and the assertion is immediate.
For \(d=1\), the condition reduces to pairwise intersection of convex subsets of a line.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite infeasible convex system admits a dimension-bounded subfamily certificate.
The conclusion remains valid for mixtures of open and closed convex sets because finiteness, not topological closure, is decisive here.
boundary_notes: The same assertion for an arbitrary infinite family is false without an additional hypothesis.
The empty set may occur as a member, in which case the singleton subfamily already violates the local condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Helly Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families of convex subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p>n\) and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex sets. Then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^p C_i\neq\varnothing\) if and only if every subfamily of \(n+1\) sets has nonempty intersection. Equivalently, \(\bigcap_{i=1}^p C_i=\varnothing\) if and only if some subfamily of \(n+1\) sets has empty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of more than n convex sets in R^n has nonempty intersection exactly when every subfamily of n+1 sets has nonempty intersection. Equivalently, emptiness has a witness consisting of n+1 members.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact Helly family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be a possibly infinite family of compact convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\), with \(|I|\geq d+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-family extension using compactness of every member. A weaker sufficient formulation only requires one compact member together with the finite-intersection property, but the cited canonical regime assumes compact convex members throughout.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family is a compact Helly family if every \((d+1)\)-member subfamily has nonempty intersection. In this regime, finite-dimensional Helly feasibility extends from finite subfamilies to the entire index set: \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Equivalently, the \((d+1)\)-wise condition gives the finite-intersection property, and compactness converts that property into a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact Helly family is a possibly infinite family of compact convex sets for which every d plus one members intersect. The finite Helly theorem makes every finite subfamily intersect, and compactness upgrades this finite-intersection property to a common point of the whole family.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The family of closed subsets \(C_{i_0}\cap C_i\) of any fixed compact member \(C_{i_0}\) has the finite-intersection property.
Every finite subfamily intersects, and the family is anchored in a compact set.
special_cases_latex: For a finite index set, compactness is unnecessary and the definition reduces to the finite-family Helly regime.
The conclusion remains valid when one member is compact and all members are closed and convex, provided the same local intersection condition holds.
immediate_consequences_latex: Infinite compact convex feasibility is determined by subfamilies of size \(d+1\).
Failure of the total intersection forces failure of some finite subfamily and hence of some subfamily of at most \(d+1\) members.
boundary_notes: Compactness cannot simply be omitted: infinite families of closed convex sets may have all small subfamilies intersect but empty total intersection.
The statement is finite-dimensional; infinite-dimensional compact-convex Helly numbers require separate hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral-Exception Replacement of the Helly Recession Hypothesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded hypothesis-replacement result stated relative to Corollary 21.3.2; its other hypotheses and conclusion are inherited rather than reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Subject to all hypotheses of Corollary 21.3.2 other than its recession hypothesis, that hypothesis may be replaced by the existence of a finite set \(I_0\subset I\) such that \(C_i\) is polyhedral for every \(i\in I_0\), and every common recession direction of \(\{C_i\}_{i\in I}\) is a direction in which \(C_i\) is linear for every \(i\in I\setminus I_0\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the referenced Helly theorem, the recession assumption can be weakened by allowing finitely many polyhedral exceptional sets, provided every direction recessionary for all sets is a linearity direction for each remaining set. All other inherited hypotheses are retained, and the referenced Helly conclusion remains valid.

assumptions_latex: The finite system \(Ax\leq b\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Helly support refinement of the ordinary Farkas certificate for finite non-strict linear inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). If \(Ax\leq b\) is infeasible, then there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+\) such that \[A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-1,\qquad |\operatorname{supp}(\lambda)|\leq d+1.\] Conversely, any \(\lambda\geq0\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}\lambda<0\) certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every infeasible finite system in d variables has a Farkas multiplier certificate supported on at most d+1 inequalities; any nonnegative multiplier that cancels the variable coefficients and gives a negative right-hand-side value certifies infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Helly subsystem certificate for linear feasibility
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and write the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^\top\). Associate the closed halfspace \(H_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:a_i^\top x\leq b_i\}\) with inequality \(i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems of weak affine inequalities in a finite-dimensional variable space. The same intersection formulation applies to strict affine inequalities, but this record uses the canonical weak system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Helly infeasibility certificate for \(Ax\leq b\) is an index set \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|J|\leq d+1\) such that \(\bigcap_{j\in J}H_j=\varnothing\). The system has the Helly subsystem property when infeasibility of all \(m\) inequalities is equivalent to existence of such a certificate. Finite affine inequality systems in \(\mathbb R^d\) have this property; equivalently, if every subsystem of at most \(d+1\) inequalities is feasible, then \(Ax\leq b\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Helly certificate for an infeasible linear inequality system is an infeasible subsystem containing at most d plus one inequalities. Every finite weak affine system in d variables has this property, so feasibility of all small subsystems guarantees feasibility of the full system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The halfspaces \(H_i\) have a common point if every subfamily of at most \(d+1\) of them has a common point.
The implication is an instance of finite Helly applied to the convex feasible regions of individual inequalities.
special_cases_latex: In one variable, an infeasible finite affine system has an infeasible subsystem of at most two inequalities.
Equality constraints may be represented by two opposite weak inequalities, although that representation can affect the counted subsystem size.
immediate_consequences_latex: Large finite linear-feasibility failures always possess dimension-bounded combinatorial witnesses.
The bound depends on the dimension of the variable space, not on the total number of inequalities.
boundary_notes: This is a subsystem certificate, not a nonnegative-multiplier certificate such as Farkas' lemma.
If feasibility is restricted to an additional convex set \(C\), that set must be included as another convex member or absorbed into every feasible region.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-dimensional Helly bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(L\) be a real affine space of dimension \(k\), and let \(\mathcal C(L)\) be the class of all convex subsets of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families in an effective affine ambient space. The bound is sharp for the class of all convex subsets and may be smaller for restricted subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Helly dimension bound of \(L\) is the least integer \(h\) such that every finite family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal C(L)\) with empty intersection contains a subfamily of at most \(h\) members with empty intersection. For a \(k\)-dimensional real affine space, this least integer is \(h=k+1\). Consequently, a family contained in a proper affine subspace is governed by that subspace's dimension rather than by a larger ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Helly dimension bound is the smallest maximum size of an empty-intersection witness for finite convex families. In a k-dimensional real affine space the sharp bound is k plus one, so effective affine dimension controls the certificate size.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If every \(k+1\) members of a finite convex family in \(L\) intersect, then the entire family intersects.
The contrapositive witness formulation and the local-to-global intersection formulation define the same number.
special_cases_latex: For \(k=0\), every nonempty convex subset of \(L\) is the single point \(L\), and the Helly number is \(1\).
For \(k=1\), intervals have Helly number \(2\).
For \(k=2\), the sharp bound is \(3\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If all sets lie in an affine subspace of dimension \(k<d\), testing \(k+1\) members suffices instead of \(d+1\).
The witness bound is invariant under affine isomorphism.
boundary_notes: The sharp lower bound can be witnessed by \(k+1\) convex sets arranged so that their total intersection is empty while every proper subfamily intersects.
Special classes, such as axis-parallel boxes, can have Helly numbers below the general convex-set bound.

notation.meaning: class of convex subsets of the affine space L

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Helly number \(h(\mathbb{R}^d)\), defined as the least integer \(n\) for which every finite family of convex sets with empty intersection has an empty-intersection subfamily of size at most \(n\), equals \(d+1\). The upper bound is Helly’s theorem. Sharpness is witnessed by the halfspaces \(H_i=\{x:x_i\ge0\}\) for \(1\le i\le d\) and \(H_{d+1}=\{x:\sum_{i=1}^d x_i\le-1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Helly number of R^d is exactly d+1; every empty intersection has a witness of that size, and smaller universal bounds fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Helly-Number Thresholds

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be an affine subspace of dimension \(r<\infty\), let \(T:L\to\mathbb{R}^r\) be an affine isomorphism, and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(L\). Each \(T(C)\) is convex in \(\mathbb{R}^r\), and for every subfamily \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), \[T\!\left(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C\right)=\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}T(C).\] Thus finite-family intersection witnesses transfer between \(L\) and \(\mathbb{R}^r\), with Helly bound \(r+1\).

children.title: Finite-Witness Dependency Map
children.top_down_role: Navigation among hull, partition, and intersection witnesses.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Witness Dependency Map in Euclidean Dimension
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix an integer \(d\geq 0\). All points and convex sets lie in \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), write \(\operatorname{conv}S\) for its convex hull; for a finite family \(\mathcal F\), write \(\bigcap\mathcal F\) for its intersection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convexity; the map records witness types and their standard logical dependency, not computational reductions or infinite-dimensional analogues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-witness dependency map is the labeled directed graph \(\mathfrak D_d=(V_d,E_d)\) with vertices \(V_d=\{\mathsf A_d,\mathsf H_d,\mathsf P_d,\mathsf I_d\}\). Here \(\mathsf A_d\) is affine dependence among more than \(d+1\) points; \(\mathsf H_d(S,x)\) is a hull witness \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i\), where \(r\leq d+1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\); \(\mathsf P_d(X)\) is a partition witness consisting of disjoint nonempty \(I,J\subseteq X\) with \(\operatorname{conv}I\cap\operatorname{conv}J\neq\varnothing\); and \(\mathsf I_d(\mathcal F)\) is an intersection witness consisting of \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\), \(|\mathcal G|\leq d+1\), and \(\bigcap\mathcal G=\varnothing\). Its dependency edges are \(E_d=\{\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf H_d,\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf P_d,\mathsf P_d\to\mathsf I_d\}\). The first two edges encode coefficient elimination and sign partitioning of affine dependences; the last records the Radon-to-Helly witness route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed Euclidean dimension d, the finite-witness dependency map is a directed graph whose objects are affine-dependence, sparse hull, Radon partition, and small empty-intersection witnesses. A hull witness represents a point using at most d+1 generators. A partition witness divides selected points into two nonempty disjoint parts with intersecting convex hulls. An intersection witness is an empty subfamily of at most d+1 convex sets. The directed dependencies are affine dependence to hull sparsification, affine dependence to partitioning, and partitioning to intersection certification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak D_d=(\{\mathsf A_d,\mathsf H_d,\mathsf P_d,\mathsf I_d\},\{\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf H_d,\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf P_d,\mathsf P_d\to\mathsf I_d\})\), with the witness predicates defined above.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The intersection vertex may equivalently be defined contrapositively: \(\bigcap\mathcal F=\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) with \(|\mathcal G|\leq d+1\) and \(\bigcap\mathcal G=\varnothing\).

A partition witness may be encoded by coefficients \(\gamma_i\), not all zero, satisfying \(\sum_i\gamma_i x_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), with the positive and negative supports forming the two parts.
special_cases_latex: For \(d=1\), hull witnesses use at most two points, Radon witnesses use at most three points, and empty-intersection witnesses use at most two convex sets.
If \(S\) lies in an affine subspace of dimension \(r<d\), the bounds \(d+1\) and \(d+2\) may be replaced by \(r+1\) and \(r+2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The map separates three certificate formats: convex coefficients, signed affine coefficients, and an index subfamily.
The edge \(\mathsf P_d\to\mathsf I_d\) records that the dimension-controlled partition principle supplies the finite obstruction size in Helly-type feasibility.
boundary_notes: The graph is an organizational dependency object; it does not identify the three witness predicates as logically equivalent for the same input data.
No uniform finite bound of this form is asserted for arbitrary infinite-dimensional spaces.
